C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about adaptive prompt retrieval, automatic loss-based supervision, and transferability. The highlighted 10.2% VizWiz and 3.8% MMMU improvement examples are unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix H.1 newly attributes a failure to semantic relevance misleading retrieval when an abstract query requires noticing a reflected visual cue. This adds a concrete failure condition to the otherwise retained interpretations of robustness and generalization.

D1.justification: v4 adds an explicit code-repository link on the first page, absent from v3. Appendix C's hardware, annotation time, and training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Appendix B drops the earlier BLEU/CIDEr metric examples.

E1.justification: The training sources and reported benchmark coverage are retained. The seven-benchmark extended evaluation moves from v3 Table 2 to v4 Appendix E, Table 8. The added failure example remains within the existing visual-question-answering task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain FGVP, RedCircle/Circle, API, and the fixed-prompt, random, regression, MoE, and list-wise retrieval alternatives. Comparator membership is unchanged in Table 1 and the retrieval comparison renumbered from Table 3 to Table 2.

E3.justification: Previously specified experimental settings are retained, including the backbones and Appendix C's 40 epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 1e-3, and eight A100-40G GPUs. Appendix B removes generic BLEU/CIDEr examples without specifying a changed captioning evaluation procedure.

E4.justification: v4 adds a failure-case analysis in Appendix H.1 and Figure 7, examining retrieval that misses a mirror cue in an abstract question. Existing retrieval, pool-size, layer-selection, filtering, teacher-scale, and loss-reliability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.7 and Table 9 retain the paired t-tests and five seeds, 10 through 50. The reported mean improvement, standard deviation, and p-value are unchanged in the statistical appendix, renumbered from F to G.

E6.justification: The new failure case reports AutoV's ranking of 2 > 1 > 3 > 4 and its incorrect selection of VP2. Numerical entries in the matched tables are unchanged. Section 4.2 condenses the earlier per-model improvements into a 3.5% overall summary.

M1.justification: Following Equation (2), v3 defines the fused text features as T_tilde = product_i H_i[-l_t:], whereas v4 uses H_i[-l_t:] directly. This locally revises the ranking computation as specified. The remaining architecture, reward loss, and inference filtering are retained; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation or experimental execution changed.

P1.justification: v4 makes limited prose edits, condenses Section 4.2, expands discussion of the relocated extended evaluation in Appendix E, and adds a failure subsection and acknowledgements. Author information and running headers are updated; most wording and the main section order are retained.

P2.justification: v4 adds failure Figure 7, renumbers the training example as Figure 8, and moves the extended evaluation table into Appendix E. Figure 1's caption clarifies the crown symbols, and table spacing and float placement are adjusted. Existing visualizations and table structures are largely retained.

R1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds citations to SparseVLM, FreeKD+, and ChainV while dropping DINOv2. References to COCO Captions, BLEU, and CIDEr are also removed. The main related-work discussion and positioning of AutoV remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The definition following Equation (2) removes the product over candidate outputs from the fused text-feature expression. This changes a mathematical definition beyond equivalent notation. The other equations, including the reward loss and Appendix A's attention-prompt formula, are unchanged; no proofs or theorems are added.

improvement.justification: The added failure analysis, explicit code pointer, and clearer Figure 1 caption modestly improve transparency and usability while retaining the empirical evidence. Existing reporting problems remain unresolved: for example, Table 9's listed gains average 2.46%, while both versions report 2.06%. The revision therefore provides limited overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoV and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds a qualitative retrieval failure case in Appendix H.1.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, retrieval comparisons, ablations, efficiency measurements, and statistical and teacher-scale analyses.

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on both benchmarks; v2 instead emphasizes consistent pre-training gains across architectures, especially with limited labels. The methodological contribution is redefined around Gaussian rendering and prototype alignment, and the failure of naive pseudo-label supervision becomes a central claim. The Internet-video occupancy novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 introduces geometric-scale and semantic-taxonomy mismatch as conjectured explanations for weak pseudo-label supervision, and interprets the new alignment mechanisms as addressing noisy supervision. Its limitations now include invisible/occluded voxels, extension to temporal or multi-view networks, and dependence on the wall-height assumption. v1 mainly emphasized object-level grouping and identified dynamic/static separation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds class-name prompting instructions, Gaussian parameterization details and the default prototype momentum of 0.999. It promises public code and data, whereas v1 withheld the dataset and promised code upon acceptance; actual release is not established. Conversely, v1's explicit YouTube train/validation counts and Occ-ScanNet scene-disjoint resplitting description are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet and YouTube-Occ for indoor semantic occupancy prediction. The larger Internet-video collection, additional architectures and revised label fractions change experimental settings without establishing a new domain, population or task.

E2.justification: The NYUv2 comparison adds ISO and EmbodiedOcc; the Occ-ScanNet comparison adds EmbodiedOcc++ and RoboOcc. v2 Table 4 additionally evaluates HASSC, GaussRender and Pri3D against the proposed training strategy, substantially broadening v1's architecture and random-initialization comparisons.

E3.justification: YouTube-Occ grows from 14,592 to 100,372 frames, with a new 50K-subset comparison. Pre-training is evaluated on three architectures instead of only Symphonies. The stated pre-training learning rate changes from 8e-4 to 2e-4, and Occ-ScanNet/YouTube-Occ training changes from 30 to 10 epochs. v2 also adds pseudo-label and joint-training controls and revises the evaluated label fractions.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's annotation-efficiency and qualitative analyses, v2 adds pseudo-label quality and naive-supervision diagnostics, a 50K-versus-full-data scaling analysis, and component ablations. Tables 5–6 isolate the two losses and test projection choices, learnable Gaussian parameters, prototype momentum and semantic thresholding.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimates or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges 'No error bars' in its checklist; that acknowledgment disappears, but v2 retains the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main proposed-method NYUv2 result changes from 30.74/51.12 to 31.65/52.15 mIoU/IoU. Occ-ScanNet changes from 58.15/67.75 to 49.38/61.25, while its Symphonies baseline also changes from 57.85/67.50 to 47.71/59.89. Numerous architecture, scaling, strategy and ablation results are added, and the NYUv2 zero-shot result is removed. These are revised results under changed methods/settings, not controlled cross-version performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v1 back-projects pixels into voxels and contrasts pooled superpixel/supervoxel features. v2 replaces this correspondence mechanism with voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering into the image plane and adds an online class-prototype memory bank and cross-scene contrastive loss. These substantially change the pre-training procedure and objective.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. The narrative now develops manual annotation, automated curation and pseudo-label failure before presenting the revised framework; experiments are reorganized around pipeline evaluation, pre-training and ablations. The checklist is removed, and authorship, affiliations and acknowledgments are updated.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different layout and substantially restructures its displays. Figures 1–2 are retained with resizing/relocation, and v1 Figure 4 becomes v2 Figure 5. The NYUv2 qualitative figure and radar plots disappear; new framework and pseudo-label figures appear. Benchmark and few-shot displays are consolidated, with new strategy and ablation tables.

R1.justification: New Section 4.3 explicitly distinguishes the approach from GaussTR, AGO, AutoOcc and other outdoor self-supervised methods through calibration assumptions and architectural coupling. References and discussion also expand to alternative training strategies and the manual occupancy-annotation pipeline, while v1's CrossPoint/MM-Point discussion disappears. This materially revises research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for class prototypes, the prototype contrastive loss and the combined objective in Equations 3–4. The region loss retains the earlier contrastive form. This is a limited extension of the formal objectives; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidentiary weaknesses: multiple-architecture tests support model-agnostic applicability, Table 4 adds relevant competing training strategies, and Tables 5–6 test component contributions absent from v1. It also replaces the unsupported abstract claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance with claims centered on demonstrated pre-training benefits and states more specific limitations. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and omitted split documentation weakens reproducibility, but the new comparisons and diagnostic evidence substantially strengthen the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe YouTube-Occ, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial revision. All pages were inspected, including v1's concluding NeurIPS checklist. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate scientific appendix.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original pseudo-label evaluations, experiments across multiple architectures, data-scaling comparisons and component ablations.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original pre-training, limited-annotation, cross-dataset and zero-shot experimental results for the proposed approach.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that direct motion guidance struggles on distilled generators and that training-free teacher-guided endpoint interpolation with adaptive supervision improves motion quality while preserving speed. The trajectory-restoration framing and expanded supporting experiments retain the central claims and contributions.

C2.justification: v1's limitations paragraph focuses on missing inference-time quality checking. v2 adds substantive limitations concerning underrepresented object-motion combinations, source-target structural mismatch, and fine-grained latent attention, linked to the human-to-monkey climbing failure (Appendix D). It also adds interpretations of runtime/memory tradeoffs and discusses unpaired teachers with unshared latent spaces.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies DDIM inversion steps, extraction timestep and attention blocks, guidance schedules, resolutions/frame counts, and VB LoRA, scheduler, and optimization details. Some earlier baseline-initialization and AnimateDiff threshold details disappear. Reproducibility remains limited by Nmax being described as a per-sample event cap while Algorithm 1 caps inner denoising steps. The project link and promised code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: TurboBench and AnimateBench remain. v2 adds LOVEU-TGVE's broader appearance and motion editing scenarios, comprising 76 videos and 304 edit pairs, and easy/medium/hard prompt conditions on DavisBench (Section 4.1, Appendix B.4). This expands the tested editing conditions; DAVIS source data itself was already represented in v1.

E2.justification: The original TurboBench and AnimateBench comparator sets remain. v2 newly evaluates MOFT and DiTFlow on DiT systems, including direct distilled-model controls, and adds Tune-a-Video and PointMotion to the LOVEU-TGVE comparison (Tables 2, 7–8, 10–11). Tune-a-Video and the work called PointMotion were previously cited but not evaluated as these comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds DiT model configurations and Flow-sim, Appearance Diversity, and Pick Score evaluations. Reported TurboV2 settings also change: activation thresholds move from 380–420 to 480–500, truncation becomes motion-dependent, and noise blending changes from k=0.01 to 0.05 or 0.3. The motion-strength sweep changes from 500–2000 to 0.05–0.2. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 expands guidance-strength sweeps and adds activation/truncation sensitivity tests, motion-type and optical-flow analyses, direct VB-only controls, memory/time analysis, and a climbing-motion failure case (Tables 4–5, 9–10, 12; Figure 8). Conversely, v1's separate inverted-noise component ablation and both noise-blend-factor sweeps are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The 50-participant, 36-pair user study retains the same reporting practice and percentages.

E6.justification: TurboBench scores, AnimateBench scores, and user-study percentages are retained. v2 adds extensive DiT, LOVEU-TGVE, subgroup, sensitivity, and resource results. For example, its new Table 10 reports VB+DiTFlow at MF 0.540 and 34 seconds versus MotionEcho at 0.733 and 54 seconds. These are newly reported comparisons, not v1-to-v2 performance gains. Noise-initialization ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: v2 adds DiT/flow-model adaptations using MOFT, DMT, and DiTFlow objectives, reference key/value injection, and iterative latent optimization (Section 3.5, Appendix A.1). Algorithm 1 also changes teacher re-noising from the student's motion-unguided prediction to its motion-guided prediction. Appendix C still uses the unguided estimate, leaving that particular procedural change internally ambiguous.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method explanation, incorporates Preliminaries within Methods, and reorganizes the appendices around implementation, results, derivation, limitations, and ethics. AnimateDiff discussion moves to the appendix. The narrative restructuring extends beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and diagnostic figures, adds runtime bars and DiT/failure panels, restructures tables with backbone and component columns, merges guidance-strength tables, and relocates the AnimateBench table. It also changes typography and page layout and resizes or relocates many retained qualitative figures.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands from the earlier emphasis on UNet diffusion and motion customization to DiT generators, trajectory distribution distillation, and additional guidance approaches. Newly discussed works include Wan, CogVideoX, Video-Blade, DiTFlow, MOFT, OPAD, and FlexiMMT, broadening the research context beyond citation renumbering.

T1.justification: The endpoint interpolation already appears in v1 Equation 5. v2 corrects the squared-loss gradient step factor from lambda to lambda/2 and adds derivations of its proximal formulation and equivalent noise-prediction correction (Appendix C). These provide a limited formal extension of the existing update.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the framework's broad applicability through DiT adaptations and comparisons, broader editing tests, teacher controls, sensitivity/resource analyses, and explicit failure boundaries. Detailed implementation recipes address much of v1's sparse reproducibility documentation. These gains outweigh the loss of noise-initialization ablations and remaining inconsistencies between endpoint formulas, pseudocode, and teacher-budget descriptions, although those inconsistencies still impede exact reproduction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MotionEcho, with matching authors, core framework, and retained experiments despite the changed title. All 33 pages of v1 and 48 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds DiT-based evaluations, LOVEU-TGVE results, sensitivity tests, motion-type analyses, memory measurements, and a failure case.

before.justification: v1 reports original TurboBench and AnimateBench experiments, component and hyperparameter ablations, qualitative results, and a 50-participant user study.

C1.justification: The central claims of model-agnostic, reward-guided escape from local optima and improved conditional generation remain. v2 makes the efficiency advantage of fewer, deeper searches an explicit experimental contribution and revises the abstract's stated NFE increase from approximately 7.6× to 6.72×.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and limitations concerning high-reward plateaus, fixed-threshold instability, late-stage reward overfitting and diminishing returns. It discusses the Hunyuan-DiT numeracy exception and hypothesizes mechanisms behind spatial-relation results. The supplement explicitly limits conclusions about large-scale inference because of resource constraints, extending v1's more general quality–efficiency discussion.

D1.justification: v1 already documents core hyperparameters and an RTX 3090. v2 adds image resolutions, CPU specifications, a second RTX 4090 setup, Ubuntu and CUDA versions, and PyTorch 2.4.0/Diffusers 0.32.2. It also documents revised configurations and expands baseline descriptions. These refine reproducibility information; no code or data release instructions are added.

E1.justification: Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench are retained. v2 adds systematic compositional evaluation on T2I-CompBench, reporting color, shape, texture, spatial-relation and numeracy results in Tables 2 and 4. This substantially extends the evaluated prompt population and explicit compositional requirements.

E2.justification: The main comparator set remains DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling and SOP; Resample is renamed Resampling. Within the reward-model comparison, v2 Table 3 adds a CLIPScore-guided variant to the HPSv2, AES, PickScore and ImageReward variants evaluated in v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Reported main settings change from λ=15, N=20, unrestricted depth and δ=0.01 to λ=40, N=4, maximum depth 3 and δ=0; SOP candidates change from 5 to 4. v2 adds Hunyuan-DiT evaluation, compositional category scores and approximately compute-matched controls. These changes prevent treating revised scores as same-setting gains. Figure 4's exact threshold sweep is ambiguous because its caption and legend disagree.

E4.justification: v2 adds depth-versus-width analysis in Figure 2, approximately compute-matched Always-explore comparisons in Table 5, exploration-probability sweeps in Table 6 and exploration-window sensitivity in Table 7. It expands reward-model testing and qualitative cases. The existing threshold/depth analysis is retained in revised supplementary Figure 4, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Increased search candidates and additional result rows do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added under revised settings. For example, Ctrl-Z's SD2.1 ImageReward scores change from 0.776 to 1.138 on Pick-a-Pic and from 0.685 to 1.025 on DrawBench. SOP now exceeds Ctrl-Z on SD2.1 PickScore in both benchmarks, reversing v1's ordering. Hunyuan-DiT, CompBench and additional ablation results substantially expand the evidence. HPS rescaling and equivalent rounding are excluded from this judgment.

M1.justification: The core reward-guided inversion sampler remains. Algorithm 1 changes the exploration condition from t ≤ T−λ to t ≥ T−λ, aligning it with the early-exploration prose already present in v1. It also moves the stopping test outside the N-candidate loop. These are localized revisions to the reported procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and consolidates related work, revises method explanations, compresses the main experimental-settings section and moves expanded settings into the supplement. The ablation narrative is reorganized around depth versus width, with threshold analysis moved to supplementary material and new interpretation and limitations sections added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn using layered two-dimensional landscapes. Tables gain model groupings, NFE columns and revised highlighting, alongside new benchmark and ablation tables. The threshold plot is relocated and redrawn, and qualitative displays gain changed examples, colored borders and an additional image grid.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for T2I-CompBench, Hunyuan-DiT and Choi et al.'s Fair Sampling through Switching Mechanism. The overall positioning against fixed-depth exploration and other inference-time techniques remains. Bibliographic formatting changes do not represent additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: The substantive DDIM, clean-image estimation, inversion and reward-threshold mathematics in Equations 1–6 is retained. Noise-schedule and index notation is cleaned up, but no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited to one architecture and two benchmarks: Hunyuan-DiT and compositional evaluations test generality, while depth-versus-width and approximately compute-matched ablations directly examine the claimed exploration advantage. Added implementation details and substantive failure conditions improve assessability. Figure 4's conflicting labels and Algorithm 1's unclear stopping check remain weaknesses, but the broader, more diagnostic validation provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ctrl-Z Sampling work. Text, equations, algorithms, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 has no separate appendix; v2 includes readable supplementary material on PDF pages 11–16.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT, adds T2I-CompBench results, and includes additional quantitative ablations and qualitative examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Stable Diffusion 2.1 experiments on Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench, including baseline comparisons, ablations and generated-image examples.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about adaptive escape from local optima, generation quality, efficiency and compatibility. Changing the abstract from a 6.72-fold increase to 7.72 times the original NFEs clarifies the cost already reported in Table 1 rather than changing the underlying claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for architecture-dependent aesthetic tradeoffs and variable computation, diminished benefits under coarse solver schedules, and differences between full and partial CFG++ integration. It also discusses redundant exploration after reward saturation and explicitly leaves pixel-space applicability unvalidated. The earlier scheduling and scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies that NFEs are averaged per denoising step and documents implementation choices for the new integrations, including schedule-matched inversion and where CFG++ replaces CFG. Existing default hyperparameters, hardware and software versions were already disclosed in v2 and remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same three text-to-image benchmarks and compositional requirements. The additional checkpoint, solver combinations and trajectory examples do not establish new datasets, domains or task coverage.

E2.justification: The original DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling and SOP comparisons remain. New Tables 7–10 evaluate DPM, AYS and CFG++ against their Ctrl-Z combinations, substantially extending the evaluated comparison methods beyond approaches merely cited in v2.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain, but Appendix C.5 adds substantially different protocols: Stable Diffusion 1.5 with a 10-step second-order DPM/AYS schedule and exploration at every step, plus CFG++ comparisons using guidance weight 0.6. Section C.6 adds a 500-prompt diagnostic with exploration window 50, four candidates and maximum depth three.

E4.justification: Existing depth, width, threshold and initiation ablations are retained. New analyses test compatibility with alternative solvers and guidance, compare full versus partial CFG++ integration, measure exploration initiation and termination depths, and inspect intermediate trajectories and redundant late searches in Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new exploration histograms describe search behavior rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: All matched pre-existing table values remain unchanged, including the relocated Hunyuan-DiT results. New Tables 7–10 add substantial results: for example, the new SD1.5/10-step experiment reports Pick-a-Pic ImageReward of -0.145 for AYS and 0.433 for Ctrl-Z + AYS. Figures 5 and 7–11 add exploration distributions and intermediate image/reward outcomes.

M1.justification: The core adaptive reward-guided search remains. Algorithm 1 caps rollback at T-t, changes the exploration-window boundary from >= to >, and tests best_score rather than the last candidate when stopping search. Appendix C.5 also introduces solver integrations and full versus partial CFG++ variants that change which forward updates use CFG++.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted prose revisions, numbers sections and appendices, reorganizes supplementary discussions, and adds an LLM writing-assistance disclosure. The main narrative, contribution list and conclusion remain largely intact; much of the added text documents new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, with resized and relocated displays and colored algorithm lines. v3 merges v2 Tables 2 and 4 into one main-text table and adds four experimental tables and six figures. Existing qualitative image grids are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially broadens related work to distillation, parallel and speculative diffusion sampling, LLM inference scaling and verifier-guided search. Section 2 also adds pruning research. This expands the distinction between Ctrl-Z's quality-oriented inference search and approaches primarily targeting sampling speed.

T1.justification: The existing DDIM, inversion and reward-criterion mathematics are retained with notation and indexing corrections. Appendix C.5.2 presents standard CFG/CFG++ update formulas to explain the integrations; it adds no substantive theoretical derivation, proof or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens previously asserted compatibility through experiments, makes practical limitations clearer through exploration diagnostics, and corrects procedural inconsistencies in Algorithm 1. These improve support and clarity while retaining the original benchmark evidence. The new combination tables omit NFEs and uncertainty estimates, limiting stronger conclusions about efficiency and reliability; the overall gain is useful but limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ctrl-Z Sampling work. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds DPM/AYS and CFG++ combination experiments, exploration-frequency measurements and intermediate sampling case studies.

before.justification: v2 reports original text-to-image experiments on Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench and T2I-CompBench, including quantitative comparisons, ablations and generated examples.

Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now foreground quality–compute trade-offs across multiple budgets instead of the earlier approximately 7.72-NFE headline. The hill-climbing contribution is qualified as an interpretation in surrogate quality space. Adaptive escape and model compatibility remain the central contributions.

C2.justification: V4 explicitly distinguishes sample-quality optima from model likelihood in Sections 1 and 4.1. Section 5.3 qualifies improvement under different reward models from all metrics to most metrics and explains how scorer choice affects realized NFEs through triggering and acceptance. Appendix D's substantive limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Sections 5.1 and B.3 add explicit settings for the named low- and higher-budget Ctrl-Z variants. However, their conflicting maximum-depth specifications for Ctrl-Z† limit reproducibility. Hardware, software versions, image resolutions, and the existing solver-integration details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate text-to-image generation on Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, and T2I-CompBench with the same task coverage. The new library-on-a-flying-whale example adds another compositional prompt without establishing a distinct task or test scenario.

E2.justification: The comparison algorithms remain DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP, with DPM/AYS and CFG++ comparisons retained in the appendix. V3's SOP matches v4's SOP-4; the additional SOP-1 configuration varies the existing method's search budget, assessed under E3.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 add comparisons near three times DDIM's NFE cost using SOP-1 and Ctrl-Z†, alongside the retained higher-budget settings. Ctrl-Z† uses lambda=30 and N=2, but its maximum depth is inconsistently specified as 3 in Section 5.1 and 2 in Appendix B.3. Existing benchmark protocols otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 1 adds a qualitative case examining composition as SOP and Ctrl-Z receive increasing compute. Existing depth/width, reward-model, initiation, exploration-window, solver-combination, and trajectory analyses are retained. Table 6's added zero-window row redisplays previously reported DDIM results.

E5.justification: V4's Figure 3 caption newly states that the depth/width results aggregate the same prompts and seeds; v3's corresponding Figure 2 lacks this disclosure. This does not establish additional runs. Neither version provides run counts, confidence intervals, or error bars for these comparisons.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add low-budget result rows across both backbones. For example, SD2.1 Pick-a-Pic HPSv2 is 26.44 for Ctrl-Z† at 2.77 NFEs and 26.34 for SOP-1 at 3.00 NFEs. Existing higher-budget scores, appendix table values, and intermediate trajectory rewards are retained. Figure 1 adds qualitative outcomes.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same reward-based trigger, random inversion, candidate selection, adaptive inversion depth, and exploration window. The AYS and CFG++ adaptations already appear in v3. The new low-budget variant changes hyperparameter settings, not the algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method rationale, experimental commentary, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting around surrogate quality and compute scaling. Numerous run-in headings become numbered subsections, and the exploration-window discussion is folded into Appendix C.3. These changes substantially reshape the exposition while retaining much appendix content.

P2.justification: V4 changes typography, text area, running headers, and float placement throughout, including expanding the wrapped algorithm to full width. It adds the Figure 1 teaser, expands Tables 1–2, redisplays DDIM in Table 6, and annotates the existing trajectory tree. Most original plots and generated samples are retained.

R1.justification: V4 adds references on Tweedie's formula, diffusion tree sampling, noise trajectory search, and direct noise optimization. Section 2 acknowledges concurrent deep rollback searches and distinguishes Ctrl-Z by selective, adaptive exploration. The changed Ma et al. SOP reference is a publication update of the retained work.

T1.justification: The DDIM, inversion, acceptance, and CFG/CFG++ equations are unchanged, with no added theorem or proof. The surrogate-quality notation in Section 4.1 and Tweedie interpretation explain existing scoring and estimation quantities without introducing a substantive mathematical result.

improvement.justification: The added low-budget comparisons in Tables 1–2 provide useful evidence for the compute–quality trade-off, while the surrogate-quality explanation and qualified reward-model discussion improve conceptual precision. Appendix E tests whether separability gains extend across event categories, and Appendix K examines dependence on the MMAudio backbone. These substantially extend the retained guidance-strength and generation-order analyses.

E5.justification: v4 replaces rating standard deviations with 95% confidence intervals and adds Wilson preference intervals with evenly split ties (Appendix A; Tables 3-4), without increasing the reported responses. However, the preference widths are inconsistent with the stated calculation: 50 responses imply approximately ±11.97 percentage points for audio quality, versus the reported ±7.71.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1-2 and sensitivity scores are retained. v4 adds caption-count and category findings, derived preference summaries, and results for new datasets, comparators, and ControlFoley. For example, Table A7 reports ControlFoley CLAP A-A of 60.67 without NAG and 53.81 with it. The existing random-order DeSync entry changes from 0.42 to 0.43 (v3 Table A3; v4 Table A4).

Incorrect equation cross-references introduced in v4 do not constitute a substantive change to the derivation.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v3's narrow validation on one automatically captioned benchmark and one proposed-method backbone. Human-captioned evaluation, additional datasets, alternative generation comparisons, and ControlFoley tests strengthen evidence for generality and the practical value of sequential generation. Clearer task framing also helps interpretation. Sparse details for some new experiments, incorrect cross-references, and inconsistent preference confidence intervals limit the gains, but do not outweigh the substantially broader empirical support.

C1.justification: v2 adds multi-institutional structured benchmark construction as a central contribution and extends the paper's claims to cross-institution generalization. It redefines the tokenization contribution around foreground-mask guidance and narrows patient-specific attribute extraction to localized lesion measurements. These changes materially extend and reshape v1's three-component, RadGenome-focused contribution statement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and limitations absent from v1: institutional reporting style can separate lexical from clinical scores; airway geometry may cause feature dilution; upstream segmentation misses constrain small-nodule detection; and organ-mask errors affect two visual modules, explaining their larger impact. These extend v1's discussion of component synergy and baseline behavior with explicit failure mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 documents encoder layer selection, physical spacing, multi-window processing, DSPy/Llama-based report preparation, anatomical subregions, and revised lesion-extraction pseudocode. It updates context length from 2,048 to 8,192 and LoRA rank from 16 to 128, and supplies a concrete repository address where v1 only states code availability. Conversely, v1's explicit 48-hour/two-A100 baseline comparison cap is no longer documented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates on RadGenome-Chest CT alone. v2 adds 500 AMC cases sampled from a separate hospital population and evaluates zero-shot cross-institution generalization, substantially expanding evaluation coverage while retaining the six-region chest reporting task.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains RadFM and M3D, removes MedBLIP and CT2Rep, and adds MedM-VL, Med3DVLM, and CT-CHAT (Table 1). The ablation comparison additionally introduces an M3D encoder baseline; the LITA comparator is retained under the LITAenc. label.

E3.justification: Reported training/validation and test counts change from 24,128/1,564 to 23,865/1,551. Inputs change from min-max-normalized 256×256×32 volumes to resampled, cropped, multi-window 448×448×128 inputs, and training increases from three to six epochs per stage. The clinical metric suite changes from CA-F1/GREEN/GPT-4 scoring to GREEN/CRG/GPT-CA. v2 also specifies 30% training subsets for ablations and introduces external zero-shot and 50-case blinded reader protocols.

E4.justification: v2 extends component ablations with encoder comparisons and external generalization tests, and adds analyses of anatomical-region weaknesses, nodule-size sensitivity, and organ-versus-lesion mask corruption (Tables S1, S3, S5). The earlier COVID-19 case is retained with revised outputs in Figure S1, while Figure 3 introduces a different multiregional effusion/consolidation case.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v2 introduces 95% confidence intervals throughout the main comparison and ablation tables, specifies 10,000 bootstrap replicates, and reports reader-score standard deviations. These additions do not establish repeated training runs or increased seed counts.

E6.justification: The reported results are substantially replaced and expanded. For example, the proposed model's internal GREEN score is 0.278 in v1 and 0.4555 in v2, but changed methods and protocols prevent interpreting this as a controlled gain. New results include AMC GREEN 0.1572 and reader score 6.9792±1.4065. Table S3 also reveals small-nodule detection of 0.1270, below every listed baseline.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming R2 pooling, v2 replaces all-slice averaging and representative-slice selection with organ-bearing slice filtering and mask-guided spatial token selection. It replaces RAD-DINO/SAT with MedSigLIP/TotalSegmentator, removes spatial tokens, and produces one volumetrically pooled mask token per region. Attribute extraction changes from organ volumes and lesion counts/diameters to localized, largest-component lesion measurements (Sections 3.1–3.3; supplementary Algorithm 1).

Related work is reorganized into three focused themes, structured reporting moves into a benchmark-construction subsection, component terminology changes, and the supplement is reorganized into dedicated implementation and analysis sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn with separate tokenizer and attribute-extractor panels; baseline and ablation results become separate tables with confidence-interval rows; and supplementary Tables S1–S5 are added. The COVID-19 illustration is revised and relocated to Figure S1, while the main qualitative figure shows a new case.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially refocused: much of v1's general and 2D medical MLLM survey is removed, while MedM-VL, Med3DVLM, MedGemma, TotalSegmentator, CRG, and DSPy are introduced. The extractor is positioned directly as an Osprey-based volumetric adaptation, replacing v1's explicit inheritance of MAIRA-SEG's extractor settings. These exceed citation renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v1's fixed D+T token-count account gives way to mask-dependent token-set definitions. v2 also specifies normalized volumetric pooling, largest-component mask intersection, and voxel-spacing-aware lesion geometry in Equations 2–7. These are bounded mathematical revisions to the procedure; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation through external-hospital evaluation, blinded human assessment, uncertainty reporting, and explicit failure and robustness analyses. The small-nodule and airway findings make applicability limits more assessable, while expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Changed protocols prevent attributing score differences solely to the revised method, and the reader study uses only one assessor while mask perturbations remain underdescribed. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential breadth and transparency.

The underlying claim of flexible, mutually conditioned audio–motion generation remains.

It also states that freezing Audio-DiT prevents learning a proper joint distribution and explicitly qualifies perfect articulation as impossible when fixed motion conflicts with target text. Most earlier limitations and qualitative interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands reproducibility information: mel-spectrogram settings, 24 kHz audio, 25 FPS motion, transformer width and heads, modality-dropout probabilities, and shared CFG scale 2. Reported training time changes from approximately one day for both stages to approximately one day per stage. Some metric-implementation attribution and the explicit promised CC-BY-NC model license disappear. Code/model release remains prospective, and the project-page address is unchanged.

Newly disclosed architecture and guidance settings do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

The existing joint-block, masking, and Audio-DiT finetuning ablations remain unchanged, as do the principal qualitative use cases and failure cases.

New results include Stage-1 HDTF FID 18.372 and FVD 194.27, 19-second generation of a 20-second video on H100-class hardware, transcript-error counts of 45/213 and 72/213, and source-separation WER increasing from 2.43% to 2.63%. Table 1 gains timing and parameter-count columns plus a Stage-1 row; Table 2 is shortened and embedded beside text. M1.justification: V1 uses object-mask matching, object-level registration, label recovery, and PCA orientation estimation. V2 adds background-based camera-motion estimation, motion-based orientation for dynamic objects, ego-motion correction, and Global Object Memory with persistent entries, refinement, and merging. These substantially extend the inference procedure beyond v1's local association and recovery rules.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method narrative, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The introduction replaces the contribution list with a two-challenge narrative, experiments prioritize benchmark detection, and the appendix is reorganized into method details, settings, analyses, failures, and qualitative results. References move after the supplement, and the title and affiliations change.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two columns to one, redraws the architecture illustration, adds a memory flowchart, and substantially rebuilds comparison and ablation tables. It introduces new temporal-consistency, failure, and benchmark visualizations while replacing or regrouping earlier qualitative panels. These are extensive display changes beyond pagination and numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions PLOT against temporal pseudo-labeling and tracking-based 3D perception, particularly MonoSOWA, ViPE, and Vid2CAD, and adds newer open-set and reconstruction literature. The related-work structure changes from emphasizing zero-shot perception foundations to distinguishing object-level temporal reasoning from competing approaches. This goes beyond citation renumbering or publication updates.

T1.justification: The Hungarian matching and Procrustes foundations remain. V2 extends the mathematical description with background-motion estimation, world-coordinate trajectories, and dynamic/static orientation equations. V1's explicit depth-clipping, height-prior scaling, and center-estimation formulas are omitted. These revise the applied geometric formulation; neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens v1's limited quantitative validation through KITTI-360 and Waymo experiments, direct temporal/open-set comparisons, and targeted memory, motion, and noise ablations. These improve the evidence for the proposed mechanisms and applicability. The net gain is tempered by omitted box-construction and metric details, unexplained reassignment of earlier scores to a different IoU threshold, and contradictory dataset descriptions in Appendix A3. Thus, the broader evidence supports improvement, but the documentation regressions limit its overall extent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PLOT research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Changed experimental conditions limit direct performance comparisons, not comparison of the documents.

after.justification: V2 reports original results on KITTI, KITTI-360, and Waymo, alongside component ablations, noise experiments, and qualitative video analyses in the main text and appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original KITTI pseudo-label evaluations, detector-training results, component ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative experiments, including appendix analyses.

C2.justification: v3 elaborates production–social feedback, discusses inconsistent planning and insufficient game knowledge, and adds an inference-efficiency versus capability tradeoff. Section 5 newly limits the social-intelligence interpretation to socially situated embodied decision-making rather than comprehensive open-ended social intelligence.

D1.justification: Table 6 corrects the swapped model identifiers for Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-4.1 mini, aligning them with the models already specified in the experiments. The task configurations, simulator APIs, evaluation pseudocode, prompt, and installation/access information otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Llama 4 Maverick, Qwen2.5 VL 72B, and Gemma 3 27B. Ablation comparators also remain unchanged. AvalonBench is added to the descriptive related-work comparison, not experimentally evaluated.

R1.justification: Section 2, Table 1's positioning against other environments, and all 49 references are identical. No cited work or substantive relationship to prior research changes.

improvement.justification: The revision updates affiliation references and arXiv metadata only. C1.justification: v2 elevates attention-dependent gradient vanishing and its implications for optimization to an explicit main contribution, and adds the claim of superiority over Gershgorin-based softmax bounds. The attention-distribution bound and JaSMin robustness contributions remain, but the paper's central scientific scope now includes weight-gradient dynamics.

C2.justification: v1's brief association of categorical attention with gradient growth is replaced by a weight-specific account of query/key gradient attenuation and distinct value-gradient behavior. v2 also qualifies the connection to attention sinks, explains the accuracy–robustness tradeoff, identifies the causal-masking limitation for k>1, and discusses poor classification under excessive regularization in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 adds A100 hardware for observational experiments, reports approximately 8000 total GPU hours instead of 2000, and documents settings for Imagenette and the visual-encoder study. These do not establish increased training budgets for retained experiments. The precise pretrained ViT-L checkpoint link supplied in v1 is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Imagenette classification and adversarial evaluation, plus attention-bound analysis using OmniGAIA images. CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet coverage remain. The OmniGAIA experiment evaluates images through a visual encoder; it does not establish coverage of the benchmark's full multimodal tasks.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 1 and Table 1 add empirical comparisons against Gershgorin and classical interlacing softmax-norm bounds; v1's corresponding histogram compares its bound only with exact norms. The unregularized and Specformer robustness baselines, and the prior full-attention bounds, remain.

E3.justification: The full-attention comparison changes from fine-tuned ViT-B/CIFAR-100 in v1 Figure 6, with exact measurements on 100 samples, to ViT-L over 5000 ImageNet samples in v2 Figure 4. New protocols include Imagenette with patch size 16 and batch size 128, normalized gradient correlations, and Qwen3-VL-4B visual-encoder analysis on 100 images with 1500 tokens each. Existing CIFAR training and attack settings largely remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-versus-bound correlations in Figure 5 and training-gradient analyses in Appendix H, testing vanishing-gradient risks and excessive regularization. Conversely, it removes the mean-versus-max aggregation comparison and the trained attention-map case study from v1 Figure 5. These substantially change the evidence about regularization mechanisms and failure behavior.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates, v2 Table 2 explicitly reports averages across three seeds with ± values. This reporting is localized to the CIFAR-100 summary; the uncertainty quantity is not defined. Because v1 specifies no seed count, the PDFs do not establish an increase from a particular earlier run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds softmax relative-error results of 0.035 for its bound, 20.19 for interlacing, and 0.85 for Gershgorin. New Imagenette results include AA2 accuracy of 11.95 for JaSMin k=70 versus 6.86 for the baseline, alongside lower clean accuracy. Main CIFAR-100 values become three-seed summaries, such as baseline clean accuracy 91.05 instead of 90.90. Appendix sweeps retain the earlier max-aggregation results while deleting mean-aggregation rows; these are not uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both logarithmic JaSMin penalties and their maximum aggregation remain unchanged. However, v1 Section 4 also proposes mean aggregation as an alternative; v2 Section 7 withdraws that variant, and its corresponding experimental rows disappear. This narrows the proposed method variants without redesigning the core regularizer.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces an explicit contribution list and separate related-work section, presents softmax theory before the attention bound, adds a dedicated gradient section, and reorganizes proofs across appendices. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a narrower single-column format with running headers, redraws bound histograms with comparator legends, revises heatmaps, and adds gradient and visual-encoder figures. Tables are restructured for uncertainty reporting and reduced sweeps; the trained attention-map comparison disappears. Some displays, including the whole-model Jacobian histogram, are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around gradient propagation, entropy collapse, attention sinks, and robust vision architectures. It explicitly acknowledges Nair's concurrent 1/2-Lipschitz result and distinguishes its distribution-dependent singular-value bounds from Gershgorin estimates. This changes the novelty comparison beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 introduces weight-specific Jacobian bounds for query, key, and value matrices in Proposition 2, with proofs in Appendix F, and adds a matrix-calculus derivation in Appendix E. It also establishes comparison with the Gershgorin bound and expands the existing constant-factor comparison proof. The central attention and softmax bounds remain; v2 Proposition 1 already appeared in v1 Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the theoretical explanation and validation of the retained contributions. Proposition 2 and the gradient studies replace v1's largely informal gradient discussion with explicit bounds and empirical checks, while direct Gershgorin comparisons test a closer alternative. Three-seed CIFAR-100 reporting and explicit applicability limits further improve evidential support and qualification. The lost mean-aggregation ablations and undefined ± notation are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attention-distribution bounds and JaSMin regularizer. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Imagenette evaluations, gradient analyses, three-seed CIFAR-100 summaries, and visual-encoder bound measurements on OmniGAIA images.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10/100 training and adversarial evaluations, ImageNet attention analyses, Jacobian measurements, and hyperparameter sweeps.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden applicability from DDPM-focused validation to U-Net and diffusion-transformer architectures, including SiT and 256×256 ImageNet generation. Batch resampling becomes part of the central framework description, and superiority over Dispersive Loss is newly claimed. The explicit claim of being first to adapt conditional-unconditional alignment to diffusion is removed.

C2.justification: v2 explains why resampling supplies more within-tail-class negative pairs and interprets its interaction with CCUA through precision and recall. The dimensional-collapse interpretation from v1 Appendix A.4 is removed, while the central knowledge-sharing explanation remains. The training-cost limitation is extended with a 1.48× SiT overhead alongside the retained 1.6× DDPM overhead.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds explicit U-Net/transformer feature-extraction mappings, four-A6000 SiT hardware, batch size 48, training budgets, and resampling configuration. However, it removes v1's explicit DDPM noise schedule, Adam optimizer, learning rate, and warmup settings, plus CIFAR evaluation sample-count and tail-class details. Reproducibility information is substantially revised in both directions.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five long-tailed datasets: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet, and Places, retaining conditional and unconditional generation. CIFAR experiments move to the appendix. ImageNet's changed resolution and backbone alter experimental settings rather than the represented dataset or conditioning task.

E2.justification: The ImageNet comparison changes from DDPM, CBDM, and OCLT in v1 to SiT and SiT with Dispersive Loss in v2. The CIFAR DDPM-1000-step comparison also adds the evaluated omega-scheduler baseline in Table 7. CBDM, OCLT, and ADA remain in corresponding retained DDPM comparisons.

E3.justification: ImageNet changes from 64×64 DDPM trained for 300k iterations to 256×256 SiT evaluated at 40–160 epochs. Sampling changes from DDIM-100 with tuned guidance to ODE-50 with guidance 7.5, and evaluation samples increase from 20k to 50k. v2 adds spatial FID, precision, recall, and batch-resampling settings, including factor 0.1 for ImageNet and TinyImageNet.

E4.justification: v2 Table 5 adds a controlled comparison of SiT and CCUA with and without resampling, testing whether contrastive regularization offsets resampling's diversity loss. New ImageNet and TinyImageNet qualitative comparisons appear. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.4's latent-covariance spectrum analysis disappears. The original loss-component ablation is retained as v2 Table 4.

E5.justification: The CIFAR100-LT comparison using seeds 0, 42, and 2025, its FID values, and the approximately 0.04 versus 0.01 deviation discussion remain unchanged, moving from v1 Table 7 to v2 Table 10. No additional uncertainty estimates or significance tests accompany the new experiments.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the low-resolution ImageNet results with a new SiT result series; at 160 epochs, Table 1 reports FID 19.95 for SiT and 16.41 for CCUA. TinyImageNet's reported FID/FIDtail change from 17.16/37.88 to 15.24/30.39, while head FID changes from 20.39 to 21.32. These replacements involve changed settings, including resampling. Most CIFAR and Places values are retained, with new scheduler and resampling results added.

M1.justification: The contrastive and timestep-weighted alignment losses and training algorithm remain substantively unchanged under new names. The procedural addition is optional batch resampling, introduced in Section 3.1 and enabled for ImageNet-LT and TinyImageNet-LT. The SiT implementation applies the existing losses to transformer representations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, conclusion, and experimental narrative are substantially revised to foreground transformer experiments. CLDM/InfoNCE/MSE terminology becomes CCUA/UCL/AL. CIFAR and unconditional results and limitations move to the appendix, qualitative sections are reorganized, and Appendix B adds a writing-assistance disclosure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration with SiT examples, adds an architecture diagram and ImageNet/TinyImageNet image grids, and introduces SiT and resampling tables. The original combined benchmark table is split across main text and appendix. CIFAR figures are relocated, nearest-neighbor panels are consolidated, and the latent-spectrum figure and several supplementary panels are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises the closest-work positioning around Dispersive Loss and REPA: it distinguishes unconditional regularization coupled through alignment from conditional regularization, and direct feature regularization from using an external encoder. SiT and Dhariwal–Nichol are newly cited. The BYOL analogy and explicit first-adaptation assertion disappear; the guidance-scheduler work was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds mathematical assertions that collapsed embeddings produce loss log N, that this is the maximum loss, and that optimal embeddings are uniform on a hypersphere. These claims have no accompanying proof. The existing contrastive-loss definition and KL-to-MSE derivation remain unchanged apart from notation.

improvement.justification: The SiT comparisons, separate fidelity/diversity metrics, and resampling controls strengthen evidence for architectural transfer and help distinguish loss effects from resampling. These gains are partly offset by losing a latent-spectrum diagnostic and explicit optimization details. Moreover, v2 does not reconcile its head-class improvement claim with Table 3's TinyImageNet head FID of 21.32 versus DDPM's 21.27. The evidence supports a positive but limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same long-tailed diffusion framework, renamed from CLDM to CCUA. All 20 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A retain original DDPM experiments and report new SiT results, batch-resampling experiments, and generated-image comparisons.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original generation experiments, quantitative benchmark results, loss ablations, seed comparisons, and latent-space analyses.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains improving tail-class diversity and fidelity through unconditional contrastive regularization and conditional–unconditional alignment. v3's introduction additionally claims that implicit conditional diversification is theoretically and empirically better than directly diversifying conditional latents. This strengthens the claimed justification without changing the principal research objective.

C2.justification: v3 introduces a substantive shortcut explanation for conditional contrastive learning and interprets alignment as distilling diversified unconditional representations. Appendix A.4 newly discusses the feature-depth tradeoff between overall FID and recall/sFID. The main ImageNet interpretation shifts from improved recall at similar precision to FID, IS, and tail-FID gains. Appendix A.2 also refines the training-cost limitation through an explicit speed–memory tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 adds batching pseudocode, throughput and memory measurements, explicit latent normalization, and selected loss weights α = γ = 0.05. Most existing training details remain. However, it drops v2's explicit 50-step ODE sampling specification for ImageNet and 100-step DDIM specification for the main TinyImageNet/Places comparisons, creating some reproducibility losses alongside the added detail.

E1.justification: Both versions cover ImageNet-LT, TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, CIFAR10-LT, and CIFAR100-LT, including conditional generation and CIFAR unconditional generation. The added ImageNet imbalance factor of 0.001 changes sample allocation within retained coverage, rather than adding a dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 compares CCUA with SiT and Dispersive Loss. v3 adds CBDM and REPA to that ImageNet-LT comparison and evaluates DiffROP in Table 11. CBDM was previously evaluated only in the U-Net comparisons, while REPA and DiffROP were discussed but not evaluated. This substantially broadens the relevant transformer comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds ImageNet evaluation at imbalance factor 0.001, adds FIDtail to the main transformer comparison, and introduces an approximately equal-training-time comparison of 700k CCUA steps against 900k SiT steps. It also evaluates controlled variations in feature depth, loss weights, and alignment schedules. Training checkpoints are now reported as 250k–900k steps instead of 40–160 epochs; matching retained results do not establish longer training or reruns.

E4.justification: v3 adds extensive ImageNet loss-weight and component ablations, four feature-depth choices, alignment-scheduler comparisons, extreme-imbalance testing, and expanded batch-resampling analyses (Tables 4–6 and 12–14). The isolated TinyImageNet UCL-only and AL-only results from v2 Table 4 disappear, as does the rose/table sample case study in v2 Figure 9. Other qualitative analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A.2 and Table 10 report CIFAR100-LT FID for seeds 0, 42, and 2025, with approximate deviations for DDPM and CCUA. v3 removes this limited seed-robustness analysis without replacement uncertainty reporting. This establishes a reporting loss, not that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1's CCUA results survive unchanged as the N-layer rows of v3 Table 13. The newly emphasized N/4 configuration reports FID 15.08 and recall 17.27 at 900k steps, versus 16.41 and 21.34 for the retained N configuration; this is a configuration tradeoff, not a same-setting improvement. v3 adds substantial baseline, tail-FID, ablation, extreme-imbalance, and efficiency results. M1.justification: The two-loss CCUA framework remains. However, v3 selects features from the N/4-th SiT block for its main results instead of the final block used in v2, retaining the final-block variant in Appendix A.4. Appendix A.1 also extends the stated t/T weighting of UCL from TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT to all datasets. These are limited procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively revised around the interaction of the two losses. v3 adds a dedicated motivation subsection, reorganizes the alignment discussion, expands the framework explanation, and restructures the appendices into implementation, acceleration, quantitative, ablation, and qualitative sections. It also updates the author/affiliation block and removes the LLM-use appendix.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a substantially different page template, typography, text area, and running-header layout. It adds the conceptual contrastive-learning diagram in Figure 2, expands Table 1 with comparators and FIDtail, and introduces several analysis tables. Retained figures are resized or relocated, while v2's rose/table sample panel is removed. These changes exceed simple renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on contrastive predictive coding and resampling by Oord et al., Shi et al., and Zhang et al. It removes v2's explicit statement that UCL generalizes DiffROP and develops positioning around avoiding shortcuts in conditional contrastive learning. The broader relationships to GAN alignment, REPA, and Dispersive Loss remain.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 adds a mutual-information decomposition, I(h;x,c) = I(h;c) + I(h;x|c), and reasoning about class-only shortcuts when regularizing conditional latents. The existing Gaussian KL-to-MSE derivation remains substantially unchanged. The addition is a limited mathematical rationale, without a formal proof of comparative superiority.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens previously limited transformer validation through direct CBDM, REPA, and DiffROP comparisons, tail-specific evaluation, and controlled studies of consequential design choices. The encoder analysis exposes fidelity–diversity tradeoffs, while Appendix A.2 makes computational costs concrete. Removing the three-seed analysis and some sampling details weakens transparency, and the revised main configuration is not uniformly better. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and substantially better characterization of method behavior provide a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CCUA for long-tailed diffusion models. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and included appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original image-generation experiments, baseline comparisons, loss ablations, qualitative analyses, and a three-seed evaluation across the main text and appendices.

It removes v1's separate contribution claim to formally define object bias and softens the 'first systematic framework' novelty language. The core object-stereotyping and implicit-default claims remain.

C2.justification: V3 distinguishes demographic differences from harmful amplification and adds substantial interpretation of mitigation tradeoffs, including Flux's contrasting behavior and the nonsignificant aggregate VAC effect. It extends the prompt-adherence explanation to Imagen, adds limitations concerning discrete demographic categories and intersectionality, and discusses extractor dependence and framework extensibility. These substantially revise v1's shorter discussion of diversity, commercial risks, and limited coverage.

D1.justification: V3 adds generation parameters for the new models, explicitly documents unlabeled discovery inputs, expands the attribute taxonomies, and specifies attention checks and the dominance threshold used to select value shifts. The repository reference remains, but its availability statement now mentions code and prompts without v1's explicit inclusion of generated images; this does not establish that files were actually removed.

It also adds Latinx ethnicity prompts while retaining the existing age and gender groups (Table 1). These additions broaden represented object domains and demographic populations.

Discovery samples increase from 18 to 20 images per model-object combination. Human validation changes from discovery checks across 15 combinations and classification checks on 270 images to 1,040 assignments across six combinations, with revised annotation categories and attention checks. Imagen generation is now reported through Replicate with specified resolution, steps, and guidance, replacing the Google API/default-quality setting (Appendix A).

Qualitative analysis adds Qwen face insertion and Imagen/Flux object-category shifts, while v1's detailed Imagen door and backpack-configuration cases are dropped.

E5.justification: Reported BDS permutation counts increase from 1,000 in v1 to 10,000 in v3 Appendix F. V3 also introduces paired t-tests for mitigation effects and significance tests for cross-VLM Pearson correlations, and explicitly reports that aggregate VAC changes are not statistically significant. These extend statistical assessment beyond the original BDS tests.

E6.justification: BDS, CDS, VAC, validation, and qualitative results are extensively revised or added. For example, v1 Table 4 ranks Imagen highest in average VAC at 0.662; v3 Table 4 ranks Qwen highest at 0.633 and Imagen lowest at 0.343. These summarize different coverage and settings, not same-setting performance changes. New results include a reported 30.9% average CDS reduction under stereotype-discouraging prompts and pooled cross-VLM correlations of 0.855–0.895.

M1.justification: The four-stage SODA pipeline, two-phase attribute discovery and assignment, four fixed plus four discovered attributes, and default GPT-4o extraction remain. Alternative extractors and mitigation prompts are experimental variants; the PDFs do not establish a redesign of the proposed audit procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, results narrative, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and related work is condensed. Numbered sections and lettered appendices reorganize the document, including relocation of generation settings and detailed results. This exceeds wording changes associated solely with added experiments.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document from two-column to single-column layout, redraws example and framework figures, and adds UMAP and unseen-model figures. The main BDS table becomes a model-level summary with rank shading, while full object-level results move to Appendix G and significance counts receive a separate table. Existing concentration examples, taxonomies, and interface displays are expanded or relocated, alongside new mitigation and cross-VLM tables.

R1.justification: V3 adds references on geographic representation, representational harms, directional bias amplification, pluralistic alignment, and newly evaluated models. It sharpens the distinction from T2IAT, TIBET, and OpenBias through controlled baseline comparisons, while retaining the central positioning around demographic-conditioned object bias.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the audit's empirical credibility by directly testing dependence on the extraction VLM and prompt wording, and by examining whether mitigation improves both disparity and diversity. These address important untested dependencies in v1, while broader object and demographic coverage supports applicability. The gains outweigh narrower human-validation coverage and the abstract's overgeneralized homogenization claim, which the main text qualifies as model-dependent with nonsignificant aggregate VAC changes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SODA study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, despite substantial expansion of the experiments.

after.justification: V3 reports an 8,000-image main evaluation across five models and eight object categories, plus original prompt experiments, cross-VLM validation, and a Nano-Banana-2 evaluation in the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original analyses of 2,700 generated images across three models and five object categories, including quantitative bias measurements, qualitative findings, and human validation.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains parameter-free frequency truncation for efficient vision-token compression, with performance retention and generalization across LLaVA, Qwen, and video tasks. The headline accuracy-retention, FLOPs, and speed claims already appear in v1. The new diagnostics principally support the existing low-frequency redundancy rationale.

C2.justification: V3 extends the existing global-structure versus fine-detail interpretation with explanations involving perturbation robustness, semantic-transition stability, and possible suppression of noisy features on RealWorldQA. It removes v1's concrete discussion of compression-induced shape/location errors and hallucinations, although the stated need for additional training remains.

D1.justification: V3 adds a repository link and retains the training hyperparameter table and compressor pseudocode in the main text. It omits v1's detailed DCT/iDCT pseudocode, explicit LAION-CC-SBU identification, training hardware and runtimes, and Qwen training pixel bounds. These are documentation changes, not evidence of altered training.

Its spectrum illustration uses Qwen2-VL alone rather than both encoder families. Existing benchmark budgets, evaluation scripts, and tabulated training settings remain unchanged.

Conversely, v1 Appendix C and Figure 4, which examine caption distortions and hallucinations across compression levels without finetuning, are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new averaged spectrum is an additional descriptive analysis, not a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 Figures 1-3 add substantive findings about image/feature spectrum similarity and greater low-frequency stability under corruption and semantic morphing. V1's unfinetuned caption-error results are removed. The matched image, video, FLOPs, latency, and KV-cache results remain numerically unchanged; no improved benchmark performance is newly demonstrated.

M1.justification: The reshape, two-dimensional DCT, low-frequency cropping, inverse DCT, and flattening procedure is unchanged. V1 Algorithm 3 matches v3 Algorithm 1. Compressor placement and finetuning strategies are retained; renaming Frequency Feature Compressor to Fourier Compressor does not change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, the paper and compressor are renamed, and the architecture primer is replaced by frequency analyses. Training, complexity analysis, and experimental subsections are reorganized, with selected appendix material integrated into the main text.

It rebuilds the spectrum figure, adds perturbation and morphing plots, removes the caption-error figure, and relocates retained tables and diagrams. Several tables reorder columns and abbreviate labels without changing their scores.

Integrating the training table and compressor pseudocode also improves accessibility. The gain is limited: benchmark evidence is unchanged, perturbation strengths remain unspecified, and removing the failure case and some reproducibility details weakens transparency.

The headline grounding-performance claims remain unchanged.

In the data-volume tables, the 30K-synthetic mAP/PQ row changes from 0.773/0.670 to 0.791/0.690, and mixed training changes from 0.807/0.705 to 0.809/0.707; real-data rows remain unchanged. v2 adds annotation, transfer and robustness results.
