The three source datasets underlying EgoExo-Con remain CharadesEgo, EgoExo-4D and LEMMA.

E2.justification: InternVL3.5-8B, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated baseline against its View-GRPO adaptation in v2 Table 3. The existing benchmark comparators and Qwen SFT/GRPO comparisons remain. The external evaluations use already represented methods: TimeChat, TimeSuite and Qwen2.5-VL.

E3.justification: Reported benchmark accounting changes from 491 video pairs and 3,178 queries to 1,148 videos and 2,269 queries; the PDFs do not explain whether this reflects data revision or corrected accounting. Appendix B.3 changes the stated maximum pixel budget from 14 x 16 x 16 to 2.8 million. v2 also adds 2,000-step reasoning-length experiments and external evaluation protocols, and corrects the grounding-consistency inequality from IoU < 0.5 to IoU >= 0.5. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a reward-component ablation distinguishing semantic-only from semantic-plus-structural rewards (Table 4), tests reasoning lengths and optimization stability (Appendix C.3), and extends the existing qualitative example with baseline responses and token-entropy comparisons (Section 5.5). The judge-size, encoder-freezing and subset analyses from v1 remain.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 8 introduces token-level predictive entropy for baseline, View-GRPO and reference reasoning, adding predictive-uncertainty reporting to the qualitative example. Neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run/seed counts; the new entropy plots do not establish uncertainty in aggregate performance estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds InternVL3.5, external-benchmark, reward-ablation and reasoning-length results. Its full Qwen 7B method reports V-ExoEgo/G-ExoEgo of 45.1/18.7, versus 44.7/18.3 in v1; the latter values are retained as the semantic-only ablation in v2 Table 4. Table 5 newly reports Video-MME scores of 69.7 for View-GRPO versus 61.1 for Qwen2.5-VL. Tables 1–2 and the original appendix tables retain their numbers. Method and reported setting changes prevent treating revised headline scores as controlled, same-setting gains.

M1.justification: In v1, the reasoning reward measures similarity to reference reasoning using an LLM judge. v2 Section 5.2 adds explicit coupling between generated reasoning from paired viewpoints: spaCy extracts action and object sets, whose Jaccard overlaps form a structural reward. This is combined with reference similarity using lambda, changing the training objective.

P1.justification: Most existing sections and much of their wording are retained. v2 makes localized rewrites, updates author affiliations and citation style, adds a qualitative-analysis subsection, and inserts Discussion and Ethics review appendices. Existing visualization material is renumbered and moved without a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 substantially changes typography, headers, text-block dimensions and figure placement. It adds an evaluation-setup diagram, redraws dataset statistics and the method diagram, expands the qualitative figure with baseline and entropy panels, adds reasoning-length plots and two tables, and extends Table 3. Several appendix figures and tables are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds comparison with EgoExo-Learn and cites Dou et al. on deriving egocentric-style data from exocentric videos. It sharpens positioning against EgoExoBench by additionally emphasizing the absence of a concrete improvement method there. The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain similar.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for counterpart-view reasoning, the action/object structural reward and its weighted combination with semantic similarity (Equations 5–7). The GRPO background and format/accuracy reward mathematics remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: The reward ablation, external-benchmark tests and reasoning-length analysis provide useful validation and concrete failure analysis absent in v1. Correcting the consistency inequality also improves clarity. These benefits are moderated by unexplained benchmark-count and pixel-budget revisions alongside unchanged comparison tables, which limit reproducibility and direct interpretation of version-to-version performance differences.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EgoExo-Con and View-GRPO. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering. Revised benchmark counts and settings require caution when interpreting performance differences.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds reward ablations, another backbone, external benchmark evaluations, reasoning-length experiments and token-entropy analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model and human evaluations, supervised fine-tuning and View-GRPO experiments, judge comparisons, and appendix analyses of encoder training and dataset subsets.

C1.justification: v2 elevates circular synchronization into a central technical contribution and claims structurally enforced seamless generation without fine-tuning. Its abstract also explicitly broadens the generality claim to geometry, lighting, and semantics. The unified framework, PanoX dataset, and graphics-ready scene contributions remain.

C2.justification: v1 tentatively attributes seams to positional-encoding topology. v2 develops an operator-level explanation based on missing circular translation equivariance and argues that latent blending distorts features while synchronization preserves fidelity. It also interprets the new pretraining and completion comparisons. The speed, geometry, and metallic-generalization limitations are unchanged and merely relocated.

D1.justification: Reported training/evaluation hardware changes from four Ascend 910B NPUs to four NVIDIA L40S GPUs, and v2 specifies batch size per GPU. It adds an explicit project-page address but drops the Blender 4.2 version and graphics deployment detail. Core optimizer, learning rate, resolution, and adapter-count disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Generation training changes from HDR360-UHD to a mixture of Pano360, Structured3D, Poly-Haven, Humus, and PanoX, notably adding synthetic scene data to that task. v2 also introduces generation evaluation on Laval Indoor and SUN360. The existing perception targets, completion task, and graphics applications remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds generation comparisons with OmniDreamer, PanoDiffusion, Diffusion360, and CubeDiff, plus completion comparison with Flux.1-Fill. Figure 10 additionally compares seam handling against unmodified Flux.1-dev, circular blending, and latent rotation. The original intrinsic and geometry comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New generation and completion protocols compute FID, KID, and CLIP-FID on perspective crops and FAED on ERP panoramas; generation also evaluates text alignment using CLIP Score. Generation caption extraction changes from BLIP-2 to Florence-2. Existing PanoX splits and perception metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 5 adds a from-scratch versus pretrained initialization control. Figure 10 adds qualitative seam comparisons and tests attention masking and padding size. These examine previously untested dependencies on pretrained weights and circular synchronization. Earlier camera-ray and joint material/geometry ablations survive as Tables S2-S4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, uncertainty intervals, run-level variability, or formal significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds generation scores, Structured3D albedo scores, completion scores, and ablation results. Table 2 reports OmniX/CubeDiff FID of 7.4/9.5 on Laval Indoor but 39.4/25.5 on SUN360, showing mixed rankings. Table S1 reports completion FID of 16.14 versus Flux-Fill's 30.09. Matched original PanoX scores remain unchanged apart from rounding.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces v1's horizontal blending approach with training-free circular synchronization: circular convolution padding and RoPE attention with padded key/value tokens and attention masking across the DiT and VAE. This changes spatial processing during inference. The Separate-Adapter architecture and flow-matching losses are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, and experimental organization are extensively revised. Task formulations move into Appendix A, experimental settings are organized by task, the camera-ray analysis moves into the appendix, and limitations move into the conclusion. The appendices are reordered and expanded beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different typographic layout and extensively redesigns the teaser, pipeline, qualitative comparisons, and application figures. It adds circular-operator, seam-analysis, generation-comparison, and completion-comparison displays. Tables gain benchmark columns and controls, and the geometry table groups depth-only and geometry methods.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against latent seam manipulation and overlapping-view approaches, adding discussion and citations involving Diffusion360, PanoDiffusion, CubeDiff, RoPE, and circular-padding work. This supports a new novelty argument about intrinsic boundary consistency. Meanwhile, the broad inverse-rendering background citation list is substantially shortened.

T1.justification: The flow-matching formulation and Equations (1)-(5) are retained. Circular translation equivariance is introduced as architectural rationale, without a new mathematical definition, formal proposition, derivation, or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 supports generation and completion primarily through qualitative examples. v2 supplies quantitative baseline comparisons for both capabilities, adds Structured3D validation, and directly tests the benefit of pretraining. These additions resolve a substantial gap in evidence for the advertised unified framework. The seamlessness guarantee still lacks formal proof and generation rankings are mixed, but the stronger empirical validation represents a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniX and PanoX. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative generation and completion comparisons, Structured3D albedo results, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original perception benchmarks, adapter and camera-ray ablations, joint-modeling experiments, and qualitative generation, completion, and simulation results.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on concept-space fitting and semantic initialization. v3 makes sampling approximation the explanation for the robustness–cost trade-off and presents single-sample adversarial optimization as a central contribution with claimed theoretical and empirical support. The abstract also replaces the explicit at-least-26% erasure improvement and 90% time reduction claims with broader robustness, utility, and efficiency claims.

C2.justification: v3 develops a sampling-based explanation of computational cost and explicitly interprets zero ASR with collapsed image generation as meaningless robustness. It adds limitations concerning weaker semantic guidance with more optimization samples and vulnerability to CCE attacks. These substantive qualifications were absent from v1, although difficulty with complex concepts and the surrogate-mapping interpretation were already discussed there.

D1.justification: v3 adds explicit DDIM, CLIP-B/32, sampling, and diagnostic-model settings, while moving previously documented prompt counts and detectors into the main text. The code URL remains unchanged. However, v1 supplies prompt templates, per-concept hyperparameters, and detailed attack settings in Appendix B, whereas v3 defers essential details to absent appendices. The complete extent of retained, revised, or unavailable reproducibility information cannot be determined.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates nine concepts, including Tench, and reports transfer to SD v1.5, DreamShaper, and Protogen. v3 explicitly lists eight main evaluation concepts and omits Tench from Table 4, yet mentions analysis of all nine concepts in unavailable Appendix D and transfer experiments in unavailable Appendix G. Complete coverage cannot be distinguished reliably from relocation or removal.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged within the shared concept blocks of Tables 2–4. v3 adds a controlled comparison of Full, Few, and Single optimization strategies against Single+SG in Table 1. Few and Single represent AdvUnlearn-style and RACE-style sampling, so they should not be mistaken for entirely new erasure baselines.

E3.justification: v3 adds a diagnostic protocol using partially erased ESD models, 100 adversarial embeddings per strategy, and image-level CLIP/AD measurements with Full optimization as reference. This differs substantially from v1's 200-prompt reference spaces, text-feature centroid distances, and PCA analysis. The main adversarial learning rate changes from 0.005 to 0.001, while the total 200 erasure steps remain. These are reported protocol changes, not evidence that unchanged benchmark results were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds a controlled noise/timestep-sampling analysis and a one-iteration study of adversarial and anchor representations before and after erasure (Table 1 and Figures 2–3). Its main ablation table narrows from Nudity, Van Gogh, and Church to Nudity and omits the initialization ablation. The retained P=8/16 settings correspond to v1's 32/64 total adversarial embeddings, rather than new sample-count experiments. Supplementary analyses cannot be fully matched.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its empirical results. v3's noise/timestep draw counts describe optimization design, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantive diagnostic results: Table 1 reports average CLIP scores of 23.79 for Single and 24.73 for Single+SG, among other newly reported measurements. Figure 4 adds per-image CLIP scores to examples already shown in v1. All shared numerical entries in Tables 2–4, and the retained Nudity ablation results, are unchanged. The new diagnostic numbers do not establish a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The alternating text-encoder erasure framework remains, but important procedures change. v1 initializes adversarial inputs from concatenated LLM-generated related prompts; v3 specifies random prefixes. v1's squared-distance semantic losses become cosine-similarity objectives in v3, and adversarial semantic guidance changes from comparing the current and original encoders to using the frozen original encoder for both representations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, the pilot narrative is reorganized into method analysis, and explicit contributions and separate domain-specific experiment subsections are introduced. These are substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a different page layout and substantially redesigns the displays. Figure 1 switches from UnlearnDiff ASR with FID coloring to average ASR versus time; new Figures 2–3 visualize the surrogate/anchor analysis. v1 Figure 3 becomes v3 Figure 4 with reordered columns and CLIP annotations. Tables 1 and 5 are substantially restructured, beyond numerical or numbering edits.

R1.justification: Related work expands into separate discussions of safety approaches, concept erasure, and adversarial erasure. v3 adds substantive positioning against retraining and filtering, grounds its analysis in diffusion-based zero-shot classification, and discusses adversarial preservation and CCE. This changes the research framing beyond citation renumbering or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v3 introduces an expected adversarial objective and Monte Carlo estimator in Section 3.2 and claims theoretical evidence connecting sampling to optimization quality. However, the derivation from diffusion models' zero-shot classification property is assigned to missing Appendix A. The supplied material establishes additional mathematical discussion but does not support a reliable assessment of the full theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v3 offers a more focused sampling analysis, clearer organization, and useful explicit limitations. However, its objectives and training specifications change while the shared benchmark scores remain identical, without clarifying their relationship. Missing Appendices A–H also prevent checking promised derivations, attack details, and supplementary evidence. These unresolved issues prevent a reliable judgment that the explanatory and presentation gains improve overall scientific quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe S-GRACE and contain readable text, equations, figures, and tables. v1 includes Appendices A–C. v3 repeatedly references Appendices A–H, but the supplied PDF ends with references and contains none of them, limiting comparison of theory, supplementary experiments, and implementation details.

after.justification: v3 reports original sampling-strategy experiments, concept-erasure benchmarks, ablations, and before-and-after image analyses. Retained benchmark results also qualify.

before.justification: v1 reports original concept-erasure benchmarks, pilot experiments, component ablations, and transfer experiments, including results in its appendices.

token_usage.accounting_note: Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning output. These subsets are not added again. Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The core claims about coordinate-free intrinsic-attention grounding, anchor aggregation and data-efficient fine-tuning remain. v3 adds an explicit claim of scalability through additional desktop-domain training data and extends its headline performance claims to five benchmarks.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism interpretation: visual-sink tokens are described as functional cross-modal proxies that need not be semantically informative, and anchor-weight similarity supports that explanation. Section 4.5 interprets layer/head contributions and pruning outcomes. The results discussion adds data-scaling interpretations and explicitly qualifies UI-Vision results as in-domain, while the soft-variant tradeoff discussion disappears.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents FlashAttention combined with eager extraction of selected attention rows, a 28×28 patch setting, measured GPU-hours and inference times, and the sources of UI-Vision/MMBench comparator scores. The existing hardware, batch size, learning rate, anchor-token formatting and project access link are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds desktop-focused GroundCUA training data while retaining the original training mixture for GUI-AIMA-lite. Evaluation expands beyond ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2 and OSWorld-G to UI-Vision's basic, functional and spatial desktop tasks, MMBench-GUI-L2's basic and advanced grounding, and supplementary ScreenSpot-v1 evaluation.

E2.justification: Retained benchmark comparisons gain Qwen3-VL, GroundNext, GTA1, InfiGUI-G1 and GUI-Actor-with-verifier variants. InfiGUI-R1 additionally enters the ScreenSpot-v2 comparison, although it already appeared elsewhere in v1. Standalone GPT-4o is removed from ScreenSpot-Pro, and the new benchmark tables include additional comparators such as Holo2 and Aguvis.

E3.justification: v3 introduces the 509k-instruction training regime and larger-data ablation, verifier, timing and top/bottom-30% head-pruning protocols. The stated second-pass crop changes from 448 to 616 pixels, retaining 2× zoom. Exact counts are inconsistent: 250k versus 200k additional GroundCUA instructions, and 259k versus 254k larger-ablation examples. The unexplained OSWorld-G-Refine table label does not establish a changed test split.

E4.justification: v3 adds controls testing gradient flow through head weights, weighted labels for GUI-Actor, verifier compatibility and head importance through pruning. It also adds runtime analysis and token-frequency evidence, and replaces v1's embedding-versus-attention correlation examples with anchor-versus-query head-weight similarity analysis. Most original 45k ablations and zoom-error counts remain; the soft-weighting ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments continue to report point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: ScreenSpot-Pro base/zoom scores change from 45.2/58.6 in v1 to 49.8/57.0 for v3-lite and 53.8/61.5 for the expanded model. These are updated results under revised settings, not controlled before-and-after gains. v3 adds UI-Vision 60.0, MMBench-GUI-L2 79.1, and extensive pruning, verifier and timing results. Existing comparator entries also change, including GUI-Actor-3B's ScreenSpot-v2 average from 90.4 to 91.0.

M1.justification: The anchor token, visual-sink selection, head aggregation, patch-label loss and two-step grounding procedure remain. v3 removes the alternative soft KL-based head-weighting variant from v1 Section 3.4 and evaluates an optional GUI-Actor verifier composition in Appendix B. The new efficient-attention discussion documents implementation without establishing that the main algorithm changed.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. v1's five method subsections become three reorganized subsections, combining preliminaries with anchor aggregation and grouping labeling with training/inference design. Experimental organization, the abstract, conclusion and appendix structure are also revised substantially.

P2.justification: Benchmark tables are expanded and regrouped, with denser layouts and inline citations. v3 adds Tables 3 and 7–10, token-frequency and head-weight figures, and a new similarity visualization replacing v1 Figure 5. The zoom-analysis table replaces accuracy with net-improvement counts and relabels Relax@2 as Relax@3. Pipeline graphics, convergence curves and qualitative grounding examples are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: The central positioning against TAG and GUI-Actor remains largely unchanged. Citations expand to support newer comparators, datasets and implementation, including Qwen3-VL, GroundCUA/GroundNext, FlashAttention, UI-Vision and MMBench-GUI. Samaran et al. replaces the Nguyen et al. attention-supervision citation, and the GUI-ARP reference is removed.

T1.justification: The principal aggregation, similarity, patch-label and loss equations are mathematically retained despite reorganization. v3 removes the alternative distribution-matching definition in v1 Equation 11 and adds a complexity argument reducing attention extraction from O((|V|+|Q|+1)^2) to O((|Q|+1)|V|). No theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design and efficiency claims. Larger-data controls give GUI-Actor the same weighted labels, addressing a comparison confound, while stopped-gradient tests, head pruning and measured training/inference costs address questions left largely unresolved by v1's small-data ablations and convergence plots. Broader comparisons and clearer exposition add value. C1.justification: V1 claims training without any 3D motion annotations and entirely from 2D data. V2 narrows this to no direct 3D pose supervision while explicitly using 3D trajectories and mocap-derived projections. Contributions shift from a specifically named lifting architecture to a broader supervision-granularity framework, materially revising the central claim's scope.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly qualifies that its findings do not mean 3D data are unnecessary and interprets the new global/relative and relaxation comparisons as evidence for structural representations. The encoder-sharing explanation is removed. The underlying interpretation that relaxed supervision discourages coordinate memorization and supports diversity remains.

D1.justification: V1 specifies RVQ depth, codebook sizes, convolutional depth, Adam, batch size, learning rates, training stages, and MoMask inference steps. V2 replaces much of this with baseline references. It newly documents projected-mocap supervision and the diffusion prior treatment, but substantially reduces self-contained implementation information; referenced fusion details are not present in the supplied PDF.

E1.justification: HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and the microgravity and underwater examples remain. V2 adds a trajectory-free relative-motion evaluation setting on HumanML3D in Table 3, extending task conditions without adding a dataset or domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds a directly relevant comparison against 2D-based generation approaches: MAS under global motion and Motion-2-to-3 under global and relative motion in Table 3. MoMask also participates in the relative-motion comparison. The fully supervised comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are retained, but the new comparison substantially broadens the evidence beyond that category.

E3.justification: QM changes from sqrt(MModality/FID) in v1 Equation 16 to MModality/sqrt(FID) in v2 Equation 12, changing its weighting of diversity. V2 also introduces global/relative evaluation and full-versus-relaxed input/supervision controls, evaluated after feature fusion and fine-tuning in Table 4. These are metric and evaluation-design changes, not evidence that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Table 4 adds a central ablation separating relaxed inputs from relaxed supervision through Full/Relax, Relax/Full, and Relax/Relax configurations. Conversely, v1's encoder-sharing ablation and its discussion disappear. The regularization, VAE-versus-AE, and limb-vector representation studies remain as v2 Tables 5–7.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals in Tables 1–2 and point estimates for ablations. Neither specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, or formal significance tests. Changed interval values accompany revised results rather than a changed uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Reported 3D-finetuned HumanML3D FID changes from 0.038 to 0.034 and MultiModality from 2.090 to 2.529; KIT-ML FID changes from 0.153 to 0.135. HumanML3D MDM-based results also change, while retained MoMask-based raw scores match. V2 adds Tables 3–4 results, removes the no-sharing row, and omits MMDist from Tables 1–2. Increased QM values use a different definition and are not same-metric gains.

M1.justification: The trajectory/limb factorization and projection, cross-view reconstruction, orientation, and feature-consistency losses match across versions. MDM-based and 3D-finetuned variants already appear in v1. V2's generic generator formulation and explicit 3D-trajectory description clarify and reframe the procedure without establishing an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming Free3D to LaxMotion, v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, method narrative, contributions, and conclusion around relaxed supervision. It removes the standalone MoMask preliminary section and reorganizes the method into representation reformulation, relaxed observability, and regularization.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column format. Figure 2 is redesigned from a full generation pipeline into a regularization diagram; Figure 3 rearranges the examples and shows additional frames. Two tables are added, main comparison tables lose MMDist columns, and retained ablation tables gain QM columns.

R1.justification: V2 adds MAS, MVLift, and Motion-2-to-3 and substantially revises the weakly supervised discussion around existing motion-generation approaches. Novelty is repositioned around supervision granularity versus coordinate objectives and 3D fine-tuning. The CLIP reference disappears with the MoMask preliminary section.

T1.justification: The QM formula is substantively redefined from sqrt(MModality/FID) to MModality/sqrt(FID), a non-equivalent mathematical definition. The principal motion-factorization and regularization equations otherwise retain their substance; neither version contains theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 improves credibility by aligning its central claim with the use of 3D trajectories and adding relevant 2D-based comparisons and supervision controls. These gains are offset by reduced implementation detail and a new numerical inconsistency: Section 4.2 still gives fine-tuned HumanML3D FID as 0.038, whereas Table 1 reports 0.034. The net improvement is limited rather than substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same work, renamed from Free3D to LaxMotion, with matching authors, core equations, datasets, and retained results. Both end with references and contain no appendices or embedded supplementary files; supplementary material mentioned in the text is not included.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark and qualitative results and adds global/relative-motion comparisons and experiments varying input and supervision granularity.

before.justification: V1 reports original HumanML3D and KIT-ML evaluations, component ablations, reconstruction experiments, and qualitative motion-generation results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about MEMR-Seg, the 177K-dialogue dataset, MediRound, and JCM's mitigation of error propagation. The added evidence does not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds substantial applicability limits: single-entity segmentation per turn, sensitivity to long queries, near-complete loss of general conversational capabilities, and inability to process 3D data or videos. It also attributes the reported weaknesses to sequence-length limitations and task-specific overfitting. These qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B supply previously missing training losses and JCM quality-target construction, substantially expanding implementation documentation. Appendix D, Table B, and Figure D add reference phrasing, modality names, scenario-level split statistics, and data examples. Appendix E.2 adds a future-release statement for the dataset and model; the existing project URL is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MR-MedSeg with the same five interaction scenarios, 168 categories, and nine modalities, plus SA-Med2D-20M evaluation. The appendix describes existing modalities and provides additional examples without establishing expanded task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–3 is unchanged, including the human-guided and MLLM-assisted systems, SegLLM variants, and MediRound+READ. Table 4 specifies SAM as SAM (ViT-H), without establishing a newly introduced comparator.

E3.justification: Table A adds a controlled comparison using neither visual reference input, cropped images alone, and crops plus bounding boxes. Existing evaluation metrics, budgets, and splits remain unchanged; Table B's scenario counts sum to the split totals already reported in v1.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a focused ablation of reference-mask information. Appendix D adds category-frequency analysis, and Figure C adds interactive case studies. The existing backbone and JCM-threshold ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or performance uncertainty estimates. The new dataset-frequency displays provide descriptive counts rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 swaps regular/hard-case entries for Qwen3-VL+IMIS-Net and Gemini-2.5-Pro+MediSee, and selected Dice/gIoU entries for SegLLM. Table 3 changes MedPLIB Dice/gIoU from 39.1/40.6 to 40.6/39.1. Table 4 revises the SAM row from 44.9/27.6/31.9 to 46.7/33.1/37.2, now labeled ViT-H. The appendix adds ablation scores, dataset findings, examples, and qualitative failure observations; MediRound's headline scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture, conversation-history inputs, crop and bounding-box references, teacher forcing, and JCM inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendices A–B disclose training objectives and supervision details; they do not establish a revised method.

P1.justification: The main prose and Sections 1–6 retain their wording and order. V2 appends an overview and organized explanatory Sections A–F, including expanded descriptions of existing interaction scenarios, rather than extensively rewriting the original narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands visual documentation with a JCM training diagram, category-distribution displays, interactive prediction examples, and dataset samples in Figures A–D. Tables A–B add the reference-input ablation and detailed dataset composition. Existing main-text figures and table structures are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, research positioning, and all 51 bibliography entries are unchanged. The appendix introduces no additional cited works.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B newly specify the mathematical definitions of JCM's IoU-based soft supervision target and composite loss, together with MediRound's text-and-mask training objective. These are limited additions to the formal specification; the original inference equations remain unchanged and no proofs or theoretical guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: V1 refers readers to training and dataset details in an appendix that the supplied PDF lacks. V2 supplies central JCM supervision and training objectives, supporting analyses, and important capability limitations, substantially improving technical transparency and critical assessment. Table A's claim of best performance with both reference inputs overlooks crop-only's higher cIoU, 56.0 versus 55.8, but this limited overstatement does not outweigh the documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MediRound work, and their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. Corresponding main sections match reliably; v2 includes Appendices A–F, which are absent from the supplied v1.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by reference-input ablation results, dataset analyses, and additional qualitative examples in the appendix.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 and Figures 6–7 report original segmentation experiments, comparisons, and ablations on MR-MedSeg and SA-Med2D-20M.

C1.justification: The central task, 177K-dialogue dataset, MediRound/JCM contributions, and segmentation-performance claims remain. v5 elevates educational benefits to central abstract and introduction claims, emphasizing progressive learning by non-experts. v2 already briefly mentioned learning medical knowledge, but primarily motivated broader clinical interaction.

C2.justification: v5 removes all four explicit limitations from v2 Appendix F: one object per turn, sensitivity to long queries, near-loss of general conversational ability after specialization, and inability to process 3D images or videos. It also adds a semantic-drift rationale for JCM and interprets student ratings as evidence of educational value. These substantially change the stated applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v5 discloses Dice/BCE loss weights of 0.5/2.0, baseline fine-tuning versus zero-shot status, human prompting procedures, and historical-mask access. It recharacterizes 118K images and 569K masks as an initial candidate pool. Conversely, detailed scenario counts, modality names, reference-phrasing guidance, and the explicit release promise from v2's appendix disappear; the project link and core implementation details remain.

E1.justification: MR-MedSeg and SA-Med2D-20M segmentation coverage is retained. v5 adds a human evaluation of educational utility involving medical students, introducing a new evaluation task and participant population. The educational reframing does not establish a change to the image datasets.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods, including human-assisted segmenters, MLLM–segmenter combinations, SegLLM-7B/13B, and MediRound+READ. Single-round comparators and backbone ablations also match. Newly cited MTurn-Seg and MedVL-SAM2 are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: v5 introduces a human-study protocol with 15 medical students rating four criteria on a five-point scale. Existing segmentation splits, metrics, and stated training budgets remain unchanged. Added explanations of baseline training and historical-mask access document existing comparisons without establishing that their protocols changed.

E4.justification: v5 omits v2's category-frequency analysis and additional interactive cases in Appendices D–E, including Figures B–C. The threshold and backbone ablations remain, and the reference-input ablation moves unchanged from Appendix C/Table A to Section 5.4/Table 5. The main qualitative comparison is also retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new student-rating chart provides aggregate scores without uncertainty; its participant count is an evaluation-design detail.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes SegLLM test metric assignments: for example, SegLLM-7B regular-case Dice/gIoU/cIoU changes from 42.4/42.1/32.9 to 42.1/32.9/42.4. MediRound scores and retained ablation results are unchanged. Figure 9 adds practicality/helpfulness/convenience/potential scores of 3.80/3.93/4.33/4.07. Appendix dataset statistics and additional qualitative results are omitted.

M1.justification: The specified JCM supervision changes: v2 Appendix A computes the quality target from the corrected mask, whereas v5 Section 4.4 and Figure 6 use an uncorrected mask decoded separately from the original feature. The core architecture remains unchanged. Algorithm 1's arbitrary prior-round reference clarifies behavior already described in v2.

P1.justification: The opening narrative is substantially rewritten around medical education. The method becomes four numbered subsections, training material from Appendices A–B enters Section 4.4, and Appendix C's ablation enters the main experiments. Other appendix sections disappear, ablation and qualitative sections exchange order, and a human-evaluation section is added.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column format, substantially resizing and relocating displays. Figure 1 adopts learner imagery, the JCM training diagram is revised and moved into the main text, Table A becomes Table 5, appendix Table B and Figures B–D disappear, and Figure 9 adds the student-rating chart.

R1.justification: v5 adds MTurn-Seg as concurrent multi-turn medical segmentation work, cites MedVL-SAM2, and adds the GPT-5 system card. It also uses existing READ and MediSee references to motivate intervention at the SEG embedding. The broader relationship to LISA, SegLLM, and medical segmentation research remains.

T1.justification: v5 Equation (4) explicitly distinguishes the uncorrected mask from the corrected prediction, and Section 4.4 revises the mathematical definition of the quality target accordingly. Other forward and loss formulations are retained or relocated. Neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v5 improves the consistency of JCM's documented quality supervision, clarifies evaluation and loss settings, and adds evidence about perceived educational utility. However, it removes detailed dataset analyses and concrete limitations, including conversational degradation that matters to its stronger educational framing. The small rating study does not resolve those concerns, so the substantive benefits and losses do not support a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MediRound work, and their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2's Appendices A–F can be matched to material retained, revised, or omitted in v5, which has no separate appendix.

after.justification: v5 retains original segmentation experiments and ablations and adds an evaluation by 15 medical students in Section 5.6 and Figure 9.

before.justification: v2 reports original segmentation experiments, backbone and reference-input ablations, threshold sensitivity results, and dataset analyses in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The main contributions remain recurrent global memory combined with local attention, strong performance from simple LSTM blocks, improved continuity through overlapping frame-wise generation, and efficient attention through hidden-state prefetching. Rewritten framing and additional evidence do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 Section 7 newly acknowledges computational overhead and finite hidden-state capacity as limitations for very long contexts. Section 5.1 shifts from emphasizing SSIM for memory and PSNR/LPIPS for frame quality to treating all three as memory/consistency measures on the tailored tasks. Interpretations of the new analyses are added, while the main local/global-memory explanation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds training/inference pseudocode, explicit Maze initialization information and a project-page link. However, it omits v1's hyperparameter table, detailed memory-batching and tensor-shape instructions, and VAE checkpoints and input/latent dimensions from Appendix A.1/A.3/A.4. This substantially changes reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the underlying settings or actual code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use Memory Maze navigation and Minecraft action-conditioned video generation, with the same described evaluation scenarios. VBench metrics are applied to these retained datasets; they do not establish additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 2–3 add Teacher Forcing and VRAG to both benchmark comparisons, substantially broadening the external comparator set beyond Diffusion Forcing. The existing recurrent variants remain. Identifying TTT-c as an implementation of LaCT does not introduce another evaluated method.

E3.justification: V2 adds five VBench evaluation dimensions covering background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, aesthetic quality and imaging quality. Section 6.2 also introduces a controlled stride-10 experiment with a 20-frame window during training and inference. Existing dataset splits and stated training budgets remain unchanged; the explicit Maze training-from-scratch statement is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: V2 adds the partial-overlap ablation and a component-level FLOPs analysis, but removes v1's action-conditioning ablation, PSNR-versus-frame curve and clean/noisy-memory training-loss plot. The memory-noise endpoint comparison remains. These changes substantially revise the supporting analyses and evidence for individual design choices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. The added result tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds TF/VRAG results, VBench scores, stride-10 results and numerical FLOPs estimates, while removing action-ablation and curve results. Maze LSTM-f changes from PSNR 15.30 and LPIPS 0.50 in v1 Table 1 to 15.50 and 0.45 in v2 Table 2, with SSIM unchanged at 0.41. V2 Table 7 still reports the old clean-memory values without explaining the difference; other retained main benchmark rows are unchanged.

M1.justification: RAD retains its spatial/temporal attention, recurrent memory alternatives, overlapping frame-wise inference, clean-memory updates and hidden-state prefetching. The new Algorithms 1–2 document existing procedures. The stride-10 experiment tests a configuration rather than replacing the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and memory-related-work paragraph are rewritten, with local clarifications elsewhere. Mamba/TTT explanations move from the supplement into the preliminaries. Most methodological and experimental prose and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, redraws Figure 1, rearranges attention diagrams, and adds algorithm boxes, a prefetching diagram and new tables. Existing benchmark tables are regrouped and the complexity table moves into the main text. The Maze visualization, action-ablation table, PSNR curve and training-loss plot disappear; several captions expand.

R1.justification: VBench is newly cited, and v2 explicitly positions TTT-c as an implementation of the already cited LaCT work. The broader related-work coverage and positioning against context, hidden-state and weight-memory approaches remain substantially the same.

T1.justification: V2 Table 6 adds analytical FLOPs expressions for the two-stage pipeline and its components. The RNN equations and asymptotic complexity comparison from v1 Appendix A.2 and Table 6 are retained in v2 Section 3.1 and Table 1; their relocation is not new theory.

improvement.justification: V2 improves comparison breadth through TF/VRAG and VBench, adds a useful overlap ablation, clarifies procedures and states concrete limitations. These gains coexist with substantial loss of reproducibility details and action-conditioning evidence. The unexplained discrepancy between Maze LSTM-f results in Tables 2/8 and the clean-memory results in Table 7 also weakens internal consistency. The supplied PDFs therefore show material benefits and harms without a reliably clear net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAD work, and their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. V1's supplementary pages were inspected. V2 ends after its references; relocated supplementary content can be distinguished from material absent from the supplied PDF.

after.justification: Sections 5–6 retain original experiments and add baseline comparisons, VBench evaluations and a partial-overlap ablation.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 report original Memory Maze and Minecraft experiments, computational measurements, and action-conditioning and memory-noise ablations.

C1.justification: v2 narrows 'first neural representation' to 'first flow-matching based representation,' replaces the zero-shot framing with composition requiring no further optimization and shared landmarks, and frames competitive accuracy around landmark-based matching. The central contribution of composing flows for correspondence across representations is retained.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the interpretation of embedding failures through smoothness and frequency, explains landmark priors, and explicitly identifies partial matching and non-bijective nearest-neighbor retrieval as limitations. The supplement adds explanations of inversion deviations and anchor instability. v1 mainly discusses map smoothness and unreliable point-cloud geodesics.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the six-layer, 256-dimensional MLP, Fourier encoding, training budget, hardware, memory/time requirements, baseline implementations, spectral settings, metric normalization and ground-truth landmark transfer. These details are absent from v1. v2 also supplies a code link, although its supplement retains future-release wording; actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The datasets, representation types and downstream tasks are retained, including cross-representation matching already described in v1. v2 adds evaluation with perturbed landmark locations (Figure 4), extending coverage to noisy landmark inputs.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Diff3F and ULRSSM comparisons, including Diff3F with functional maps in Table 4. It also includes FUSE_DDIM in the main benchmark comparison, beyond the dedicated diffusion comparison retained from v1. KNN-IN-GAUSS becomes FUSE_ANCHOR; that renaming is not an added baseline.

E3.justification: v1's 45-pair embedding comparison is replaced by FAUST/SMAL comparisons with different descriptor dimensions and Euclidean-error/feature-energy reporting. v2 introduces controlled landmark, smoothing, anchor and solver settings. Its supplement also specifies SHREC20 evaluation on remaining common points after selecting six input landmarks, refining v1's stated common-landmark evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds landmark perturbation/count studies, controlled embedding-smoothness experiments, smoothing of pretrained features, alternative-anchor tests and solver accuracy/runtime analyses (Figure 4; supplement Figures 14–15 and Tables 9–11). These substantially expand the questions tested beyond v1's embedding and FM-versus-DDIM comparisons.

E5.justification: v2 adds per-pair metric distributions with medians, interquartile ranges and outliers across four benchmarks (Figure 13), supplementing v1's averages. This reports variability across shape pairs; neither PDF establishes repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces embedding results and adds extensive baseline, cross-representation, robustness and computational results. SHREC20 FUSE Euclidean error changes from 0.0846 to 0.0975; the revised evaluation description prevents interpreting this as an established same-setting regression. Newly evaluated ULRSSM leads FAUST/SMAL accuracy in Table 4. Existing SDF and volumetric table values are retained.

M1.justification: The conditional-flow objective, independent per-shape flows, shared-anchor composition and nearest-neighbor retrieval remain unchanged. v2 adds a tested spectral-smoothing preprocessing variant for WKS and pretrained embeddings (supplement Equation 11; Tables 2 and 9), constituting a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The flow rationale, embedding-selection discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Dataset descriptions are redistributed between the main text and a structured supplement, terminology is standardized, and the narrative is reorganized around prior assumptions, robustness and limitations. These changes extend beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from two-column to single-column layout, redraws the overview and application diagrams, expands the embedding and benchmark tables, and adds robustness curves, distribution plots and supplementary comparison tables. Several existing figures and tables are retained with relocation or relabeling.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted discussion of template-based methods such as 3D-CODED, FARM and NICP, revises the optimal-transport discussion, and adds references supporting smoothing, implementation and partial-matching directions. It narrows the novelty positioning while retaining the central relationship to flow matching, Geometry Distributions and functional maps.

T1.justification: v2 adds a theorem-based argument about coincident flows for identical embedding distributions and independence from training couplings (Section 4.2). Supplement Section 1.2 adds mathematical reasoning contrasting finite-time FM anchoring with asymptotic DDIM anchoring. The core objective and composition equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing implementation information and limited examination of failure conditions. Stronger comparisons, controlled robustness/smoothness studies and explicit limitations make the work more reproducible and its claims easier to assess. Some bijectivity and exact-anchoring statements remain inconsistent with the added qualifications, but these residual issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FUSE research work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes an additional 11-page supplement. All supplied material was included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, robustness experiments, smoothness analyses, runtime measurements and anchor/solver evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original shape-matching experiments, embedding and diffusion comparisons, SDF and volumetric evaluations, and qualitative application results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add RT-DM and reward-informed initial distillation as central contributions, replacing v1's reward-free dynamic cold-start contribution. Joint DMD/RL benefits and teacher-surpassing performance remain headline claims. v1's explicit emphasis on image-free training is dropped.

C2.justification: v4 introduces explanations for RT-DM saturation, loss-weight-dependent reward hacking, and CFG/RL acting as distribution 'density sharpeners.' It interprets DMD regularization as manifold projection and presents reduced diversity as potentially desirable. The earlier reward-model-bias/scaling limitation and proposed connection between reduced diversity and weaker DPO/GRPO gains are omitted.

D1.justification: v4 specifies 1.5K training steps per stage, a default RL weight of 0.5, hardware/batch details for timing, and SiT initialization and DINOv2 reward information. It removes v1's explicit baseline CFG settings and 512×512 ablation default. These are documentation changes; omitted settings do not establish changed execution. The code URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The original t2i-2M, ShareGPT-4o-Image, GenEval and DPG_Bench coverage remains. v4 extends evaluation beyond text-to-image generation to class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 generation using SiT (Section 4, Table 6), introducing a distinct dataset and conditioning task.

E2.justification: v4's system comparison adds reproduced multi-step ReFL baselines for SDXL and SD3, plus DMD2-PSO for SDXL. Its new Table 1 compares joint training against multi-step RL and RL followed by distillation. Conversely, v1's RL-only DPO/GRPO controls are absent from v4; sequential ReFL remains tested in Figure 4.

E3.justification: Dynamic-strategy evaluation changes from CLIP/HP scores at 1K and 2K iterations to DPG measurements at earlier checkpoints. New protocols include training/test reward and DPG trajectories, a 1024×1024 timing comparison with local batch size 16 on H100, and one-step ImageNet evaluation across CFG/RL configurations using FID, recall, precision and Inception Score. These are distinct experimental designs, not matched-setting performance comparisons.

E4.justification: v4 adds RT-DM versus continued RT-DM versus joint-training analysis, reward-model ablations, an RL-loss-weight sweep, and a CFG/RL diversity study. Reward-hacking analysis now includes held-out reward and DPG trajectories. v1's fixed '-Dynamic' control, RL-algorithm qualitative grid and ShareGPT LPIPS diversity comparison are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version documents repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for its performance results. v1's raw/smoothed reward fluctuations describe within-training variability, not uncertainty across repeated experiments; v4 introduces no corresponding statistical uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Reported DMDR results change across the main tables: SD3-M DPG rises from 84.96 to 85.30 and GenEval from 0.64 to 0.65, under the revised method/training description. Numerous strategy, sensitivity and ImageNet results are added. Rankings also become more nuanced: v4's added SDXL ReFL baseline exceeds four-step DMDR in HP score, 33.1874 versus 32.9832. The earlier LPIPS results are removed.

M1.justification: v1 uses dynamic DMD for a reward-free cold start before joint DMD/RL training. v4 introduces Reward-Tilted Distribution Matching (RT-DM): rewards from complete few-step trajectories become fixed weights on DMD gradients during the initial stage (Section 2.4). This changes early optimization; DynaDG, DynaRS and the subsequent joint stage are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around an explicit two-stage framework, with diagnostic experiments embedded in the method discussion. Related work moves near the end and absorbs Appendix A; appendix visual comparisons move into the main results. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. The pipeline diagram is redrawn, diagnostic plots and a multipart ablation table are introduced, and system-table columns are restructured. v1's appendix comparison grids are consolidated into v4 Figure 8, while several original showcase and ablation displays are removed.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning through works such as Flash-DMD, TwinFlow and PSO and a new reward-model discussion. v1's Appendix A is largely relocated into Section 5. The novelty framing also changes: v1 acknowledges Diff-Instruct++ integrating RL during distillation, whereas v4 groups it with work focused on RL after distillation.

T1.justification: v4 adds a mathematical definition of the reward-tilted teacher target and an asserted reward-weighted KL-gradient expression (Equation 4). The original DMD gradient remains. This is a localized formal extension; no theorem or proof establishes the new target/gradient equivalence.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens the empirical argument with held-out reward/DPG trajectories, loss-weight and reward-model controls, and comparisons against RL-improved baselines. These make the central synergy claim easier to assess. Gains are tempered by removing in-domain LPIPS evidence and some controls, losing setting details, and introducing an unexplained reward-tilted target/gradient equivalence. The net improvement is supported but qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DMDR and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. All pages were inspected, including v1's appendices. Much of that appendix material is incorporated into v4's main text, allowing relocation to be distinguished from removal.

after.justification: v4 reports original text-to-image results, training-strategy and component experiments, and an additional class-conditional ImageNet study.

Appendix D replaces the older single-slide heatmaps and pathway-count displays with two BRCA cases linking prototype heatmaps, representative patches, and hallmark pathways. Most component ablations and parameter sweeps were already present in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean±standard deviation with five-fold evaluation and Kaplan–Meier confidence regions with log-rank tests. v2 introduces no new seed counts, repeated-run procedures, confidence-interval methods, or significance-testing practices.

Retained numerical results—including TTA's 0.693 main average, 0.677 ResNet50 average, and log-rank p-values—are unchanged. Appendix D supplies new case-specific qualitative findings.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity through a more defensible joint-objective framing, corrected mathematical details, a relevant additional comparator, targeted sensitivity checks, and more informative tissue–pathway visualizations. C2.justification: v2 strengthens the earlier hypotheses into explanations involving garment leakage, competing reconstruction gradients, and train-test discrepancy. It interprets the retained guidance experiment as diagnosing these conflicts and adds a resolution-dependent interpretation of the loss ablation. Limitations shift from garment-body correspondence and pose conditioning toward validation only on UNet/CFG models, possible DiT and flow-matching adaptations, and broader inpainting applications.

It removes v1's explicit 80GB memory-fit guidance, per-GPU batch explanation, and pixel-versus-latent implementation discussion. The actual latent concatenation, principal hyperparameters, hardware, software versions, and efficiency-measurement instructions remain documented.

It introduces a randomized blind A/B preference protocol with an Equal option, 25 participants, 30 samples, and 1,500 responses across two comparisons. The progressive ablation also replaces v1's reproduced CatVTON control with an explicitly identified, source-reported full-fine-tuning control; this does not establish that the earlier experiment was rerun.

The progressive ablation's baseline comparison is revised. Existing guidance-scale sensitivity and DressCode category analyses remain, with the guidance plot moved into the main text.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A.5 adds binomial and chi-squared significance testing for the user study, reporting p<0.001 for both comparisons. This statistical addition is confined to the new study. The existing 30-run latency averaging remains unchanged, and neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals or training-seed variability.

E6.justification: The proposed model's original benchmark and efficiency scores remain unchanged. v2 adds high-resolution results, including paired FID 4.741 on VITON-HD and 2.216 on DressCode, new comparator scores, and leave-one-out results. Figure 7 reports preferences of 62.0% versus 18.5% against CatVTON and 53.6% versus 25.9% against Leffa, with remaining responses ties. CatVTON's Table 1 paired FID/KID/LPIPS changes from 5.888/0.513/0.061 to 5.425/0.411/0.057. These additions and revisions do not represent same-setting improvements between versions of the proposed model.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column layout. v2 removes the structural-comparison schematic and logo close-up panel, revises the architecture diagram, merges the main qualitative comparisons and efficiency tables, and moves the guidance plot into the main text. It adds a user-study chart and comparison/ablation tables, while appendix image grids gain RefTON columns.

R1.justification: Positioning expands from the single-versus-dual UNet efficiency gap to conditioning conflicts across architectures. Voost motivates the full-fine-tuning argument, while RefTON provides a distinct sequence-conditioning comparison. Added discussion connects the work to multimodal transformers, ControlNet, BrushNet, RePaint, and SDEdit, including explicit acknowledgment of prior known-signal anchoring approaches.

Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs; the revised conflict-based reasoning is conceptual interpretation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens validation through higher-resolution and transformer comparisons, direct human-preference evidence, and a leave-one-out control beyond v1's progressive ablation. These make practical quality and component contributions easier to assess. The gain is tempered by stronger causal and architecture-independent claims: the recipe is not tested on a DiT backbone, and Table 10 shows small low-resolution loss benefits with worse paired KID. Overall, the evidence improves more clearly than the support for the broader mechanistic claims.

C1.justification: The principal contribution shifts from a competence-driven, co-evolving reward curriculum to a Goodhart-based diagnosis of shortcut optimization and lost within-group discrimination, addressed by TaRoS. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion foreground robust reward signaling and saturated-component suppression. Broad claims of improved visual, motion, and semantic quality remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the mechanism interpretation around shortcut directions, noisy advantages, saturation, and training collapse. It argues that evaluator scaling alone is insufficient and adds a rationale for prioritizing visual fidelity. Section 5.5 explicitly acknowledges that the method mitigates rather than completely eliminates reward hacking, qualifying the stronger prevention language in its abstract.

D1.justification: Available reproducibility documentation contracts substantially. v1 Appendix A and Fig. 14 provide batch and accumulation settings, optimizer and SDE details, threshold calibration, and exact reward prompts; v2 refers these matters to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. v2 newly discloses reward normalization to [0,10] and a smoothing window of 50. It reworks the stage ablations into two- and three-component comparisons. Additional order and sensitivity-curve analyses referenced by v2 cannot be inspected.

The Wan-14B/Qwen-72B and Hunyuan benchmark values are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of LVR and Monet. Table 1 adds these methods and the already-discussed Mirage, and replaces the 3D-awareness criterion with broader perception enhancement. A visualization-of-thought reference is also added. The overall positioning among tool-assisted, textual, and latent reasoning approaches remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2, Equation 7 corrects T_i^sam = proj(T_i^sam) to T_i^sam = proj(T_i^seg), repairing the formal mapping from predicted segmentation tokens to SAM prompts. The remaining equations and derivations are retained, with no new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens comparison with relevant latent-reasoning methods, adds grounding diagnostics, supplies a code pointer, and resolves inconsistencies between the main text and appendix. These are useful incremental gains while the original method, results, and limitations remain. The new diagnostics lack sampling details, and Table 1's Mirage citation differs from Section 2's, leaving some weaknesses in the additions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoVT research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete supplementary material support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds checkpoint-based baseline comparisons, representation-similarity results, and an attention case study.

C1.justification: V2 broadens the abstract and introduction from state-of-the-art performance on VDC with one backbone to two benchmarks, cross-backbone generalization and human-validated preference quality. It also foregrounds faithfulness beyond caption length. Autonomous data generation, curriculum DPO and efficient internalization were already core contributions in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning scorer validity, length and position bias, grounding beyond VDCscore, premature exposure to difficult pairs, and directed reflection versus extra sampling. Some conclusions exceed the evidence: position-bias robustness is asserted despite GPT preference rates changing from 84.4% to 95.2% across input orders.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 32 sampled frames, 128 tokens per frame, beam size 1, temperature 0.1 and maximum caption length 1024, and supplies a project-page pointer. These are disclosures, not established changes to existing experiments. Most training settings remain unchanged; promised appendix prompts and pseudocode are unavailable.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from VDC alone to include DREAM-1K, comprising 1,000 annotated clips with diverse complexities. This adds substantial independent video coverage. Cockatiel-4K training videos, the five caption dimensions and VDC-Agent-19K remain unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3-VL-8B and InternVL2.5-8B comparisons. DREAM-1K additionally includes Tarsier-7B and LLaVA-Video-7B. New controls include Best-of-N and anti-curriculum DPO. LLaVA-OneVision's existing VDC baseline is relocated, while vanilla DPO is renamed Random DPO.

E3.justification: V2 adds DREAM-1K event-level precision, recall and F1 evaluation; applies the framework to two additional backbones; and evaluates 500 randomly sampled preference pairs using three blind human raters and GPT-5.1 in both input orders. It also introduces inference-budget comparisons. Dataset-construction totals now refer to eight A800 GPUs rather than one.

E4.justification: New analyses examine preference validity, caption-length bias, evaluator position bias, reversed curriculum ordering and reflection versus Best-of-N under comparable time budgets. Principle robustness adds Shutterstock-derived P4, and principle/iteration studies extend to DREAM-1K. The original greenhouse qualitative example is retained, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. V2's separate human judgments and averaging across GPT input orders describe its evaluation protocol, without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including 37.4 F1 on DREAM-1K and human preference rates of 67.6–75.8%, while retaining Qwen's VDC 49.08/2.50. Existing values also change: OwlCap's camera result becomes 46.90/2.50 from 41.30/2.20; Baseline+P2 becomes 45.43/2.30 from 45.83/2.32, and Baseline+P2+R becomes 46.15/2.34 from 46.55/2.36.

M1.justification: The generation, scoring, reflection, preference construction and curriculum DPO pipeline is retained. Equation (3) newly includes video x in both refinement calls, but the PDFs do not establish whether this changes the procedure or clarifies previously implicit inputs. The referenced pseudocode is absent.

P1.justification: The abstract, substantial introduction passages and results narrative are rewritten; the agent-related-work discussion, qualitative discussion and conclusion are condensed. Author and affiliation information changes, and acknowledgements are added. These are extensive prose revisions despite retaining the main section sequence.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Figure 1 is rearranged, Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, and a caption-length histogram is added. Tables gain backbone blocks, controls and DREAM-1K columns, alongside new comparison tables. The qualitative figure is relocated and reduced; several dense displays become noticeably smaller.

R1.justification: The cited literature expands substantially, including Constitutional AI, Self-Refine, PromptAgent, self-rewarding models, curriculum learning and new benchmark/model references. Several earlier captioning citations disappear. Sections 2–3 gain broader connections to self-feedback and adaptation research, while retaining the central positioning against dependence on external teachers.

T1.justification: Equation (3) adds video x to the refinement/reflection arguments, but it is unclear whether this revises the mathematical definition or makes implicit conditioning explicit. The remaining definitions, DPO loss and curriculum objective are substantively unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited validation: another benchmark and two additional backbones test generalization, human judgments assess the self-generated preferences, and new controls probe curriculum ordering and extra-compute explanations. These address important evidential gaps. Missing appendix details, smaller displays and overstrong bias conclusions remain weaknesses, but the broader and more targeted validation provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VDC-Agent work, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. Neither contains appendix pages. V2 repeatedly refers to an absent appendix for prompts, pseudocode, generation analyses and overhead details, limiting comparison of those materials.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds DREAM-1K results, additional backbones, human preference evaluation and further controlled comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original VDC benchmark results, component and training ablations, principle and iteration sensitivity experiments, and a qualitative comparison.

C1.justification: The introduction moderates its dismissal of earlier VAU benchmarks: v1 says none provides practical or scalable evaluation, whereas v4 describes limited coverage that does not comprehensively capture VAU complexity. The central claims about a synthetic, balanced benchmark, automated generation and annotation-free VAU construction remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V4 substantially revises the VAD interpretation, emphasizing biological motion and Fed-WSVAD's semantic/federated mechanisms. It adds arguments about generator-independent representations, attributes poor UCF transfer to resolution and viewpoint differences, and interprets mixed training as evidence of complementary synthetic representations. Appendix A adds an annotation-quality interpretation. The general synthetic-to-real limitation was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: V4 specifies VideoScore filtering of the bottom 5%, discloses manual VAD ground-truth labeling, names Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B for aggregation/refinement, and adds feature-extraction references and a dataset/code access URL. These improve documentation without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. Hardware, generation time and existing prompt examples are largely retained.

E1.justification: V4 adds evaluation domains generated with Cosmos-2.5 and Hailuo-2.3, extending coverage beyond the original generator and retained real-video benchmarks. It also evaluates UCF-based Holmes-VAU annotations. Pistachio's original scene and anomaly coverage remains unchanged; the ten newly enumerated anomaly types were already represented in v1.

E2.justification: Fed-WSVAD joins the VAD baselines, and Holmes-VAU becomes an annotation-pipeline comparator. UCF-Crime-to-Pistachio and reverse comparisons now report CLIP-TSA and Fed-WSVAD; v1's corresponding VadCLIP and PEL4VAD entries disappear, although those methods remain in other transfer comparisons. The VAU model lineup is unchanged.

E3.justification: V4 introduces CLIP-TSA training conditions combining Pistachio with 10%, 30% and 50% of UCF-Crime, evaluated on UCF-Crime. Appendix A adds annotation consistency and richness scoring on a 1–10 scale using three LVLM evaluators. These are substantive new evaluation designs; the original benchmark splits and AUC/AP/F1 metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing alternative-generation examples and cross-dataset analyses, v4 tests generator dependence, the effect of mixing synthetic and real training data, and annotation consistency/richness against Holmes-VAU. These additions directly examine robustness, practical transfer and annotation quality.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional annotation evaluators provide separate model scores rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V4 adds Fed-WSVAD results, including 83.2% overall AUC and 71.9% AP, plus cross-generator, mixed-training and annotation-quality scores. Table 4 newly reports 83.96/24.25 AUC/AP for CLIP-TSA with Pistachio plus 10% UCF training data. Earlier VAD scores are retained apart from rounding, and VAU scores are unchanged. VadCLIP/PEL4VAD results for transfer between UCF and Pistachio are removed.

M1.justification: V4 introduces a VLM Refiner that checks generated summaries against actual video content and corrects misalignments, extending v1's storyline-to-summary annotation procedure. The scene assignment, storyline construction and sequential Wan generation remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the annotation procedure, implementation description and VAD discussion, with smaller introduction edits. Numbered method subsubsections become unnumbered headings, and the supplement adopts lettered sections. Most introductory, related-work, generation, VAU and concluding prose is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column typesetting, substantially resizing and relocating figures, tables and the algorithm. V4 adds three experimental tables, restructures the statistics and transfer tables, and removes Table 1's camera-shot column. V1's standalone scene-ratio Figure 4 disappears, while its information remains in the retained supplementary distribution figure.

R1.justification: V4 adds references for Fed-WSVAD, Cosmos-Reason1, Video-LLaVA, I3D and ViT. Holmes-VAU, already cited in v1, becomes a direct annotation-quality comparator. The related-work survey and broad positioning of controlled generation against existing VAD datasets remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The scene-classification, anomaly-assignment and storyline equations, sequential video-generation formulation, and Algorithm 1 are mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new evaluations introduce no formal derivation.

improvement.justification: V4 adds useful tests of generator dependence, mixed-data training and annotation quality that v1 lacked, while clarifying annotation construction and filtering. These provide a limited net improvement. However, new evaluation details remain incomplete, some transfer comparisons are removed, and the new cross-generator discussion misreports its table: the stated 85.22/82.34 AUCs do not match Table 3's corresponding CLIP-TSA values of 72.17/75.89. These weaknesses limit the reliability of the expanded conclusions and prevent a major improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pistachio benchmark and generation pipeline. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: V4 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds cross-generator results, synthetic/real training experiments, and model-based annotation-quality assessments in Tables 3, 4 and S1.

before.justification: V1 reports original VAD evaluations in Table 2, VAU evaluations in Table 4, cross-dataset experiments in Table 7, and qualitative generation analyses.
