C1.justification: The main benchmark and automated-construction contributions remain intact. The introduction corrects the description of all 4,962 videos as long-form, and the conclusion more explicitly positions Pistachio as a complement to real data and a foundation for fine-tuning.

C2.justification: New Section 5 substantially expands applicability limits, including surveillance-domain transfer failures and character-identity drift, with deployment guidance. New interpretations address joint training, feature-distribution overlap and training-free detection failures. Appendix B.3 also introduces the stronger assertion that annotation hallucination is structurally impossible, which the reported evidence does not establish.

D1.justification: v6 newly discloses the 3.98 filtering-score cutoff, approximately two person-days of manual filtering, and 90% normal-video versus 80% anomaly-video acceptance rates. It also supplies acceleration timings and VRAM figures and describes VADTree processing. Core model choices, construction hardware and the project-access location are retained.

E1.justification: MSAD changes from a dataset discussed in related work to an evaluated transfer target and a dataset included in feature-distribution analysis. Existing Pistachio tasks and coverage, including Cosmos, Hailuo, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence and appendix ShanghaiTech evaluations, are retained.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds the evaluated training-free VADTree baseline while retaining the previous eight VAD methods. The VAU comparison adds InternVL3-2B, InternVL3-8B, InternVL3-14B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B variants within already represented model families.

E3.justification: v6 substantially extends evaluation design: XD-Violence-source and pooled five-dataset training, direct training-free VADTree evaluation, additional VAU model sizes, four-dimensional VLM pipeline scoring, generation-efficiency configurations, and a 100-video study with three annotators. Existing dataset splits and principal AUC/AP and F1 protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v4's qualitative pipeline comparisons, v6 adds quantitative strategy ablations in Table A.2, efficiency analysis in Table A.3, human annotation validation in Appendix B.3, and I3D feature-distribution analysis in Figure A.3. These substantially broaden evidence about generation quality, computational cost, annotation reliability and transfer.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly reports inter-annotator agreement estimates from three annotators: kappa of 0.76 at event level and 0.72 at video level. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the main VAD/VAU comparisons.

E6.justification: Matched existing scores are retained, but substantial new results cover VADTree, MSAD, XD-Violence-source and joint training, additional VAU models, and appendix analyses. VADTree reports 72.52% AUC and 25.15% AP; added InternVL3-14B becomes the VAU average leader at 29.39. Table 1 also revises MSAD's anomaly-type count from 35 to 11. Relocated statistics and earlier appendix transfer results are unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds optional four-step distilled generation and a TeaCache-assisted configuration, extending inference procedures. The core scene assignment, storyline construction, chained generation, filtering and annotation refinement remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that these accelerated configurations regenerated Pistachio.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative are retained. Local revisions correct the abstract/introduction ordering, update author information and headers, rewrite portions of experimental interpretation and the conclusion, introduce a dedicated limitations section, and reorganize appendix subsections.

P2.justification: v6 adds two compact appendix tables and a t-SNE figure, expands comparison tables, and revises Figure 2's assignment-stage display. Dataset statistics move from main Table 5 to Table A.5, while existing appendix figures and tables are reordered. The overall visual design remains similar.

R1.justification: v6 adds references for VideoScore and VADTree and discusses the latter's training-free approach through its evaluation. Existing cited works and the broader positioning against collected VAD datasets and video-generation research remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3, their mathematical definitions, and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. No formal theorem, proof or derivation is added; the new causal-inversion discussion is a qualitative interpretation.

improvement.justification: Expanded comparisons, human annotation checks and concrete deployment limits provide a modest net improvement over v4's thinner validation and brief domain-gap caveat. Gains are limited by underspecified new study protocols and new overclaims: annotation hallucination is not shown impossible, and joint-training MSAD AP of 25.69 trails Pistachio-only 54.24 despite the claim of strongest performance across all benchmarks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pistachio benchmark. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v6 retains these original results and adds baseline evaluations, pipeline and efficiency measurements, a human annotation study, and feature-distribution analysis.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the unintentional-attacker threat model, four-axis SPQR evaluation, and evidence that benign adaptation can undermine safety while preserving utility. The adaptation-dependent failure claim also remains. Added validation and backbone experiments support these existing claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly distinguishes the BFT threat from auxiliary adversarial stress tests and cautions against optimizing the scalar score alone because of detector overfitting. New sections interpret sensitivity and partial recovery as evidence about structural safety, while explicitly qualifying the recovery study as preliminary. Existing limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 provides a project-code URL, documents the human-annotation procedure and new sensitivity configurations, and explains the smoothing constant with an example value. The optimizer, base learning rate, batch size, resolution and LoRA configuration tables are retained. The PDFs alone do not verify the linked code's availability.

E1.justification: Both retain COCO, Arabic/French/Spanish/Hindi adaptations, artistic and medical data, and ViSU, I2P and Ring-A-Bell evaluations. The human audit uses an in-distribution subset of existing categories. Additional backbones and re-alignment procedures change experimental settings without expanding the represented data or domains.

E2.justification: The SD2.1 benchmark comparison narrows from AdvUnlearn, ESD, SPM and UCE in v1 Table D to ESD and UCE in v2 Table 11. AdvUnlearn and SPM remain in the separate LoRA-rank experiment. The eleven-method SD1.5 comparison and four-method SDXL comparison are retained.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 changes prompt adherence from raw CLIPScore to normalization against an unaligned SD3 reference. V2 adds SD3/FLUX configurations, a 250-image audit with three annotators and majority voting, learning-rate and aggregation variants, and post-BFT re-alignment. Existing base hyperparameters and BFT profiles remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds human validation of the safety classifiers (Table 1), learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 6), normalization/weight/temperature sensitivity (Table 10), and reversibility of safety degradation (Table 13). These test measurement validity, calibration dependence and recovery. The profile, domain, harmful-prompt and LoRA-rank analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports Spearman rank correlations against the default ranking for nine aggregation variants in Table 10. This adds a statistical ranking-stability summary. Both versions retain seed 42; v2 does not introduce confidence intervals, significance tests or documented additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Rescoring changes many reported values: RECE's SD1.5 general prompt-adherence/SPQR values change from 0.292/0.608 to 0.973/0.956, reflecting normalization rather than demonstrated performance gains. V2 also adds SD3/FLUX results, human-validation macro F1 of 0.87, sensitivity findings, and safety recovery of 86%, 81% and 60% for RECE, ESD and FMN.

M1.justification: The same existing alignment methods and full-parameter, cross-attention and LoRA adaptation procedures remain. The recovery experiment reapplies existing alignment methods. Revisions to SPQR normalization and aggregation concern evaluation definitions, rather than a new alignment algorithm or model.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, edits the introduction and conclusion, standardizes BFT/scenario terminology, adds appendix navigation and subsections, and replaces the Stable Diffusion history with focused backbone results. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, substantially altering figure sizes and float placement. Backbone comparisons are regrouped, with SDXL moved into the main benchmark table. Human-validation, aggregation-sensitivity and recovery tables and a learning-rate figure are added; existing qualitative and radar figures are largely retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for LLaVA-Guard, CLIPScore, FID and two recent unlearning/safety-drift works. The SDXL technical-report citation disappears with the removed backbone-history discussion. The main method taxonomy and positioning against existing benchmarks remain; the STEREO publication update represents the same work.

T1.justification: V2 defines SD3-normalized prompt adherence, generalizes Equation 7 with axis weights, and introduces temperature-dependent robustness in Appendix B.3. These are limited mathematical extensions of the existing scoring framework. The threat-model equations remain unchanged, and neither version supplies formal proofs.

improvement.justification: Human validation, sensitivity checks, DiT-backbone results and code-access information strengthen evidence and transparency beyond v1. However, the scoring revision is incompletely propagated: Section 4.4 still reports RECE's old 0.608 score while Table 2 gives 0.956. Appendix B.2 also calls the default learning rate a mid-range choice although Table 8 places it at the tested upper endpoint. These inconsistencies limit the overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPQR benchmark. All main-text and appendix pages, including equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite retitling, substantial reformatting and additional experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds human validation, SD3 and FLUX results, sensitivity analyses and a safety-recovery experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original safety and utility experiments across alignment methods, benign fine-tuning profiles, languages, domains and backbones, including appendix LoRA-rank ablations.

C1.justification: The central diagnosis, training-free attention correction, boundary refinement, and efficient image/video generation claims remain. v2 drops v1's sweeping statements that the method stabilizes all heads and layers uniformly and is compatible with any pretrained DiT, modestly narrowing the claimed applicability.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning modality-dependent learned RoPE biases, LR queries' reliance on coarse context, and high-resolution performance through token counts closer to training conditions. Appendix E replaces v1's discussion of unstable ultra-high-resolution details with concrete texture-transition failures and proposals for better masks and retrained positional encodings. These substantially revise the explanation of applicability and remaining limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents resizer training pairs, Pexels and Aesthetic-Train-V2 data, batch size, and weighted latent/pixel reconstruction and LPIPS losses. Appendix C adds attention-probing sample counts and offset grids, stage schedules, caching thresholds, and baseline configurations. A project-page link is also added. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing that previously unspecified training procedures changed.

E1.justification: VBench and MSCOCO coverage is retained. Beyond v1's two-resolution experiments, including its existing 480+1920 demonstration, v2 evaluates three and four simultaneous resolution grids, reaching 3840p for video and 2560 for images (Tables 8–9 and 13–14). These substantially expand the spatial-scale combinations required of generation.

E2.justification: v2 adds standalone video comparisons with UniPC, DPM++, ToMe, TeaCache, and MagCache (Table 3). TeaCache and MagCache also become standalone image comparators, whereas v1 evaluated their integration with the proposed method. Image Table 2 adds PI+NTK; RALU, Bottleneck, and ToCa were already evaluated in v1. LR+HR disappears from Table 1, although it remains a comparator in v2 Figure 10.

E3.justification: Image evaluation replaces FID with ImageReward. The main two-stage image comparison changes from 18 steps, 7 LR steps, and 30% HR tokens to 15 steps, 5 LR steps, and 60% HR tokens; the latter setting already appeared in v1's caching appendix. The faster three-stage image setting changes from 9 to 10 steps, and Appendix C specifies DeepGazeI instead of DeepGazeIIE for images. New evaluations also introduce distilled-model and matched-latency protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained boundary and RoPE-only analyses, v2 adds saliency-model robustness (Table 6), HR key/value handling ablations (Table 15), FLUX modality-specific attention curves (Figure 16), failure cases (Figure 17), and prompt-count/timestep sensitivity checks (Figure 24). It also tests generation with and without DyPE. v1's FID-versus-token-ratio plot and four-budget image comparison are absent; v2 introduces a video quality–latency comparison.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 documents attention-measurement sample counts and checks larger prompt samples, but retains the same averaging estimator and does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive acceleration, distillation, multiresolution, and ablation results. For example, Table 5 newly reports four-step DMD at 80.15 VBench total and 10.9 seconds, versus DMD plus the proposed method at 80.11 and 5.6 seconds. Image comparison entries are revised under changed settings, and FID results are removed. Many retained video and boundary-ablation scores merely receive percentage formatting or additional precision.

M1.justification: CRPA is renamed PMA, but Section 4 retains query-scale position mapping, HR key/value subsampling for LR queries, bidirectional Boundary Expand-and-Replace, and coarse/mixed/optional-fine denoising. The newly disclosed resizer training losses describe existing learned components; the PDFs do not establish an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around generation efficiency and positional scale bias. The title and method terminology change, method explanations are substantially revised, and experiments are reorganized by comparison type. The appendix gains subsections and a figure guide, with results moved before the derivation.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column main layout to a single-column format. Figure 1 becomes a sample montage, Figure 4 is redrawn to contrast both interpolation baselines with PMA, and qualitative comparisons are redesigned with detail crops. Numerous new tables and analysis figures are added, while retained material such as the boundary-ablation table moves into the main text.

R1.justification: The distinction from RoPE extrapolation and positioning relative to RALU remain. v2 adds an explicit claim to be the first work focused on mixed-resolution generation, cites additional mixed-resolution vision precedents, and adds references supporting DyPE, distillation, ImageReward, and training data. Some earlier references, including FID and VideoRoPE, disappear. The principal research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 changes S from native grid spacing in v1 to native resolution scale, explicitly larger for HR, in v2. This corrects the interpretation of alpha = S_q/S_k to agree with the retained stretching examples. The sinusoidal decomposition and its proof are unchanged apart from formatting and relocation from Appendix A to B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: new standalone video acceleration comparisons, saliency and key/value ablations, multigrid tests, and concrete failure cases address important gaps in v1. Resizer training and experimental configuration disclosures make the work easier to assess and reproduce. Removing FID analyses reduces continuity, and changed image protocols prevent straightforward historical performance comparisons. Nevertheless, the targeted evidence and documentation gains provide a substantial overall improvement without requiring a new method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite changes to the title and method acronym. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds acceleration comparisons, multiresolution evaluations, robustness studies, and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-response measurements, image and video generation experiments, acceleration comparisons, and boundary-module ablations in the main text and appendix.

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free initial-noise optimization and superior image-inpainting performance remain. v3 qualifies the novelty framing by explicitly acknowledging earlier noise optimization and identifying its gradient approximation with the straight-through estimator. It sharpens the contribution around Adam-based spectral preconditioning and reduced need for learning-rate tuning.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism explanation through Adam's per-frequency normalization and globally coupled updates. It discusses learning-rate, blur and divergence tradeoffs, qualifies trajectory linearity near the final denoising steps, and explains applicability to non-flow backbones. These go beyond v1's empirical rationale and broad future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the spatial-ablation learning rate of 0.05, identifies Claude Sonnet 4.5, and adds implementation settings and exact runtime/memory information. The original implementation recipe and prompt templates largely persist. The explicit code-release promise disappears, but the PDFs do not establish a change in actual code availability.

E1.justification: FFHQ, DIV2K and BrushBench coverage and their mask scenarios are retained. v3 adds full-image inversion of synthetic SD3.5 outputs for convergence testing and describes preliminary Wan video inpainting. The video outputs themselves are only linked externally, limiting assessment of that extension.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets remain. Appendix H/Table 7 adds InitNo, GoldenNoise and FreeInpaint, including FreeInpaint with BrushNet and BLD-SD3.5; Appendix I/Table 8 adds SD3 ControlNet inpainting. These substantially expand comparisons with relevant noise-optimization and trained methods. FlowOpt and DiNG are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a randomized, single-blind 2AFC study with 37 raters and 45 scenes, controlled synthetic-image inversion using shared initializations and RMSE, SD1.5/SDXL backbone evaluations, and 10/20/30-iteration budgets. These substantially expand evaluation design; the original main benchmark splits and inpainting settings are retained.

E4.justification: The original component ablations remain, but the single-example convergence analysis becomes a systematic Adam/SGD and learning-rate comparison. Appendices B/C add velocity-linearity diagnostics and latent/noise convergence analyses; Appendix J adds iteration sensitivity. New CLIP-scored qualitative cases examine disagreement between metric scores and visual consistency.

E5.justification: v1 contains no formal uncertainty analysis. v3 Appendix A/Table 5 introduces aggregate and per-baseline 95% confidence intervals for human preference and claims statistically significant advantages. The interval construction and significance test are unspecified, and uncertainty across repeated benchmark runs remains unreported.

E2.justification: The real-world comparison expands from the Wu and Yang 4DGS methods to include Grid4D and FreeTimeGS (Table 1). FreeTimeGS was already cited as a methodological foundation in v1, but was not an evaluated comparator. All four baselines also participate in the new motion and video-quality comparisons.

E3.justification: The two 4DGS baselines change from reported random initialization to COLMAP initialization. V2 introduces density-weighted volumetric evaluation and full-video CGVQM with soft masking of synchronization hardware. Synthetic evaluation uses 50 frames per camera over two seconds and 640-cubed velocity grids. NoSync changes from v1's one-frame or up-to-one-frame offsets to half-frame offsets; the real-data every-eighth-frame holdout remains unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds the NoMask ablation, evaluates component effects on simulated motion, and introduces a RoMa matching-failure analysis (Figure 12). It removes the quantitative GlobalShutter ablation and detailed per-scene ablation tables, although Appendix B retains the finding that explicit shutter handling did not improve image metrics. These changes substantially revise the evidence about component roles and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly identifies Table 1 entries as means and standard deviations across scenes. V2 retains the plus-or-minus format but omits that explicit definition, including for its new motion and video metrics. Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests; additional result rows do not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Real-world results are extensively replaced: the proposed method's flame PSNR changes from 27.46 to 26.93, full-image PSNR from 33.61 to 35.89, and depth RMSE from 0.0412 to 0.094. The full-image ranking changes from Yang 4DGS leading to the proposed method leading. Settings also change, preventing interpretation as controlled performance gains. New results include motion cosine similarity of 0.744 and CGVQM of 86.1; per-scene baseline and ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: The two-stage, flow-initialized Gaussian model retains its lifetime and constant-velocity equations. V2 adds a motion-mask opacity loss weighted by 0.1 and bounds dynamic Gaussian scales using a voxel-scaled sigmoid (Section 3.2; Appendix H). Rolling-shutter modeling is presented as an optional extension. These refine the existing procedure rather than replace its core representation.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, with substantial revisions to results interpretation and methodological explanations. Rolling-shutter treatment moves from the main methodology to Appendix B. The supplement is reorganized from Sections 8–14 into thematic Appendices A–J, with reordered dataset, implementation, visualization and resource sections.

P2.justification: Comparison figures are redesigned for four baselines, and new motion visualizations, synthetic-scene montages and a RoMa matching illustration are added. Existing fire-removal and capture-setup images move to the appendix. Real-world comparisons and ablations merge into a color-highlighted table, with new motion and video tables. Six per-scene baseline/ablation tables and the rolling-shutter illustration are removed; retained dataset and per-scene tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from a FreeTimeGS-based reconstruction pipeline toward a transient-Gaussian formulation claimed to overcome general failures of existing Gaussian representations. V2 also introduces an efficiency-based rationale for excluding non-Gaussian comparisons. It adds references to RoMa, Grid4D, CGVQM+D and MotionGS and removes R3D3; the broad related-work survey is otherwise largely retained.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 adds mathematical definitions for density-weighted motion comparison: opacity-volume weights, expected ground-truth velocities approximated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and weighted relative L2 and cosine scores. It also removes duplicated depth-loss weighting from the displayed formulation. Existing flow-reconstruction and rolling-shutter derivations are substantially retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central motion-reconstruction claim. V1 relied on image metrics, monocular-depth proxies and qualitative evidence; v2 adds direct comparison with simulated ground-truth velocities, video-quality evaluation and two additional baselines with better-documented initialization. This addresses an important evidential gap rather than merely increasing reported performance. The gains outweigh the loss of detailed per-scene comparisons, less explicit uncertainty labeling, and remaining weaknesses in the broad baseline-failure claims and contradictory JointOpt interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Gaussians on Fire and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material. Content can be matched across the substantial reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original real-world reconstruction experiments, adds three simulated fire scenes with ground-truth velocity evaluation, and reports video-quality results.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on 17 captured fire scenes, including baseline comparisons, component ablations and per-scene results.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the expert-grounded CoE benchmark, two-stage REVEAL framework, and claims of better detection, generalization, and explanation fidelity. Although v2 moderates wording in its abstract and conclusion, its introduction retains the state-of-the-art claim and Table 1 retains the first-reasoning-dataset claim. Added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning expert aggregation, annotation reliability, complementary Pixel Noise cues, and limited gains from stronger annotation models attributed to saturation. Appendix C qualifies model-size scaling under limited data, and Appendix H acknowledges failure on a convincing synthetic cat. The multi-view reward discussion also drops v1's assertion of self-supervised discovery of novel transformation-invariant artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 supplies expert-to-input mappings, clarifies that experts operate offline without additional training, and identifies Qwen3-VL-8B as the reward assessor. It documents loss/reward weights and training details including 58K samples, 10 SFT epochs, one RL epoch, AdamW at 1e-5, and eight A800 GPUs. These are newly available disclosures, not demonstrated changes to prior settings. V2 promises future code and data release but supplies no release location.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on REVEAL-Bench++, covering FLUX, FLUX2, Z-Image, Qwen-Image, and SD3.5 as generators stated to be absent from training. This substantially extends the evaluated generator population beyond v1's REVEAL-Bench and GenImage coverage; merely citing some generators in v1 did not establish their evaluation.

E2.justification: V2's main comparisons include AIGI-Holmes alongside retained detectors, and Table 6 adds the best individual expert, majority voting, and decision trees. AIDE and VIB-Net disappear from the full-data in-domain comparison but remain in the GenImage comparison. V2 also supplies large-model comparisons in Appendix D; v1 references such an appendix without providing its contents, so those comparisons cannot all be called newly conducted.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a balanced 10,000-image recent-generator test and an anonymized explanation study using 100 images and three annotators with majority voting. New controls test answer-first supervision and alternative annotation configurations. Section 3 also revises the reported curation sequence: v1 selects 60K images before expert annotation, whereas v2 describes selecting 60K from approximately 6M annotated samples. Newly supplied training settings do not establish changes to earlier training budgets.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained backbone, CoE/GRPO, and perturbation analyses, v2 adds an answer-first ablation, expert-guided versus direct-LLM annotation analysis, Pixel Noise expert removal, and stronger-annotator experiments. Appendices provide explanation preferences, agent-versus-embedding examples, and detailed success and failure cases. These substantially expand tests of reasoning, annotation quality, and applicability.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new three-annotator majority-vote procedure defines the human evaluation protocol; it does not introduce uncertainty estimation or inter-rater agreement statistics.

E6.justification: V2 adds recent-generator scores, answer-first accuracy of 82.39%, human preference of 63% versus 37% for AIGI-Holmes, and annotation-ablation results. Matched GenImage per-generator scores remain unchanged; the REVEAL mean changing from 95.00 to 94.96 reflects exclusion of the in-domain column. Figure 5 also revises REVEAL's robustness results under the same stated perturbations: JPEG quality 60 rises from approximately 58% to 72%, without an explanation of the revision.

M1.justification: The stated reinforcement-learning objective changes substantially: v1 Equations 7 and 16 use advantage-weighted log probabilities with KL(old policy || current policy), whereas v2 Equations 7 and 13 use clipped probability-ratio objectives with KL(current policy || reference policy). This revises the specified optimization procedure, although implementation changes or reruns are not established. The two-stage framework and three reward components remain.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative, expands expert and optimization explanations, incorporates backbone comparisons into the ablation section, and adds dedicated explanation and annotation sections. The author list also changes. The new template introduces unfinished running headers, including 'F. Author et al.' and 'Abbreviated paper title'.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V1's introductory figures are replaced by a redesigned comparison diagram, while its dataset and training pipelines are retained as v2 Figures 2–3. Generalization tables are reorganized, the backbone table is transposed, and numerous analysis displays and qualitative panels are added. Figure 5 receives new styling, axes presentation, and legends alongside its separately assessed numerical revisions.

R1.justification: The related-work framing remains largely intact. V2 adds references for DeepSeekMath, Qwen3-VL, FLUX2, Z-Image, and Qwen-Image, removes the VAR citation, and adds a limited contrast with interpretable rule-based classifiers. This updates supporting literature without substantially redefining the work's research positioning.

T1.justification: V2 substantively revises the mathematical definitions of the GRPO and R-GRPO objectives through probability-ratio clipping and a different KL direction and reference policy. The basic GRPO advantage also gains standard-deviation normalization and a denominator safeguard. These are non-equivalent mathematical revisions, unlike the simplification of already normalized R-GRPO advantages. The SFT factorization and loss remain, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited support for its generalization and explainability claims through recent-generator testing, controlled annotation and reasoning analyses, and an anonymized human preference study. Supplying previously unavailable training and expert details also materially improves auditability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including unexplained Figure 5 revisions, unfinished presentation, and the new claim that alpha=0.1 prioritizes answers despite Equation 5 weighting reasoning by 0.9. The added evidence strengthens evaluation without establishing causal faithfulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REVEAL, and their supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 cites Appendices A–D but ends after its references; v2 includes Appendices A–I. This limits comparison of earlier supplementary details, while the main-text changes remain reliably comparable.

after.justification: V2 retains original detection results and reports additional generator evaluations, annotation ablations, human preferences, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments, backbone comparisons, training ablations, and perturbation results in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5.

It also narrows v1's blanket quantitative-superiority claim to superior fidelity and competitive perceptual quality. The central full-frame geometry contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets lower MEt3R scores as evidence of stable 3DGS structures with fewer geometric conflicts, and matching counts as evidence of pixel-level geometric consistency. It also discusses GPU-memory overhead from loading VGGT. Existing explanations concerning imperfect conditioning and token filtering largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents simultaneous training of the adaptation and diffusion modules, inference output sizes, GPU memory capacities, parameter accounting and total two-stage timing. These are additional disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing settings. v1 Appendix B's supplementary-video filenames are omitted; the project-page address remains equivalent.

E1.justification: Both versions train on DL3DV and evaluate on RealEstate10K and Tanks and Temples for camera-controlled novel-view synthesis and 3D scene generation. The new geometry measurements evaluate these existing outputs; the omitted example galleries do not establish a distinct change in task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1-2 replace DimensionX with Hunyuan-Voyager, and Table 2 adds ViewCrafter to the 3D scene generation comparison. See3D and FlexWorld remain, while ViewCrafter was already evaluated for novel-view synthesis. This is a focused update to the comparator sets.

E3.justification: Sections 4.3-4.5 add adjacent-frame MEt3R evaluation on 49-frame 3DGS renderings, two-view MASt3R matching, no-geometry and depth-only controls, and computational-cost evaluation with specified hardware and method-specific output sizes. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Existing Section 4.1 training budgets, sampling procedures and standard benchmark metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of removing geometric conditioning and replacing it with depth maps (Figure 8), plus multi-view consistency and image-matching analyses (Figures 6-7). These directly examine the geometric benefits of the method. Existing component, training-duration and token-weighting analyses remain; the discard-ratio study moves from Appendix A into Section 4.5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. The new per-frame MEt3R curves show variation across frames, not repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark and numerical ablation values remain unchanged, including GeoWorld's RealEstate10K PSNR of 17.28 in Table 1. v2 adds Hunyuan-Voyager results, ViewCrafter reconstruction results, MEt3R curves, matching counts including 1250 for GeoWorld, and cost measurements. DimensionX results and the additional appendix galleries are removed, substantially changing the reported evidence.

M1.justification: The two-stage generation procedure, VGGT geometry features, alignment loss, adaptation module, 50% token removal and cross-attention fusion remain unchanged. Explicit two-stage terminology and the additional conditioning ablations do not establish a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, central introduction passages, contribution statements and conclusion are substantially rewritten around full-frame conditioning and two-stage efficiency. The experimental narrative is reorganized, Appendix A is integrated into the main text, and Appendix B is removed. Most methodological prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 changes the predominantly two-column layout to a single-column format, redraws the pipeline comparison in Figure 2, revises qualitative comparison panels and adds geometry-analysis figures and a cost table. Existing ablations are relocated and reformatted, while the additional appendix galleries disappear.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to MEt3R, Depth Anything 3, WorldMirror and newer video world models, and emphasizes efficiency relative to Hunyuan-Voyager. The related-work taxonomy and core geometry-guidance positioning remain. Voyager was already cited in v1, although it was not an evaluated baseline.

T1.justification: Equations 1-4 retain the same diffusion loss, geometric feature loss, combined objective and cross-attention formulation. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the new evaluation measures introduce no mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: The new geometry diagnostics and conditioning controls strengthen evidence for the central mechanism, while updated baselines and narrower performance claims improve the comparison. The gain is limited by the illustrative scope of the new geometry tests and removal of extra appendix examples. Cost reporting adds transparency, but its broad efficiency claim needs qualification: Table 3 uses unequal output sizes and lists ViewCrafter at 2.6B parameters versus GeoWorld's 3.9B.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GeoWorld and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. Inspection included v1 Appendices A-B. v2 incorporates Appendix A's discard-ratio study into Section 4.5 and has no separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and ablation results and adds geometry-consistency tests, conditioning ablations and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: Sections 4.2-4.3 and Appendix A report original benchmark results, component ablations and generated-scene examples.

C1.justification: The four central contributions and 86-92% model-compression claim remain. v2 extends the abstract's superiority claim to multi-teacher distillation through a reported 5.3-point advantage over GPFM, qualifies the earlier novelty positioning, and strengthens deployment language to describe the model as already suited for clinical settings.

C2.justification: v2 adds a CKA-based explanation of teacher complementarity and flags training/evaluation overlap for relevant baseline results. Its rewritten discussion no longer contains v1's explicit single-institution/scanner and correlated-teacher-bias limitations, while asserting clinical suitability and interpreting compression as evidence that large models underutilize their capacity. These substantially alter the qualifications and implications presented to readers.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-and-weights location, explicit equal teacher weighting and segmentation-head information. v1's implementation section specifies eight GPUs, batch size 1024, AdamW, 300,000 iterations, learning-rate and decay schedules, and EMA evaluation; these details are unavailable in v2. Its missing supplement prevents determining whether this substantial reproducibility information was relocated or lost.

E1.justification: v2 adds segmentation on ConSep and MoNuSAC, extending evaluation from classification and retrieval to spatial mask prediction. The original internal training dataset, ten classification benchmarks and CCRCC retrieval task remain.

E2.justification: GPFM becomes an evaluated multi-teacher pathology baseline in the classification, efficiency, retrieval and nested-embedding comparisons. These corresponding v1 experiments included the teachers and H0-mini but not GPFM. Its citation in v1 did not constitute an evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include Dice-based segmentation with a convolutional decoder receiving patch tokens and raw images, and CKA analysis on 10,000 training images with DINOv2 reference controls. UNI2-h's k-NN evaluation extends to dim/128, while the PCA visualization tests truncation through dim/256. The shared classification and throughput protocols remain unchanged as documented.

E4.justification: v2 adds teacher-complementarity analysis using CKA and quantitative segmentation tests under embedding truncation, while expanding k-NN compression analysis from three to six existing classification datasets. The cropping ablation is retained and moved from v1 Table 7 to v2 Table 3. A new single-teacher ablation is summarized, but its cited Table S6 is unavailable.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 adds one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across datasets, reporting p-values of 0.042, 0.010 and 0.019 against UNI2-h, H0-mini and GPFM. This adds an inferential layer while retaining the existing five-run reporting and 500-batch throughput statistics; increased repetition counts are not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPFM scores, segmentation results, CKA measurements and additional k-NN results. Examples include GPFM's median classification score of 80.3 and Pathryoshka-B's ConSep Dice scores of 63.6 at full dimensionality and 62.6 at dim/16. Existing classification and Recall@5 entries are largely retained with rounding. Table 2 changes Pathryoshka-B throughput from 885.1 ± 7.1 to 842 ± 4 images/s under the same stated measurement protocol.

M1.justification: The documented procedure retains the same teachers, aligned and non-aligned crops, nested embedding prefixes, projection heads and cosine/MSE losses. Explicit equal teacher weighting in v2 clarifies the existing unweighted sums. The new evaluation heads do not establish a change to Pathryoshka itself.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the method subsections, moves teacher selection into Methodology, and extensively rewrites related work and the discussion. The standalone implementation section disappears from the supplied main text, while author information, terminology and explanatory passages are revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference formatting. Figure 4 becomes six separate panels with uncertainty bars and absolute embedding sizes; Figure 5 uses a different tissue example and stronger truncation. Other diagrams are revised, Table 2 is transposed, the cropping table moves into the main text, and a segmentation table is added.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the assertion that multi-teacher distillation had not been explored in pathology with explicit discussion of GPFM, positioning Pathryoshka around compression relative to larger teachers and nested embeddings. GPFM was already cited in v1, but this substantive relationship was absent. Related work also expands discussion of unsupervised distillation, teacher-head accessibility and embedding efficiency.

However, v1's appendix includes an O(nd) k-NN runtime argument, whose retention or revision cannot be checked because v2's supplementary material is unavailable.

improvement.justification: GPFM comparisons, segmentation validation, significance tests and more accurate prior-work positioning strengthen v2. However, the supplied version lacks v1's detailed training recipe and its own referenced supplement, while replacing explicit limitations with stronger clinical-suitability language without corresponding clinical validation. C2.justification: v2 develops a new loss-landscape/GNC interpretation, attributing robustness to avoiding sharp local minima. It assigns distinct geometric and appearance roles to position and color smoothing, interprets MonoGS results as evidence of wider applicability, and attributes runtime gains to approximately 40% fewer iterations. These materially expand the causal interpretation; no substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: CUDA integration, A40 hardware and principal smoothing hyperparameters remain documented. v2 removes v1's explicit 40 tracking/60 mapping iteration budgets and several implementation details, including first-frame initialization, current/latest/top-overlap keyframe selection and mapping's SSIM term. These are losses of documentation rather than established implementation changes.

ScanNet 0207 already appeared in v1's trajectory analysis. These address mechanisms and portability absent from v1. Conversely, v1's targeted RPE analysis is removed.

Section 2 newly positions RAP against virtual-correspondence approaches DeepVCP and DeepPRO, while Section 4.3 introduces the claimed absence of cross-domain evaluation as a research gap. These changes extend the positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The main flow equations, rigid projection, training loss and standard error formulas remain equivalent after renumbering. v1 Equation 8's explicit rigidity-residual definition is absent from v2. Appendix B.6 introduces definitions for edge/graph success and normalized global RMSE. Neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: The broader evaluation, matched-training-data BUFFER-X control and threshold/view-count analyses strengthen the empirical case beyond v1. These gains are tempered by unresolved support for the central zero-shot claim: nuScenes appears in both training Table 4 and benchmark Table 10 despite Section 4.3 claiming no dataset overlap. Conflicting learning rates and removal of several diagnostic ablations further limit reproducibility and transparency, making the net quality improvement modest.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAP research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original registration experiments, cross-domain benchmark comparisons, ablations and offline SLAM results, including Tables 2, 3, 8 and 9.

before.justification: v1 reports original pairwise and multi-view registration experiments, ablations, runtime measurements and extensive validation results, including appendix Tables 8–10.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: tightly coupled visual-inertial estimation, robust initialization, time-varying biases, consistent loop-closure updates, robust real-time tracking and high-fidelity mapping. Expanding evaluation from four named benchmarks to five datasets supplies broader support rather than redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific explanations involving DBA-Fusion's linearization gap and VINGS-Mono's depth generalization and loop-closure failures. Its limitations paragraph replaces the multicamera/fisheye and high-end-GPU caveats with marginal gains from Gaussian-assisted pose refinement, attributed to insufficiently sharp online renderings. These refine mechanisms and applicability discussion without overturning the main interpretation.

D1.justification: v1 describes partially NumPy-based IMU processing and future CUDA optimization; v2 reports C++ preintegration, CUDA Jacobian/Hessian computation and TensorRT inference. It also adds baseline configuration details, smartphone-demo implementation, and Odin acquisition, calibration, undistortion and anonymization information. The project-page link is replaced by promises to release code and data, which do not establish current availability.

E1.justification: The four original benchmarks remain. Self-captured evaluation expands from one extreme-condition sequence to 18 indoor/outdoor sequences covering long trajectories, dynamic objects, glare, low light and reflective/transparent surfaces. Controlled motion-blur, overexposure and low-light variants of EuRoC introduce additional input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds DBA-Fusion and VINGS-Mono to tracking comparisons on the original benchmarks, increasing the stated baseline set from 13 to 15. VINGS-Mono also enters rendering comparisons, including Table 3 and Figure 3. It was discussed but not evaluated in v1; these additions directly address closely related visual-inertial competitors.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled blur, exposure and noisy low-light transformations, success-curve AUC through 6 meters, and peak GPU-memory measurement. Newly evaluated baselines use specified adaptations: forced EuRoC keyframes, a reduced UTMM initialization threshold, and disabled monocular depth and loop closure for VINGS-Mono. The original ATE, recall and rendering metrics remain.

E4.justification: Table 6 expands from three tracking ablations to six, adding zero-bias, shared-global-bias and removal-of-inertial-only-initialization tests. v2 also adds controlled corruption sensitivity tests and broader trajectory/rendering case studies. Conversely, v1's appendix Tables 17–18 with per-sequence mapping and tracking ablations disappear, although their aggregate results remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's synthetic-noise parameters describe input corruption, not uncertainty in estimated performance.

E6.justification: Original benchmark accuracy/rendering results are largely retained, but v2 adds extensive baseline, self-capture, corruption and ablation results. Table 10 reports self-captured mean ATE of 0.588 m for VIGS-SLAM versus 1.850 m for DBA-Fusion. Runtime Table 9 changes mean tracking/full-system FPS from 16.40/7.09 to 39.83/12.02, while mean keyframes change from 491 to 366; this is not an isolated same-workload speedup. Some per-sequence ablation results are removed.

M1.justification: Both versions retain joint pose/disparity/velocity/bias optimization, three-stage IMU initialization, IMU-based keyframe initialization, pose-graph loop closure and consistent Gaussian updates. v2 adds solver and sampling details and reports implementation acceleration; these do not establish a different estimator, objective or core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose remain. v2 makes targeted introductory and related-work rewrites, expands optimization and ablation explanations, updates author/front matter, and adds dedicated supplementary sections for the demo and baselines. References move behind the supplementary narrative.

New self-capture Figures 5–6 replace the earlier single-case display. Tables gain comparator, ablation and memory rows, new experimental tables appear, and two detailed appendix ablation tables are removed.

The existing VINGS-Mono discussion is recast around that relationship and specific weaknesses. Additional references support implementation and acquisition; KITTI and KITTI-360 citations are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds the block normal equations and Schur-complement update in Section 3.1, Equation 4, including the argument that the depth block is diagonal. v1 states the residual objectives without this algebra. Other core mathematical formulations remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1: missing empirical comparisons with closely related dense visual-inertial systems and limited tests of staged initialization and bias modeling. The added comparisons, targeted ablations, controlled corruptions and diverse self-captured sequences substantially strengthen support for robustness. Implementation documentation also improves. Removed per-sequence ablation tables and less explicit hardware/camera caveats reduce transparency, while changed keyframe counts limit runtime comparability, but these losses do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds self-captured-dataset evaluations, baseline comparisons, visual-corruption experiments, additional ablations and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original VIGS-SLAM tracking, rendering, robustness, ablation and runtime results in the main paper and appendix.

Figure 1 gains red highlights, Figure 5 revises panel labels, and Figures 6-7 are added. Tables 3-4 exchange numbering, v1 Table 7 moves into the main text as Table 5, and the other appendix tables and algorithm disappear.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning inadequate global replay, CLIP/model-space mismatch, and local score-field protection. It introduces limitations concerning candidate coverage, overlapping style features, long deletion sequences, and teacher–student resource costs. It also describes UCE as achieving high erasure with retention collapse, replacing v1's contrary prose and aligning with the reported tables.

However, v1 supplies detailed prompt templates, hyperparameters, and evaluation counts, while v2 defers full details to an unavailable supplement and leaves Kf/Kr unspecified. The extent to which earlier reproducibility information was retained or revised cannot be established.

This changes the evaluated target population modestly; the overall task still covers sequential removal of objects, styles, and named individuals or characters.

New selection and no-LLM controls add experimental configurations. These are reported setting differences, not evidence of otherwise identical experiments being rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's fixed/adaptive mapping comparison and component ablations, v2 adds naive, LLM, CLIP, and score-based selection comparisons, a no-LLM variant, and alternative-VLM judge sensitivity. Component ablations are revised for the new selection procedure. Whether v1's supplementary timestep and base-model analyses persist cannot be checked without v2's referenced supplement.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports averaging results over five random deletion orders; v1 provides a fixed order without comparable repeated-run reporting. Neither supplied PDF reports confidence intervals or dispersion across runs. This establishes a reporting addition, not a verified increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Results are substantially revised and expanded. v1 Table 5 reports final fixed-context UA/RRA/GRA of 0.86/0.81/0.85, while v2 Table 1 reports LACU Uacc/RRacc/GRacc of 0.90/0.72/0.87. MACE's final unlearning/related-retention values change from 0.29/0.81 to 0.97/0.03. These are results under revised targets and order aggregation, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v1 uses LLM-generated fixed-context or adaptive-context mappings and related/random replay prompts. v2 adds explicit score-prediction-distance ranking to select both per-prompt mapping targets and nearest replay concepts, recomputed using the current teacher. These change the selection procedures while retaining teacher–student distillation and parameter regularization.

P1.justification: The title changes from Distill, Forget, Repeat to Locality-Aware Continual Unlearning for Diffusion Models. The abstract, introduction, related work, failure analysis, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around locality, with new metric explanations, trajectory interpretation, and limitations. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

Its Figure 3 reworks v1's opening qualitative comparison, replacing the MACE row with SMem. Main quantitative presentation shifts from radar plots to compact, highlighted comparison tables, with additional selection-ablation displays.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a mathematical definition of averaged squared score-prediction distance and explicit argmin target and top-Nr neighborhood selection rules (Equations 2–5). These extend the formal specification beyond v1's contextual mappings. The basic distillation and regularization losses remain, without new theorems or proofs establishing stability.

improvement.justification: v2 benefits from broader baseline comparisons, randomized-order evaluation, new controls, clearer methodological positioning, and explicit limitations. However, its referenced supplement is unavailable, leaving important protocols and supporting results unverifiable. LACU's final Uacc/RRacc also differs between Table 1 (0.90/0.72) and Tables 2–3 (0.92/0.74) without an explained setting distinction. These benefits and unresolved reproducibility and reporting gaps prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

The supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 includes supplementary Sections 7–12, while v2 references supplementary methods and results that are absent from the supplied PDF, limiting appendix-level comparison.

The introduction also adds a statistical-power claim based on comparisons with other agent benchmarks.

C2.justification: v3 explains ChatGPT Agent's relative advantage on Structure tasks through native GUI handling, contrasting this with PPTPilot's tendency to over-edit master XML. It also adds a plateau-based rationale for the three-pass refinement cap. The detailed failure examples and limitations concerning ambiguous instructions, cross-application workflows, and specialized domains are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix I and Table D document baseline interfaces, backbones, context limits, retry budgets, timeouts, latencies, and an approximately $700 evaluation cost. Appendix J changes the release statement from planned to released and specifies screenshots, structural diffs, judge prompts, and raw outputs. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although availability itself cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate PPTArena's 100 decks and 2,125 slides across the same editing taxonomy, plus T2US and PPTC-R. Revised edit totals and sourcing-pool sizes do not establish additional task or domain coverage. The human and batching studies assess existing editing tasks.

E2.justification: v3 adds Kimi-K2.6 to the matched subset comparison and reports Gemini CLI and ChatGPT alongside the subset baselines in Table 4. The other principal comparators remain. The earlier Poster2Agent label corresponds to Paper2Poster, which remains reported in v3's text and Appendix Table A.

The hard-subset selection description shifts from poor model performance to structural difficulty plus breadth. v3 also reports 1,340 edits rather than 800+, introduces a blind 25-expert evaluation on a stratified 10% subset, and adds a 105-slide-pair page-wise control. These are documented setting changes and new protocols, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial validation of the evaluation pipeline: human–judge alignment, repeated-call consistency, and batched versus page-wise visual scoring. It also reports the router's 66% programmatic versus 34% XML usage. The executor ablations, alternative-judge comparison, and illustrated failure cases already existed in v1 and are largely retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no corresponding repeated-judge uncertainty analysis. v3 Table 8 first reports five judge runs per example, majority agreement of 78%/95% for IF/VQ, and standard deviations reported as 15.4%/9%. It also introduces Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall human–judge correlations. This adds statistical validation and variability reporting, rather than establishing an increase over a previously specified run count.

E6.justification: PPTPilot's full-benchmark IF/VQ changes from 2.36/2.69 to 2.57/2.69, and its subset scores from 1.71/1.54 to 1.87/1.91 (v1 Table 3; v3 Tables 4–5). v3 adds Kimi scores, human ratings, latency measurements, and judge-validation outcomes; reported average operations change from 5.1 to 13.4. The ablation and T2US scores remain unchanged. Revised models and settings prevent interpreting the changed scores as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The semantic planning, routing between programmatic and XML editing, validation, and reflection procedures are retained. SSIM screening and the detailed two-stage editing paths already appeared in v1's appendix. Updated backbone versions are experimental configuration changes; no new algorithmic component or procedure is established.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: detailed ablations move from main Section 5.2 to Appendix E.3, difficulty analysis moves into the main benchmark section, and separate sections present judge reliability and human comparisons. The abstract, conclusion, and dataset explanation are rewritten or expanded, and the title, author list, and bibliographic text are revised.

New latency, human-validation, and configuration tables accompany extensive resizing and restyling of appendix figures and code listings.

R1.justification: v3 adds an explicit comparison with the concurrent, independent PPTArena benchmark, contrasting its GUI tasks over 12 source files with this work's scope. It also adds SWE-bench Multimodal scale positioning and a Kimi reference. Much of the extensive bibliography revision supplies author, title, and publication metadata for already cited works rather than changing research positioning.

The expert study, repeated-judge analysis, and batching control directly support the benchmark's credibility, while matched comparisons and baseline budgets improve interpretability and reproducibility. Reporting problems temper these gains: revised counts and configurations are not fully reconciled, and Figure G retains older PPTPilot scores despite Tables 4–5. These limit precise performance interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial new validation.

improvement.justification: The VBD comparison and separate phase-alignment control strengthen evidence for portability and scheduling benefits. C1.justification: v1's abstract claims 98% of CLIP performance at half cost; v2 strengthens this to matching or beating full-cost frozen CLIP. The introduction also extends the efficiency claim across multiple architectures. The central NoisyCLIP, benchmark, and early-stopping contributions remain.

C2.justification: v1 treats NoisySigLIP's weaker retrieval performance as limited transfer across backbones. v2 attributes it to sigmoid-versus-softmax discrimination and emphasizes robust transfer for visual selection (Section 5.4). It also interprets the new DiT results as architectural transfer and revises failure-case explanations in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page address where v1 only promised future code and data, and documents DiT VAE decoding and shorter generation schedules. Core training hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged. The PDFs alone do not establish whether the linked resources are actually available.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation from SDXL-generated representations to zero-shot transfer on SD3.5 and FLUX.1 [dev] trajectories, testing substantially different latent input distributions (Section 5.4). The two caption benchmarks remain, and renaming factual consistency as latent-to-text retrieval does not introduce another task.

E2.justification: LatentCLIP-8 and LatentCLIP-4-plus become evaluated comparators in the main Best-of-N experiments and Appendix C tables. LatentCLIP also enters qualitative comparisons. v1 cited LatentCLIP but evaluated primarily frozen CLIP and SigLIP, so this materially strengthens comparator coverage.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a blind preference protocol using 100 randomly sampled GenAI-Bench Basic image pairs, comparing selections at latent step 20 and excluding strict ties (Appendix C.3). New DiT experiments use zero-shot evaluation, VAE decoding, and shorter generation schedules, including 28 steps. Existing SDXL training and benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 adds tests of robustness to changing the generating architecture, and Appendix C.3 independently checks automatic evaluation through human preferences. Appendix F expands and revises failure examples with LatentCLIP. Training-range, encoder-training, and model-size ablations already existed in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: The new human study reports inter-rater agreement, κ = 0.724, adding a statistical reliability assessment absent from v1. Neither version reports confidence intervals or repeated-training-run variability; the revision does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: v2 adds LatentCLIP scores, DiT alignment-versus-cost curves, and 61.3% human preference for NoisyCLIP among non-tied trials. Existing Table 1 and encoder-ablation scores remain unchanged. It also replaces some qualitative selections and removes the dedicated latent-30 Best-of-N panel and Appendix C average-gap columns.

M1.justification: The contrastive objective, frozen text encoder, and training interval 20–29 remain unchanged. v2 adds an inference adaptation for DiT inputs: model-specific VAE decoding replaces the linear latent-to-RGB conversion used for SDXL (Section 4.5).

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around three challenges, and the results narrative is reorganized. Factual consistency becomes latent-to-text retrieval within alignment analysis, while training-range analysis moves ahead of Best-of-N and backbone discussion becomes generalization analysis.

P2.justification: v2 changes from two-column to single-column layout, extends Figure 1 with an early-stopping schematic, redesigns alignment plots, adds DiT plots and LatentCLIP rows, and expands qualitative grids. The combined appendix benchmark table becomes separate Basic and Advanced tables, and the latent-30 Best-of-N panel is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to FLUX.1 Kontext, SANA 1.5, and b-CLIP. It sharpens positioning against the already-cited LatentCLIP by emphasizing early noisy-latent ranking rather than final-stage superiority. The related-work survey is otherwise largely retained.

T1.justification: The definition accompanying Equation 3 relaxes Φ from a linear transformation to a general transformation, consistent with the added VAE decoding. Equations 1–3 otherwise retain their mathematical form, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing v1's missing latent-specialized comparison and SDXL-only, automatic evaluation through LatentCLIP tests, cross-architecture transfer, and human preferences. These additions make the central efficiency argument more credible. The stronger abstract overstates the retained SDXL results, which still report a small drop against full-cost CLIP, and the human study lacks annotator counts and uncertainty estimates. These shortcomings limit, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential gains.

C1.justification: The contribution list expands from one benchmark to two, making prompt-camera entanglement evaluation an explicit contribution. v1's conclusion claims the first absolute camera-control method for text-to-video; v2 drops that priority claim and positions the contribution around extreme and full-360-degree rotations. Gravity alignment and null-pitch conditioning remain central.

C2.justification: v1 attributes reduced CLIP and visual-quality scores primarily to training-data differences. v2 develops a substantive alternative interpretation: prompt-based CLIP can penalize correct camera views when requested content should be outside the frame. It also explains why null-pitch captions can induce capture artifacts and qualifies GEN3C comparisons because that method cannot generate scene motion.

D1.justification: v2 documents resolution and pose-quality filtering, retention of 4,798 of 7,797 training videos, 720-by-480 sampling, and variable prompt lengths. It adds camera-encoder initialization, AdamW settings, and a one-day training duration on eight H200 GPUs, replacing v1's four-A100 training description. Both still defer some implementation details to unavailable supplementary material.

E1.justification: v2 adds PolyHaven panorama evaluation with viewpoint-specific reference content for prompt-camera disambiguation, alongside the retained SpatialVID-extreme video benchmark. The reported training source changes from WEB360 to a filtered PanoVid YouTube subset. Figure 2 also introduces a full-rotation, return-to-start test scenario.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UCPE and PreciseCam+GEN3C while retaining both AC3D variants and PreciseCam+WAN. The SpatialVID qualitative comparison replaces PreciseCam+WAN with PreciseCam+GEN3C and adds UCPE. UCPE also joins the prompt-camera entanglement comparison in Figure 6.

E3.justification: The reported training setup changes from a 2B backbone trained for approximately 8,000 iterations to a 5B backbone jointly finetuned for 30,000 iterations. SpatialVID evaluation now specifies ViPE-derived metric translations instead of reusing original translations. The new entanglement protocol evaluates 20 panoramas at 19 static pitches and computes CLIP against pitch-specific reference captions.

E4.justification: The existing null-pitch ablation is retained under the revised setup and incorporated into Table 1. Section 4.6 adds a systematic pitch-sensitivity analysis testing prompt-camera conflicts across 380 conditions, extending v1's qualitative illustration. Figure 2 adds a full-rotation case study comparing trajectory adherence and return-view consistency.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars for the experimental results. The new aggregate curves in Figure 6 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical results for the proposed method and retained baselines, and adds comparator results. Reported pitch/gravity errors for Ours change from 23.79/27.06 to 9.35/11.67 under changed training and method conditions, not a controlled same-setting comparison. Unlike v1's ablation, v2 shows that null-pitch conditioning improves camera metrics but worsens CLIP, FID, and FVD relative to its ablated model. Figure 6 adds pitch-dependent findings.

M1.justification: The main model changes from CogVideoX-2B with an AC3D-style ControlNet to WAN-2.2 5B with a convolutional camera encoder and joint backbone finetuning. Section 3.2 adds gravity estimation from eight perspective views and changes pose composition. Section 3.3 adds downward-view captions and negative-prompt guidance to suppress tripods and other capture artifacts.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around extreme rotations and two evaluation goals. Related-work explanations are expanded and reorganized, gravity annotation precedes path sampling, and experimental exposition is reworked. The separate discussion and conclusion sections are merged into Section 5.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the teaser and reference-matching examples, redraws the pipeline, and replaces Euler-angle plots in the training examples with spatial camera trajectories. It redesigns the qualitative comparisons and expands Figure 6 into qualitative and quantitative panels. The ablation table is merged into a grouped Table 1; v1's distribution plot is absent from the supplied v2 pages.

R1.justification: Section 2 introduces UCPE as a concurrent gravity-aware alternative and substantially expands positioning against panoramic video generation and static novel-view synthesis. New discussions include GEN3C, ViewCrafter, PanoWAN, and PanFlow, with arguments about rotation diversity, cropped resolution, prompt visibility, and translation control. This changes the novelty argument beyond adding citations.

T1.justification: Equation (2) substantively revises the absolute-pose construction by introducing gravity alignment through psi and separate translation and rotation expressions. This is a focused change to the mathematical definition of pose composition; neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap by adding a controlled test of prompt-camera entanglement across pitches, beyond v1's general ablation and illustrative example. View-specific reference captions address a concrete metric mismatch, while UCPE provides a directly relevant gravity-aware comparator. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. Changed backbones and data prevent controlled cross-version performance claims, and centered CLIP curves and visual-quality tradeoffs limit stronger conclusions, but the gains in mechanism testing and comparison relevance substantially improve the paper.

Losing explicit optimizer, training-budget and hardware details weakens reproducibility in the supplied v3, but the stronger experimental controls provide a substantial net improvement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning ignored global illumination and wavy normals causing specular effects to enter albedo. It explains diffusion's artifact suppression and limited hallucination under late activation. The dense-view discussion replaces v1's segmentation-versus-fine-roughness tradeoff with an explanation involving Ref-Gaussian's appearance fitting and continued densification.
