C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the claimed empirical applicability to feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction and emphasize integration into generic multi-view models. The central contribution—ray-based positional encoding satisfying the four stated desiderata—and the existing performance claims remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix B explains why the TokenGS latent-query adaptation uses global coordinates and does not preserve SE(3) invariance. Section 5.3 also newly interprets the retained EscherNet results as evidence that depth predictions tolerate diffusion noise. The limitations concerning uncertain cameras and unposed inputs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds TokenGS configuration and training details and newly discloses EscherNet's three training reference views, 70K iterations, and batch size 32. Conversely, v3 omits v2's three-corner-ray implementation note and RTX A6000 runtime-profiling disclosure. These omissions do not establish actual implementation or hardware changes; the project-page access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction through TokenGS, substantially extending task coverage beyond image synthesis and stereo-depth estimation. DL3DV-10K was already used for EscherNet in v2; the addition concerns reconstruction of an explicit scene representation, not a previously unused dataset. Earlier coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 Table 5 introduces original TokenGS as an evaluated comparator, alongside a PRoPE adaptation using the same latent-query treatment. Comparator membership in the retained LVSM, EscherNet, UniMatch, and runtime comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: The added TokenGS experiment introduces a distinct protocol: training with four views, 150K iterations at 256×256 with 1024 Gaussian tokens, then 10K iterations at 256×448 with 4096 tokens, followed by evaluation with 2, 4, and 6 views and test-time tuning. These are settings for a new experiment; existing evaluation protocols are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: v3 Table 2 extends the four existing component ablations to Objaverse; v2 Table 4 reported only CO3D and RE10K. The questions tested remain uncertainty modeling, depth adaptiveness, multiple frequencies, and value/output encoding. Existing depth, attention-similarity, pose-variation, and generalization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Section 5.1 newly states that models are trained with three random seeds and mean results are reported, except for the large-scale experiments. v2 provides no corresponding run-count statement. This is newly disclosed statistical reporting, not evidence that the number of runs increased; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v3 adds quantitative and qualitative results for the new reconstruction task (Table 5 and Figure 9). With four input views, TokenGS PSNR is 22.85 for the original model, 23.04 with PRoPE, and 23.40 with RayRoPE. It also adds Objaverse ablation scores, including PSNR 20.37 without uncertainty versus 22.42 for full RayRoPE. Matched performance tables from v2 retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: The core RayRoPE procedure remains unchanged. However, the new TokenGS adaptation in v3 Section 5.3 and Appendix B changes latent-query cross-attention: it skips query-frame projection and applies ray encoding only to image features in global coordinates because the Gaussian query tokens lack explicit positions.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: runtime discussion moves from the appendix into Section 4.4, known-depth material is consolidated with analysis, and stereo depth and EscherNet join TokenGS under Broader Applications. The introduction gains an explicit contribution list, and prose and captions are revised throughout.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, restructures the ablation, depth, and known-depth tables, and extensively relocates figures. v3 Figure 3 combines the attention diagram with runtime curves while omitting the separate three-view timing bars. A new TokenGS table and qualitative figure are added; other qualitative images and generalization plots are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references for TokenGS, Gaussian Splatting, acceleration, and camera-control methods such as ReRoPE. Section 2 qualifies the comparison with Positional Encoding Field as lacking exploration beyond two views. Unified Camera Positional Encoding and LLaVA-3D citations are removed, while the central positioning against CaPE, GTA, and PRoPE remains.

T1.justification: The attention equations, uniform-distribution assumption, expected-RoPE derivation, and Appendix A.2 proof retain their mathematical substance. Section 4.2 rewrites projection using lifted 4×4 matrices and normalized homogeneous coordinates, yielding the same six-dimensional representation; this is an equivalent reformulation.

improvement.justification: The TokenGS study adds useful evidence of transfer to latent 3D representations, while Objaverse ablations strengthen support for the design choices. Newly disclosed seed counts and training settings improve transparency. These are incremental gains over v2's already broad evaluation, partly offset by losing the corner-ray implementation note and runtime-hardware specification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RayRoPE work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds TokenGS reconstruction experiments and Objaverse ablation results.

before.justification: v2 reports original LVSM and EscherNet novel-view synthesis experiments, UniMatch stereo-depth experiments, ablations, generalization tests, and runtime measurements.

C1.justification: V2 adds downstream robot trajectory planning as an explicit contribution and extends the painting-generalization claim to manipulation. The abstract's maximum SCS improvement is corrected from 80% to 65%, consistent with the retained Table 1 values. The central claims of architecture-independent conditioning and appearance-independent structural evaluation remain.

C2.justification: V2 interprets its ablations as evidence that temporal alignment improves control and better preserves pretrained priors. It adds arguments for automated and long-horizon SCS applicability, explains modest planning gains through the restrictive trajectory prior, and proposes policy-evaluation use. The failure discussion retains object-permanence and structural problems but removes v1's specific attribution of Cosmos painting collapse to its pretraining distribution.

D1.justification: V2 adds Wan learning rates and bfloat16/float32 precision details, together with planning and automated-segmentation instructions. It removes v1's backbone-specific sinusoidal-versus-MLP encoding description and the eight-day training-time/100-hour dataset disclosure. Existing hardware, learning rates, strides, resolutions, and chunk lengths largely survive, sometimes relocated.

E1.justification: The four principal datasets remain RECON, SCAND, TartanDrive, and 1X. V2 substantially extends task coverage to goal-conditioned navigation planning and held-out humanoid manipulation planning, and extends painting-domain demonstrations from navigation to object manipulation. DROID and Panda-70M are cited context, not newly evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds evaluated global-conditioning and chunked-conditioning Cosmos variants, plus an SVD cross-attention comparator based on Ctrl-World. These substantially broaden comparisons of the central conditioning mechanism. NWM and the SVD-from-scratch comparator remain; Wan is an additional EgoWM backbone.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 14B Wan configuration, SCAND-only training for transfer evaluation on RECON, 64-frame testing on sufficiently long trajectories, and automated SAM3-based SCS. Planning adds 120 navigation candidates, ATE, validation/test partitioning, and human-rated manipulation success. Section 5 newly states 4 FPS while Appendix E retains 5 FPS, leaving the actual evaluation frame rate unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scratch-training comparison and qualitative SCS/failure examples, v2 adds conditioning-design ablations and cross-domain generalization analysis in Table 3. Appendices B–C add quantitative tracking robustness under Gaussian noise, manual-versus-automatic SCS comparisons, visibility attrition, and action-consistency analysis through 64 frames. The original appendix illustrations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional success rates and robustness scores do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing numerical rows in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. V2 adds Wan scores, conditioning ablations, planning results, and Tables 6–9. Examples include navigation-planning ATE of 3.25 for NWM, 3.18 for SVD, and 3.13 for Cosmos, and 64-frame navigation SCS of 0.15, 0.41, and 0.33 for NWM, SVD, and Wan. V1's shorter-horizon latency plot entries disappear; its 64-frame table values remain.

M1.justification: The core action projection, temporal downsampling, timestep modulation, initial-state conditioning, and training objective remain unchanged. Section 6 adds a CEM planning procedure that samples actions, scores predicted terminal frames against a goal image, and selects trajectories. The Wan experiments reuse the existing conditioning recipe.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanation are substantially rewritten to foreground temporal compression and precise control, with revised related-work and failure-mode prose. The experimental narrative is reorganized around dedicated ablation and planning sections, and the appendix changes from three sections to six, separating qualitative results, metric analysis, long horizons, compute, implementation, and failures.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting with extensive resizing and reflow. V2 adds seven tables, expands Figure 4 with Wan, and replaces the painting visualization. V1's latency plot and campus-generalization figure are removed. Its compute table and appendix illustrations remain as v2 Table 10 and Figures 7–8.

R1.justification: Seven references are added, including DreamDojo, SAM3, DROID, and Panda-70M. Comparisons with GrndCtrl, IRASim, and Ctrl-World become more specific about conditioning precision and temporal compression. These refine the existing positioning around adapting pretrained video models; publication and bibliography-format updates do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same diffusion objective, conditioning operations, and mean mask-IoU definition of SCS. Temporal alignment receives clearer explanation, but no new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced.

improvement.justification: The conditioning ablations, third backbone, and quantitative SCS and long-horizon tests substantially strengthen central claims that v1 supported mainly through benchmark comparisons and qualitative examples. Correcting the 80% headline to 65% also improves accuracy. These benefits outweigh removed implementation details and reporting inconsistencies, including conflicting FPS statements and the miscomputed relative gain in Section 5.3. Planning supplies additional preliminary evidence, although manipulation success is assessed within generated rollouts rather than physical execution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EgoWM and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, references, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds Wan experiments, conditioning ablations, planning evaluations, metric validation, and long-horizon prediction results.

before.justification: V1 reports original navigation and humanoid manipulation experiments, including LPIPS, DreamSim, and SCS results in Tables 1–2, a training-from-scratch comparison, and latency measurements.

C1.justification: The central shortcut diagnosis remains, but the methodological contribution is redefined around CPR's synthesized supervision and hard-negative regularization plus TORC. V2 extends its principal effectiveness claim to multiple VLM backbones. The abstract's earlier assertion of consistently positive compositional gaps is dropped, and the diagnosis is framed as a key failure mode rather than the primary explanation for failure.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies CG as a supporting diagnostic rather than a standalone criterion, explicitly discusses seen–unseen performance trade-offs, and explains why full-space training can suppress unseen classes. It adds interpretations concerning persistent shortcuts after video pretraining and zero optimal calibration bias, plus a substantive rationale for restricting the study to encoder-based VLM interfaces.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds InternVideo2 adaptation and frame-level pooling details, backbone-specific input lengths and hyperparameters, and model-selection information. Training schedules, augmentation strengths, and margin parameters are revised or expanded relative to v1 Appendix B.2. V2 also removes v1's explicit code-availability statement and repository link; this does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions use Sth-com and EK100-com, the same controlled 10-by-10 and biased 4-by-4 subsets, and the same original and reconstructed Temporal/Static scenarios. Dataset construction and reported split counts are retained. Added backbones and metrics do not expand data or task coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator suite loses several distinct controls: C2C without conditioning disappears from the Sth-com comparisons, CutMix disappears from augmentation comparisons, and L-softmax disappears from margin-loss comparisons. V2 adds independently trained InternVideo2+LoRA comparison rows. C2C, AIM, Jung et al., and Mixup remain in their relevant comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported CLIP training increases from 30 to 40 epochs; new InternVideo2 configurations use eight-frame inputs and 40–50 epochs. Augmentation and loss schedules change substantially. V2 specifies primitive accuracies from joint top-1 composition predictions instead of v1's separate component logits, revises FCP normalization, and adds macro-CG evaluation. These are reported setting changes, not proof that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds verb/object/dual-collapse analyses, macro-CG checks for class imbalance, CPR label-space and penalty-set ablations, and backbone-size analysis. It removes v1's confidence-distribution study and top-K margin sweep. Random-initialization, temporal-reversal, failure-case, and Temporal/Static analyses remain, with several relocated rather than newly introduced.

These substantially expand validation beyond v1's retained layer/head and Gram-alignment analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds significance reporting for the cross-model association and supplementary analyses, subject-level dispersion statistics, and the noise ceiling's standard deviation of 0.037. The existing 10 seeds per fold and 20 subject splits remain unchanged; no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Table 1's grouping accuracies and the main plotted results are retained, but substantial supplementary findings are added. These include linear-readout association r=0.917, condition-specific correlations, raw model–human correlations, and behavioral sensitivity/bias results. CLS distillation yields 0.59→0.59 and 0.59→0.58 for the two ViTs, compared with Gram alignment's 0.59→0.72 and 0.59→0.70. These are additional comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed patch-feature readout, object-centricity analysis, and Gram-alignment procedure are retained. Section 6.2 newly documents architecture and training details without establishing a changed method; linear readout and CLS distillation are additional comparison methods.

Human correlations cover only 11 aggregate entities without uncertainty for comparative superiority, and estimator tests exclude nuScenes; these constrain the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds geometry-estimator robustness experiments and a blinded human study with 1,050 judgments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 1,296 videos, controlled geometric perturbations, component ablations, motion analyses, PCA cross-validation, and segmentation-sensitivity experiments.

C1.justification: The introduction adds an explicit priority claim that Em-Garde is the first proactive streaming framework to decompose triggering into query-time proposal generation and streaming-time matching. The abstract, conclusion, and principal accuracy and efficiency claims otherwise retain their scope.

C2.justification: v2 attributes the component gains to the propose-match decomposition rather than model capacity, and explains threshold robustness through similarity changes and RL adaptation. It newly emphasizes stability across lambda values from 0.5 to 1, while removing the earlier task-specific threshold interpretation. The limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.5.1 newly specifies how the controls are constructed: Qwen2.5VL-7B for prompt rewriting, Qwen2VL-2B for yes/no decisions, and the query plus a two-second segment for the sliding-window baseline. Existing training hardware, training times, dataset-generation prompts, and code-access information are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use Parse2Prop-1K drawn from COIN, Ego4D, and BEHAVIOR, and evaluate the same StreamingBench, OVO-Bench, and ProactiveVideoQA tasks. The additional ablations introduce no new datasets, domains, or task scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds direct prompt-rewriting and yes/no decision replacements, their combined variant, and a naive sliding-window comparator. The comparison methods in the existing benchmark tables, including the appendix tables, are unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled component-replacement experiments and explicitly crosses training and testing thresholds of 0.03, 0.035, and 0.04. It also adds lambda = 0.75 to the reward sweep. These extend the experimental settings; the primary setup, metrics, and default threshold remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands component validation by testing removal or replacement of IGPP, LPMM, and both together, plus a sliding-window control. It replaces the per-task threshold precision-recall analysis with a training/testing threshold grid and extends the reward sweep. The existing qualitative SFT-versus-RL analysis is retained in Appendix B.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for these experiments. The added results retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Headline benchmark results remain unchanged. New diagnostic results include 24.0/28.8 without IGPP and 14.6/23.2 without LPMM in v2 Table 5, expressed as OVO-Bench F1/StreamingBench accuracy. Table 6 reports threshold-grid F1 values of 26.59-30.99, and Table 7 adds 28.6/36.4 at lambda = 0.75. The per-task precision-recall points in v1 Figure 5 are removed.

M1.justification: The IGPP proposer, SFT/GRPO training, LPMM embedding matcher, similarity-change triggering rule, and visual encoding cache remain unchanged. The component replacements introduced in v2 are experimental controls, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Section 4.5 is locally rewritten and reordered, and its proposal-quality discussion moves into Appendix B.4. v2 also adds acknowledgements and author asterisks. Most prose and the overall section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds component-ablation and threshold-grid tables, extends the reward table, and removes v1's precision-recall Figure 5. The proposal-quality Figure 4 moves to the appendix and is enlarged as Figure 7. Other tables and figures are largely retained with relocation, renumbering, and page reflow.

R1.justification: The new explicit first-framework claim strengthens the paper's novelty positioning. The related-work discussion and cited-work membership otherwise remain unchanged; the bibliographies contain the same works.

T1.justification: The mathematical problem formulation, proposal and matching definitions, reward function, triggering rule, and recall/precision equations are unchanged. No formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added or removed.

improvement.justification: The component controls and training/testing threshold grid strengthen evidence for the decomposition and its robustness. These are useful, limited gains, tempered by losing task-specific precision-recall diagnostics and a new prose mismatch: Section 4.5.1 says removing both modules performs worse, although Table 5 reports OVO-Bench F1 of 18.6 versus 14.6 when removing LPMM alone.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: order marginalization improves AR classification, surpasses diffusion classifiers with up to 25-fold faster inference, and competes with DINOv2. The additions provide supporting evidence without changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization beyond RandAR and practical differences between equivalent-in-expectation scoring objectives. Appendix H hypothesizes that perceptual fidelity increasingly dominates FID at low values, while Appendix I distinguishes fast generation from fast classification. Existing error explanations and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies sources for the MaskGIT-B checkpoint and COCO-to-ImageNet mapping, documents disabling RAR order annealing, and makes the WILDS tokenizer description consistent with Appendix A. The original core training schedules, hardware disclosure and code/model access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds ObjectNet and COCO evaluation while retaining the earlier ImageNet and WILDS coverage. These introduce non-image-centric object views and multi-object recognition, with COCO requiring recovery of multiple ImageNet-mapped objects rather than one class.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds comparisons involving adapted RAR-B, MaskGIT-B and RandAR scored as masked diffusion. The WILDS comparison adds raster-order RandAR at both model sizes. Appendix I additionally evaluates three MeanFlow classifier variants against DiT, substantially expanding the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include B-scale AR/MD comparisons with evaluation-budget sweeps through K=60, COCO-to-ImageNet mapping with K-recall@K, and three MeanFlow scoring strategies. The WILDS tokenizer statement changes from MaskGIT to LlamaGen with noise, matching the existing Appendix A; this correction does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds architecture generalization through RAR, AR-versus-MD scoring sensitivity to computation, an XL no-noise ablation, raster-order controls on WILDS, and generation-quality versus classification analysis. Appendix I also tests whether few-step generation translates into efficient classification. These substantially extend v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed averaging for the WILDS discriminative baselines. v2 introduces no additional repeated-run disclosures, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practices. The new evaluation-budget sweeps concern scoring procedures rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises the relabelled A-VARC+ rows: ImageNet-Val scores change from 0.683 to 0.717 for L and 0.661 to 0.719 for XL; RandAR's main scores remain unchanged. Substantial new results cover RAR/MD, XL augmentation, WILDS raster controls, ObjectNet/COCO, generation FID and MeanFlow. Table 12 places RandAR above DiT but below DINOv2 on both added datasets.

M1.justification: The central RandAR classifier and Equation (5) remain unchanged. Section 6.6 adds an adaptation of RAR trained without order annealing, and Section 6.7 introduces alternative masked-prefix scoring of RandAR. These extend the procedures without replacing the core method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the narrative sequence are retained. v2 inserts Sections 6.6–6.7 and several appendix sections, introduces AO-AR terminology, adds the HSE affiliation and corrects names such as ResNet-151 to ResNet-152. These are localized additions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds the paired B-scale/MD tables, ObjectNet/COCO and FID tables, and a MeanFlow runtime plot. Table 4 gains model-size groups and the WILDS table gains raster rows. These substantially expand the visual evidence; the earlier qualitative Figure 9 is retained as Figure 10. Page margins also increase throughout.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly connects its objective to masked-diffusion research and extends the efficiency discussion to contemporary few-step diffusion methods. These relationships, supported by new any-order/diffusion and MeanFlow/distillation citations, substantially broaden the research positioning beyond v1's discussion. Existing cited works are retained.

T1.justification: Unlike v1, Appendix D derives a claimed equivalence between the order-averaged AR objective and a masked-diffusion ELBO using expectations over masked subsets. This is a substantive theoretical addition. As written, Equation (6) introduces a 1/N normalization inconsistent with the earlier full-sequence likelihood definition.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in support for generality and efficiency through another AR architecture, WILDS raster controls, multi-object/non-image-centric evaluation and MeanFlow comparisons. These strengthen the central argument while documenting DINOv2's remaining advantages, and the WILDS tokenizer correction improves consistency. Equation (6)'s normalization problem weakens the theoretical addition, but the broader empirical validation provides a substantial overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same order-marginalized generative classification study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds RAR, masked-diffusion, ObjectNet/COCO and MeanFlow evaluations, among other analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier training, ImageNet and WILDS evaluations, token-order experiments, tokenizer ablations and runtime measurements.

These improve documentation without establishing implementation or experimental changes. Optimizer settings, GPU hardware and project-access information remain unchanged.

Other documented settings remain stable, including training hyperparameters, voxelization resolution and F-score threshold. Table 3's new 'fixed random subset' description is additional disclosure, not evidence of a changed split or rerun.

E4.justification: Removing the Text+Image ablation reduces evidence isolating the benefit of relational inputs when text and image are already supplied. Component, token-count, parser, rare-part and held-out-relation analyses otherwise remain; their relocation does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Both describe 20 annotation-audit repetitions with 200 triplets per repetition. Neither introduces generation-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 3 and the conditioning table exchange CD/EMD assignments; for example, Table 3's full-model pair changes from 0.771/0.145 to 0.145/0.771. These are reporting revisions, not demonstrated performance gains; most results and rankings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The DPL/RSL architecture, synchronization updates, diffusion objectives, inference procedure, and application procedures remain unchanged. Newly specifying that fusion coefficients are learnable documents an existing component without establishing a procedural change.

P1.justification: Most prose is retained with localized clarification and correction. Qualitative and quantitative ablation discussions are reordered, dataset and implementation appendices exchange order, inference efficiency moves into the main text, and acknowledgments are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column design to a single-column format, with pervasive changes to typography, headings, figure/table sizing and placement, and text wrapping around displays. Appendix timing Table 10 becomes main-text Table 4. Existing illustrations are retained with caption and label edits.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds AutoPartGen, FullPart, PARIS3D and PartSLIP, while removing five earlier citations, including DreamBooth3D and PALM. It more explicitly distinguishes vision-language-based part perception from generation. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–6 retain the same substance. Explicitly describing global tokens as non-diffusion variables clarifies the previously documented deterministic update; no theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the unsupported ST-alone superiority interpretation and replaces the 53%/33% headline with 60%/41%, consistent with approximately 59.8%/40.7% mean reductions calculated from unchanged Table 1. These repairs modestly improve accuracy. The benefit is limited by unexplained KID rescaling and removal of the useful Text+Image control; there is no substantive expansion of empirical evidence.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint stochastic recovery from a single image with known geometry, four architectural components, complementary information across objects, and ambiguity-aware evaluation. Renaming scheduling and adding supporting experiments do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds discussion of the no-cross-talk limitation and a prospective material-patch extension. It also interprets scheduling and attention as suppressing non-shared global-illumination signals and attributes DPI's FID/NIQE trade-off to hallucinated detail. The existing known-geometry and near-field-lighting limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies rendering and latent resolutions, the 80% triplet probability, object arrangements and rotations, and 50-step single-pass texture refinement. Appendix D identifies the MegaPose variant and perspective rendering. The runtime disclosure and project-access link are updated. These are additional implementation disclosures, without evidence that the underlying training procedure changed.

E1.justification: The training sources, synthetic datasets, Stanford-ORB, nLMVS, and captured MultiGP dataset remain the same. The GI-off inputs in v2 Tables 1–2 introduce a limited additional lighting condition. Stanford-ORB texture estimation was already evaluated qualitatively in v1, so its new numerical scores do not introduce another task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds StableNormal-assisted DRM alongside the retained Marigold-assisted DRM comparison, with corresponding MultiGP variants. The principal baseline sets remain intact. IID was already evaluated in v1 Table 5; its additional mean-of-10 row is not a new method.

E3.justification: v2 adds FID/NIQE evaluation, runtime comparisons on one A100 for 1024×1024 inputs, and GI-off controls. The normal-noise sweep extends from a maximum standard deviation of 0.15 to 0.35, corresponding to 25.13° angular error. Existing splits and principal accuracy protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The diagnostic evidence expands substantially: Tables 1–2 test removal of global illumination and extend texture-refinement ablation to illumination and reflectance; Appendix H adds stronger normal corruption and StableNormal-based robustness tests. New Appendix J investigates perceptual-quality differences and includes a visual case of scene-inconsistent DPI details. Existing component, diversity, and fewer-object analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 6 adds an IID mean-of-10 summary alongside the retained result under the general top-three-of-ten protocol, introducing an alternative sample aggregation. This does not establish additional runs or seeds. The existing sampling counts and distribution analyses remain unchanged, with no new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover real texture accuracy, GI/refinement ablations, robustness, runtime, and perceptual quality. For example, v2 Table 5 reports Stanford-ORB texture RMSE of 0.0255 for MultiGP versus 0.0441 for DPI; Table 8 favors DPI on FID but MultiGP on NIQE. Existing matched accuracy entries remain unchanged. Reported pipeline runtime changes from 28.4 to 25.3 seconds, but v1 does not specify the input resolution, preventing a verified same-setting speedup claim.

M1.justification: The texture-extraction cascade, reflectance-map diffusion, scheduling, attention, ControlNet refinement, and losses remain unchanged. Coordinated Guidance becomes Coordinated Scheduling, while new implementation explanations do not establish a procedural change. The material-patch extension in the conclusion is prospective.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and typo corrections, changes scheduling terminology, expands explanatory passages, renames Appendix B to include inference, and adds Appendix J. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds training examples in Figure 9, a DPI comparison in Figure 16, and new Tables 5 and 8. Several existing tables gain rows, and retained figures and tables move or receive new numbers. These are localized display additions and layout adjustments rather than a document-wide visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds the StableNormal citation and its experimental role. Appendix J further positions MultiGP against DPI's panorama prior, while related work adds regression-to-the-mean as an explanation for smooth predictions. The broader research positioning remains intact; reference renumbering and access-date additions are bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, scheduling equations, losses, and Appendix A derivation remain unchanged. Added descriptions of the rendering operator, residual expectation, and model assumptions clarify existing mathematics rather than introducing new definitions or proofs.

improvement.justification: The added GI controls, stronger geometry tests, and concrete training/inference details improve scrutiny of the method's physical assumptions and reproducibility. New texture and runtime comparisons also strengthen the supporting evidence. The gains are limited by noisy texture pseudo-ground-truth and Appendix J's inference of scene-specific hallucination from FID/NIQE, which those metrics alone do not establish. Overall, v2 modestly strengthens the existing paper without changing its core method or established benchmark results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MultiGP research work. All 24 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison. Equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite relocation and renumbering.

C2.justification: v2 adds a World-Action Models interpretation and explicitly acknowledges Ross3D's stronger QA scores while emphasizing VEGA-3D's grounding performance. Omission of Appendices E–F removes qualifications about fine-grained instance confusion, manually chosen extraction settings and indoor-centered validation. D1.justification: v2 loses Algorithm 1, detailed training-data mixtures, per-backbone resolutions/tokenization and feature stages, and correspondence preprocessing details, including depth handling and coordinate alignment. This introduces a materially different deployment environment, although coverage is limited to one real-robot task. The five scene-understanding benchmarks, VSI-Bench and four LIBERO suites remain.

E3.justification: The new Click Bell experiment introduces a RoboTwin-based physical-robot evaluation with 20 trials per policy and success-rate reporting. Existing benchmark settings, including 32 sampled frames, timestep 300, layer 20 and batch size 128, remain unchanged. Missing supplementary settings do not establish changes to those experiments.

Tables A3 and A5 also supplied multi-metric ablation evidence beyond the ScanRefer curve retained in Figure 6. Main backbone, fusion and Wan2.1 noise/depth analyses remain, but supplementary diagnostic coverage is substantially reduced.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix C.1 specifies calculating correspondence-score means and standard deviations over valid scenes; this statistical aggregation/reporting description is absent from v2. Neither version provides training-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new robot trial counts describe evaluation sample size, not repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Retained VEGA-3D benchmark scores are unchanged. Table 1 adds Ross3D/Omni-View results and recomputes average ranks, including VEGA-3D's 1.8 to 2.2 under the expanded comparator set. v2 newly reports Click Bell success of 55% (11/20) versus 40% (8/20). It also loses substantial appendix-only results, including SEVA/Vmem sweeps, unplotted ablation metrics and qualitative success/failure outcomes.

M1.justification: The frozen video-diffusion feature extractor, noise injection, intermediate-layer extraction and adaptive gated fusion remain unchanged in Sections 3–4. v2 clarifies the existing VLA integration; neither this clarification nor omission of the supplementary training pseudocode establishes a procedural or architectural change.

P1.justification: The organized technical, implementation, scoring, probing, qualitative-results and limitations supplement disappears entirely. v2 also rewrites the video-generation related-work and manipulation discussions, adds World-Action Models and real-robot paragraphs, and adds acknowledgments and corresponding-author information. The principal main-text section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 omits supplementary Tables A1–A5, Figures 8–12 and the Algorithm 1 display. Table 1 gains two comparator rows, supervision markers and an expanded caption; Table 2 explicitly identifies its baseline. Main Figures 1–7 are retained, with several displays relocated through text reflow rather than replaced by new analyses.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces a broad contrast with generation/control work by explicit positioning against Ross3D, Omni-View, MILO, GaussianDWM, DyVA and JEPA-VLA. It emphasizes frozen feature extraction relative to auxiliary generation, geometric supervision and predictive world-model approaches. This substantially develops the closest-prior-work discussion; twelve cited works are added.

This reduces formal specification, particularly the normalization population, without establishing a changed underlying computation or adding new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 improves comparison with close prior work and adds a useful, limited real-robot experiment. Their omission substantially weakens reproducibility and scrutiny of the central evidence, while the retained benchmark performance is unchanged.

D1.justification: Filtering documentation explicitly identifies first-turn MCQA predictions, the six-of-22 cutoff, and the pool spanning ten model families. These clarify the existing procedure. E2.justification: Model membership is unchanged in the retained MCQA, single-turn open-ended, reference, and hinted comparisons. The new multi-turn experiment evaluates 12 models already represented in the existing suite; it introduces no new baseline method.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 adds a supplementary multi-turn open-ended protocol that maps inapplicable suggestions to random valid actions and measures trajectory accuracy and intervention rate. This replaces the earlier cross-format comparison using aggregate accuracy. The original evaluation settings remain.

E4.justification: v2 examines whether weak open-ended performance persists with multiple interaction turns. Appendix A.8 also adds a modeled recall comparison for filtering thresholds. Existing invalid-action, hint, history, few-shot, and reward analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.8 adds binomial-based recall estimates: 92.8% for the chosen filtering rule versus 37.6% for a binomial-test alternative at a 0.05 threshold, assuming 40% first-turn success. Neither version reports experimental confidence intervals or repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: The MCQA aggregate results in v1 Table 10 are removed and replaced by multi-turn open-ended results for 12 models. Qwen2.5-VL-7B leads the new comparison with 3.9% accuracy and 0.1 intervention rate. These are different-protocol results, not performance changes. Retained numerical tables and single-turn component scores are unchanged.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively retypeset with a narrower text block, different typography and headers, and widespread resizing and relocation of displays. Table 2 now separates category and suggestion scores, Figure 6c displays suggestion percentages instead of aggregate accuracy, and Table 10 presents a different experiment.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 72 works and retain the same positioning relative to MLLM benchmarks and active vision. Reference formatting and bibliographic metadata changes do not alter research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.8 introduces binomial-model reasoning under an assumed 40% success probability to justify the six-of-22 filtering cutoff. v1 supplied empirical filtering curves without this mathematical rationale. The MDP formulation and training reward rules remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Separating suggestion frequency from successful answering makes the findings easier to interpret, and the new multi-turn comparison adds relevant evidence. The gain is limited: core results are unchanged, the earlier MCQA aggregate comparison is removed, and the replacement relies on approximate action substitution. The added filtering rationale is also assumption-dependent.

The added transparency supports a net improvement, but conflicting quantitative reporting limits its overall strength.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments in Figure 5 and Tables 3–7 and additionally reports scene-level results and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original geometric-consistency measurements and experiments on aerial retrieval, cross-view matching and reconstruction in Figure 4 and Tables 2–6.

C1.justification: Both versions claim efficient, long-tail-aware training through cluster scaling and dynamic sampling, with competitive full-training performance at approximately 3% of training cost. v2 foregrounds cluster scaling and restates the existing diversity and upsampling rationale without changing the claims' substantive scope.

C2.justification: Appendix C extends the existing offline-cost discussion by explaining how combined embedding/clustering overhead becomes proportionally smaller as training scales and discussing potentially faster clustering. Earlier interpretations of long-tail benefits, retrieval shortcomings, and unusual frequency-performance cases are retained.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents sampling with replacement when the target cluster size exceeds its original size, details the greedy cosine-similarity merging rule, and reports a 0.25 GPU-hour merging cost. The code URL moves from an introduction footnote to the abstract; this does not establish newly available code.

E1.justification: Training datasets and classification, retrieval, long-tail, and robustness coverage are retained. Table 9's caption changes from 25 to 22 datasets, but both versions contain the same 22 dataset columns.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in corresponding experiments is unchanged, including DFN and reproduced DFN*, RECLIP, CLIPA, HQ-CLIP, and full-training baselines. Corrected citations do not introduce replacement methods. SuperKMeans is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New Table 17 evaluates seven fusion thresholds from 0.6 to 1.0 using DataComp, 106 million samples seen, ViT-B/16, and 112×112 images. Table 15 adds end-to-end GPU-hour totals and preprocessing/training overhead ratios. Existing experimental settings, including the default 0.7 threshold, are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a sensitivity study testing how centroid-fusion thresholds affect ImageNet accuracy and retained centroid counts. Appendix C additionally analyzes preprocessing overhead across training budgets. Earlier sampling, scaling-factor, cluster-count, batch-size, and robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The added results retain the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark-table scores are unchanged. New Table 17 reports, for example, 39.2% accuracy with 10,808 retained centroids at threshold 0.7 versus 34.9% with 50,000 at 1.0. New Table 15 gives totals of 119.25, 187.25, and 323.25 GPU-hours. Several prose summaries are corrected against unchanged tables: Section 6.2 now reports a 0.5-point margin over DFN* instead of 2.6 over DFN, and Section 6.5 corrects long-tail margins against OpenAI-WIT/OpenCLIP from 7.7/6.4 to 14.1/12.9 points.

M1.justification: Cluster scaling, epoch-wise sampling, centroid merging, and model architectures remain unchanged. The replacement-sampling statement and greedy-merging description clarify existing components; they do not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 corrects grammar, terminology, cross-references, and author affiliation/contact information. It reorders contribution bullets and explanatory paragraphs to discuss cluster scaling before dynamic sampling, while preserving the overall section structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds the cost-breakdown and fusion-threshold tables, relocates several existing tables, and revises captions. v1 Tables 15–17 correspond to v2 Tables 16, 18, and 19. Figures 1–3 retain their visual content; there is no broad graphical redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Reproducible Scaling Laws for Contrastive Language-Image Learning paper and SuperKMeans, while retaining the OpenCLIP software reference. T1.justification: Equations 1–2, scaling-factor cases, and assumptions about semantic embeddings are retained. Explaining the existing symbol N and correcting the cluster index clarify notation; no new theoretical result, derivation, or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reporting accuracy by correcting numerical summaries to match existing tables, makes implementation details clearer, and supplies evidence for the existing refinement threshold. The expanded cost breakdown makes preprocessing overhead easier to assess. These are useful, limited gains in correctness, reproducibility, and transparency; the central method and benchmark evidence remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central scientific claims: a shared RGB–event manifold, lightweight LoRA alignment, transfer of RGB-trained heads and state-of-the-art event feature matching. The additional experiments support these retained contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: V3 moderates the depth discussion from surpassing specialized architectures to competitive accuracy with lower decoder cost. It expands the existing resolution and temporal limitations by identifying tiling and memory holding as workarounds. It also states potential applicability beyond DUNE and interprets the new reconstruction and transfer results as broader latent-space generalization.

D1.justification: V3 adds reconstruction-head size and training-data quantity, hardware annotations for depth timing, and runtime settings. It consistently states code/model availability, replacing v1's mixed release-upon-acceptance wording while retaining the existing project address. S5.2 revises segmentation input width from 1024 to 768, although Table S8 retains 11,275 head parameters, leaving that specification unresolved. Most detailed training and preprocessing instructions were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V3 adds image reconstruction on VECtor and M3ED using a head trained on NYUv2. M3ED, previously used for distillation, also becomes an evaluation dataset for depth and segmentation under cross-dataset head transfer (S6). These extend task and domain coverage beyond the retained original benchmarks.

E2.justification: New Table 2 substantially extends the depth comparison with EReFormer, Depth AnyEvent and Depth Any Event Stream. These methods did not participate in v1's comparisons. The original depth, segmentation and matching comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V3 introduces extended depth metrics and efficiency comparisons, LoRA rank/module controls, a masking control and cross-dataset head-transfer protocols. The main-text learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 1e-3 and depth-head training from 100 to 300 epochs, matching settings already stated in v1's appendix rather than establishing reruns. The stated depth-bin interval changes from 1–81 m to 1.95–82 m. The new segmentation transfer protocol remains ambiguous: S6.2 names NYUv2 training, while Figure S5 names DSEC.

E4.justification: Tables S1–S2 add LoRA rank and attention-versus-feed-forward ablations and a quantitative masked-versus-unmasked comparison at rank 16. The latter supplements v1's qualitative masking analysis with downstream depth and segmentation measurements. S6 also adds cross-dataset generalization analysis; the earlier representation ablation and wide-viewpoint analyses are retained.

E5.justification: New Table S9 reports 1000 timing runs and mean times with ± values for the backbone and task heads. This is a separate experiment, not an increase to the retained 50-iteration matching benchmark. Neither version reports training-seed uncertainty or significance tests for the accuracy comparisons.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores and corresponding appendix results are retained; VECtor AUC fractions are simply converted to percentages. V3 adds extended depth and efficiency results, ablation outcomes, reconstruction examples and M3ED results. For example, Table S2 reports masked versus unmasked mIoU of 55.47 versus 53.97 and depth RMSE of 8.06 versus 8.42. Table S10 newly reports M3ED mIoU of 26.95 for REALM versus 24.08 for DUNE. These are additional comparisons, not improvements over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: V3 adds a 5M-parameter convolutional image-reconstruction head in S6.1. The core DUNE alignment encoder, LoRA adaptation, dual masking and losses remain unchanged. Existing head specifications are also revised, but the changed segmentation input width alongside unchanged parameter counts does not establish an actual architecture replacement.

P1.justification: V3 makes targeted prose edits, defines zero-shot explicitly, separates limitations from the conclusion, and adds appendix subsections for the new analyses. It also updates author/publication text and standardizes terminology and references. The main narrative and most existing paragraphs retain their structure.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the displayed evidence with an extended depth comparison, LoRA and masking tables, backbone/head timing and domain-transfer tables, plus reconstruction and M3ED segmentation panels. Existing figures and tables are largely retained with relocation and caption edits. The VECtor comparison is reformatted to display AUC percentages rather than fractions.

R1.justification: V3 adds the three recent depth-method references, NYUv2 and MegaDepth, and sharpens its positioning relative to distillation between other sensor modalities. The overall related-work organization and claimed relationship to DUNE remain stable. Reference deduplication and publication-detail updates do not constitute additional substantive changes.

T1.justification: The LoRA formulation, spatial dilation curriculum and loss equations retain their mathematical substance. Equation 1 makes summation limits and mask indexing/time dependence explicit, without introducing a different derivation or formal result. Neither version provides theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens support for its design choices through quantitative masking and LoRA ablations, updates depth comparisons, and presents a more measured accuracy–efficiency interpretation. It also reconciles the main-text learning rate and training duration with existing appendix details. These are clear benefits, but ambiguous training provenance in S6.2/Figure S5, the segmentation-width inconsistency and mixed-hardware latency comparisons limit the strength and reproducibility of the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REALM, with readable main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete supplementary materials. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds quantitative ablations, extended depth comparisons, reconstruction examples and cross-dataset evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original depth, segmentation and feature-matching experiments, alongside representation ablations, masking visualizations and runtime measurements.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a simple, scalable generative vision encoder with competitive performance and strong data efficiency. The revised abstract explicitly states 8B versus SigLIP2's 40B seen samples, quantifying an existing claim. The new diagnostics support the retained alignment rationale rather than redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4.4.2 and new Appendix E argue that pretrained language initialization can encourage language-side shortcuts and weaken visual grounding, whereas training from scratch promotes attention to visual evidence. This adds a substantive mechanism hypothesis and qualification on initialization benefits. v2 also softens the claim that ungated models 'fail' at discriminative tasks to substantially degraded performance; the existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1 identifies Recap-DataComp-1B and the 27M BLIP3o-Long-Caption/10M Infinity-MM mixture. v2 replaces this provenance with unmapped Dataset-S1/S2 labels in Section 3.3 and Table 1. Conversely, it adds exact frozen-evaluation resolutions, per-head gating specificity and implementation details for new comparisons. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish an actual training-data replacement.

E1.justification: The Cambrian-style evaluation adds knowledge, mathematical reasoning and perception coverage through MMMU, MathVista, MMVP, SEED-Image and CV-Bench2D/3D (v2 Tables 5 and 12). MMBench and RealWorldQA already appeared in v1's unfrozen evaluation. The unmapped Dataset-S1/S2 labels do not establish whether training-data coverage actually changed.

E2.justification: v1 discusses SAIL without experimentally comparing it. v2 Table 9 evaluates SAIL-style Qwen3-0.6B models with initialization and gating variants, while Table 10 adds one-register and four-register alternatives against gated attention. The comparator sets in the retained main evaluations are unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include projector-only versus projector-plus-LLM perplexity evaluation, matched 1B-sample initialization/register experiments, and attention-map analysis using 128×128 images, six prompt tokens and 30 generated tokens. Appendix aggregation is corrected from 15 to 14 benchmarks, matching the already stated main-text suite; this does not establish rerunning existing experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds objective-mismatch diagnostics, controlled tests of pretrained language initialization, and comparisons of gating against register tokens. Expanded Figure 3 and new Figures 10–11 investigate attention allocation and language-side sinks. Existing scaling, resolution-sensitivity and qualitative failure analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new layer-averaged attention curves are descriptive measurements, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark and ablation results. Table 9 reports 56.0 for scratch-trained SAIL-g versus 54.8 with initialization; Table 10 reports 56.3 for gating versus 55.1 with four registers. Table 8 adds captioning results and replaces subgroup averages with an overall average. Figure 3 replaces the earlier single attention curve with separate measurements. Retained headline tables are unchanged; the additions do not establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed GenLIP architecture, prefix-LM attention, MRoPE, autoregressive objective, gated attention and vision-feature extraction remain unchanged. Describing the gate as per-head adds implementation specificity without establishing a procedural change. The new SAIL and register-token variants are experimental comparisons.

P1.justification: The qualitative 'Let ViT Speak' section moves from Section 4.1 to 4.6, allowing setup and quantitative results to lead the experiments. Appendix sections are reorganized, and terminology, grammar, captions, conclusion wording and an author affiliation are edited. Most existing prose and the overall argument remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, 9, 10 and 12, appends a perplexity panel to Figure 1, expands Figure 3 into three panels, and introduces attention plots and heatmaps in Figures 10–11. The controlled VLP table gains captioning columns and changes its averages. Existing qualitative and scaling figures are relocated, while several tables receive revised layouts.

R1.justification: v2 extends the existing distinction from SAIL with an argument about initialization, adds benchmark citations and attention-sink alternatives such as DINOv3 and Systematic Outliers, and removes four training-data-related references. The broader positioning among contrastive, encoder-decoder and single-transformer approaches is retained.

T1.justification: The sequence definition, autoregressive loss and gating equations (1–3) are unchanged. The added language-prior discussion provides empirical interpretation, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The SAIL/register comparisons, broader benchmark coverage and attention analyses strengthen empirical support for important design choices. However, removing identifiable training datasets and mixture provenance materially weakens reproducibility and leaves continuity of the training data unresolved. The PDFs provide no mapping for Dataset-S1/S2, so the gains and this substantial reporting loss do not support a reliable net-quality judgment.

Together these substantially extend robustness and scaling analyses; the earlier component, projection-head, alignment-layer, and loss-weight ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without specifying repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The new tables follow the same reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables F.1 and G.1 add results for independent annotations and a large-model configuration. Table F.1 shows a mixed depth finding: M2-REPA's delta1 is 0.124 versus 0.127 for naive multi-expert REPA. Retained tables and plotted results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The GV coordinate construction, collinearity fallback, rotation loss in Equation 1 and appendix decoder/rotation equations are unchanged. No mathematical derivation, theorem or proof is added or removed.

improvement.justification: The project-page link and editorial corrections offer limited benefits, but deleting Section 4.3 removes useful qualifications about incomplete geometry and gravity-alignment generalization without evidence that these limitations were resolved. Appendix G preserves some failure discussion but does not replace those specific caveats. With the method and empirical evidence unchanged, this modestly reduces transparency about applicability.

E4.justification: The new text-only BAGEL control tests performance without visual evidence. Existing resolution, thought-modality, inference-mode, discrete-codebook, grayscale/depth, and qualitative failure analyses are retained, including v1 Tables 11–12 as v3 Tables 13–14.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing deterministic seeds for answer-choice shuffling are retained, and the new baseline table adds no uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 4 changes generated-image IPT accuracy on MVC from 63.1% to 67.3%, although Table 3 and Section 5.3 retain 63.1%. M1.justification: The BAGEL architecture, imaginative intermediates, flow-matching and language-modeling objectives, mixed training, and inference procedures are unchanged. The discrete-token alternatives in v3 Appendix G already appeared in v1 Section 11.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion receive limited rewriting, terminology is standardized, and author/affiliation information, keywords, and acknowledgements are updated. Appendix headings are relabeled and two sections inserted, while most exposition and narrative order are preserved.

P2.justification: The document changes from a dense two-column layout to a single-column format with running headers, different typography, extensively repositioned tables, and resized figures. Two appendix tables are added; the existing twelve figures and retained tables are redistributed and renumbered where necessary.

R1.justification: New Appendix C/Table 10 positions IPT against SpatialViz, SITE, OmniSpatial, SpatialScore, and MMSI through a feature comparison, emphasizing its combined training data, generation pipeline, thoughts, and framework. Four benchmark references are added; the main related-work discussion remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4 retains the same two-stage probabilistic formulation and training objectives. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: The added ThinkMorph/Show-o2 comparisons, human and nonvisual reference points, and benchmark feature comparison modestly improve assessment of effectiveness and novelty. These benefits are limited by sparse documentation of the new evaluations and the unreconciled MVC revision: Table 4 now reports 67.3%, while Table 3 and nearby explanations retain 63.1%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Imaginative Perception Tokens work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds human, text-only BAGEL, ThinkMorph, and Show-o2 baseline results in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original BAGEL fine-tuning experiments, spatial reasoning evaluations, transfer results, ablations, and appendix experiments with discrete tokens in Qwen2.5-VL.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that DLA bypasses the decode-encode loop, MESSy transfers auxiliary priors without harmful rigid feature matching, and image-only students exhibit synesthetic alignment without extra inference overhead. The new contribution list and title reorganize claims already present in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations attributing gains primarily to latent representations rather than resampling, and to auxiliary prediction targets rather than predictor architecture alone. It newly argues that handcrafted-feature alignment excludes label co-occurrence and interprets transfer results as evidence against capacity interference. The conclusion also identifies frozen generators as limiting task-specific latent co-adaptation.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies generator variants, four acoustic codebooks, eight-head resamplers, two-layer prediction heads, caption regeneration using class-name synonyms, and the weighted training objective. Section 4.1 adds 50-epoch teacher/student budgets, student training from scratch, AdamW, cosine scheduling, temperature 2.0, and loss weights. These substantially improve documentation without demonstrating that existing settings changed.

E1.justification: V2 retains Imagenette2-320, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100, while adding full ImageNet-1K classification and CIFAR-100 linear-probe transfer from ImageNet-100-trained students. These substantially expand class coverage and introduce evaluation on a different downstream population.

E2.justification: V2 adds the architecture-matched Raw+Perc teacher comparison in Table 1 and the CLS-Pred student comparator in Table 4. Figure 6 also adds LUGPI to the alignment comparison previously containing only the image baseline and MESSy. These substantially strengthen comparisons around the method's central mechanisms; the original KD/LUGPI accuracy comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include freezing ImageNet-100 students for CIFAR-100 linear probing, matching raw and latent teachers' Perceiver resamplers, and controlling prediction targets and teacher representations in Table 4. Existing ViT-B/16, token budgets, dropout, and clustering counts remain; newly disclosed training hyperparameters do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 tests whether gains arise from resampler architecture, predictor heads versus auxiliary-modality targets, and latent versus raw teachers. It also adds transfer evidence concerning visual discriminability, LUGPI alignment analysis, and four additional class cases. These extend the original modality ablations and synesthesia analyses substantially.

E5.justification: Both versions state three independent runs. V2 explicitly identifies table entries as means with standard deviations and plots as means, clarifying v1's unspecified ± notation. However, the new ImageNet-1K and approximate raw-teacher results omit uncertainty despite that general statement; no increased run count is established.

E6.justification: Original accuracy entries and baseline/MESSy alignment values are retained. Added outcomes include CLS-Pred's 67.04% on ImageNet-100, CIFAR-100 probe accuracies of 42.4% for LUGPI and 48.1% for MESSy, and ImageNet-1K accuracies of 64.17%, 71.32%, and 69.05% for image-only, teacher, and MESSy respectively. Raw+Perc, raw-teacher students, LUGPI alignment, and additional class results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: Both versions use undecoded audio/3D latents, Perceiver-based teacher fusion, and multilayer prediction of pooled auxiliary-modality features from student classification tokens. V2 specifies predictor architecture, filtering, and loss weights more fully, without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and expands the introduction, related work, method exposition, and experimental narrative. It introduces an explicit contribution list, separates the method into motivation and three stages, and gives setup and scalability their own subsections. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. V2 adds Figures 3–5 redisplaying existing table results, redraws alignment as three dataset panels with LUGPI, expands the class chart from six to ten examples, restructures Tables 1–2, and adds ablation and scalability tables. The original conceptual and pipeline diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: The short prior-work discussion becomes three substantive subsections. V2 discusses BYOL, data2vec, AV-data2vec, JEPA, CRD, and projector-based cross-modal distillation, explicitly identifying AV-data2vec as the closest architectural predecessor. It positions MESSy around synthetic auxiliary-modality targets while acknowledging that predictive heads follow established designs.

T1.justification: V2 retains the original data-processing inequality and adds a chain-rule derivation showing that joint modalities cannot decrease mutual information with the label (Section 3.1, Equations 2–3). This is a limited extension of the mathematical argument, without a new substantial theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's attribution gaps through Raw+Perc and CLS-Pred controls, while transfer and ImageNet-1K experiments broaden validation. Fuller implementation details and explicit acknowledgment of architectural predecessors also improve assessability. Supplementary material remains unavailable, some new results lack uncertainty, and several causal and information-theoretic interpretations overstate the evidence, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: The authors, DLA/MESSy pipeline, and matching original results establish the same research work despite retitling. All supplied pages are readable, but both PDFs end with references and omit the supplementary material cited for generation details, layer ablations, and clustering checks. Those referenced materials cannot be compared.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds controlled comparisons, CIFAR-100 transfer results, and ImageNet-1K evaluation.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original teacher and student classification experiments, modality ablations, latent-alignment measurements, class-level analyses, and generation-efficiency measurements.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly acknowledges that force- and co-contraction-driven variation at a fixed joint angle remains unmodeled. D1.justification: The supplement supplies extensive previously unavailable reproduction details: marker encoding and annotation, dataset organization, mesh specifications, trajectory refinement, network dimensions and activations, Adam training for 20 epochs with batch size 128 and learning rate 0.0001, loss weights, metric definitions, and muscle binding. The project URL and code/data availability claim are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the five-subject SKIM dataset for pose-driven skin and muscle deformation. V2 supplies demographics, acquisition routines, and more examples from that dataset; it does not establish an added dataset, population, or distinct evaluation task.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains LBS and HIT via SMPL as comparators. Tables 3–4 retain the same architecture and regularization variants. Supplementary baseline descriptions clarify these existing comparisons without adding evaluated methods.

E3.justification: Supplementary Section 5 introduces a visibility-evaluation procedure aggregating coverage across frames and subjects, separating motions, and plotting per-frame elbow-flexor visibility during curls. No protocol revision is reported for the retained benchmarks; newly supplied training settings document existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds an analysis of marker coverage and pose-dependent occlusion, including elbow-flexor visibility histograms, plus a biceps case study at minimum and maximum flexion. The original architecture and loss ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experiments. The new visibility histograms describe variation across observed frames rather than uncertainty in estimated model performance.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, including SOMA's 13.43 mm MPME. Supplementary Figure 3 adds coverage results, including 82.1% overall, 94.6% for triceps extensions, and 65.0% for push-ups. Supplementary Figures 4–5 add motion-specific and biceps deformation results.

M1.justification: The pose-driven muscle/skin decomposition, two U-Nets, canonical marker-residual supervision, regularizers, LBS, and barycentric muscle transfer remain unchanged. The supplement documents previously described components without establishing a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations through a structured supplement covering dataset construction, marker refinement, experimental setup, volume computation, visibility, qualitative examples, and muscle transfer. The main narrative remains largely intact, with limited conclusion/caption edits and an added acknowledgements section.

P2.justification: The supplement adds subject and annotation illustrations, visibility histograms, extensive deformation panels, and tables documenting demographics, meshes, motions, and dataset size. Existing main figures are retained but resized or reflowed, notably Figures 6–7; Figure 4 and ablation-table captions are refined.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including Dynamic FAUST, detailed moving-body capture, SFLsh, SoftSMPL, biharmonic weights, muscle incompressibility, and elasticity theory. These broaden supporting references without substantially changing the positioning against surface-only models, inverse anatomy methods, and simulations.

T1.justification: Supplementary Section 4 adds a focused derivation of signed prism volume using FEM shape functions, Jacobian integration, and polynomial-degree arguments establishing exact two-node Gauss–Legendre quadrature. V1 states this computation but does not contain the derivation; the existing regularizer is unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 defers essential reproduction details to a supplement absent from the supplied PDF. V2 supplies architecture, optimization, preprocessing, and volume-computation details, substantially improving reproducibility and scrutiny. Visibility evidence and the fixed-angle force limitation also improve transparency. Local documentation problems remain, including 2,310 markers versus the stated 1,000 IDs with two instances, but do not outweigh these substantial gains. The main benchmark evidence is unchanged.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds measured marker-visibility results and additional qualitative deformation examples in supplementary Sections 5–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original SKIM experiments comparing SOMA with LBS and HIT, quantitative architecture and regularization ablations, and qualitative deformation results in Section 5.

E3.justification: The new DeepLabv3+ experiment introduces a control that replaces softmax with sigmoid for one-hot outputs and applies the same projection and error score, while explicitly retaining the remaining setup. Existing splits, training budgets, attack settings and metrics are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds an ablation separating the contribution of prediction inconsistency from Hadamard encoding. Existing loss-function and classification-weight ablations, perturbation-strength analyses and ROC comparisons remain.

E6.justification: v2 Table 3 adds 76.9 ± 0.3% global AuROC for one-hot+(17). Its entropy and Hadamard comparison values, 72.5 ± 0.1% and 80.4 ± 1.1%, already appear in v1 Table 2. Existing benchmark and appendix results are retained.

M1.justification: HadamardNet, simplex decoding and the three anomaly scores remain unchanged. v1 Section 5 and Supplement J already select the MSE-only encoded-space loss; v2 foregrounds this choice in Section 3.4 and relocates the general loss formulation to Supplement H. The new one-hot variant serves as an experimental control.

P1.justification: Section 3.4 is shortened to emphasize the selected training objective, with the general loss discussion moved to a new Supplement H. v2 adds the control-experiment discussion and makes limited cross-reference and bibliography edits; the broader narrative remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the compact comparison Table 3 and moves the training schematic from main-text Figure 2 to supplementary Figure 6. Existing displays are retained with modest sizing, spacing, placement and numbering adjustments.

R1.justification: The cited research and substantive positioning remain unchanged. v2 removes a duplicate SegFormer reference while retaining the same work, renumbers subsequent citations and edits bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The probabilistic formulation, error-minimization equivalence proof and simplex-projection derivation remain unchanged, including Supplements A–E. Relocated loss equations and the explicit statement of the previously selected loss do not introduce new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: The new Table 3 provides a more informative control for attributing detection gains to Hadamard encoding, strengthening the evidence in the tested Cityscapes/DeepLabv3+ setting. Clearer presentation of the selected loss and the code-access pointer also help. These are limited improvements; the broader methods, experimental findings and limitations remain unchanged.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds a Cityscapes comparison of inconsistency-based detection with one-hot and Hadamard outputs.
